lessons.plain: AI is the broad goal of getting computers to do things that normally take human judgment, like recognizing a face or understanding a sentence. Machine learning is one way to get there: instead of writing every rule by hand, you show the computer many examples and it finds the pattern itself. Deep learning is a style of machine learning that uses neural networks, which are layered networks of simple numeric units loosely inspired by brain cells. Computer vision is AI that works on images and video, and natural language processing, or NLP, is AI that works on human language. Knowing these six words, and which one sits inside which, lets you tell what a team is actually proposing.
lessons.guessPrompt: A colleague says we should use AI to flag damaged parcels in warehouse photos, and another says we should just write a rule that flags any photo where the box corner is dark. Which of these two is machine learning, and what makes you think so?
lessons.teach:
Start with the nesting. Artificial intelligence (AI) is the broad field of making computers perform tasks that usually need human judgment. Machine learning (ML) is a part of AI in which a program learns its behavior from data instead of following rules a person wrote. You give it examples with known answers, it adjusts its internal settings to fit them, and then it applies what it found to new inputs. Deep learning is machine learning built on neural networks, which are stacks of layers of simple numeric units; each unit multiplies its inputs by adjustable numbers called weights, adds them up, and passes the result on. Stacking many layers lets the network learn increasingly abstract features, such as edges, then shapes, then whole objects in an image.

Computer vision is the area of AI that interprets images and video. Natural language processing is the area that works with human language in text or speech. Both can be built with classic machine learning or with deep learning.

Worked example: a warehouse wants to tell whether a photo shows a damaged or intact parcel. Step 1: collect photos and have people tag each one as damaged or intact, which is the labelling step. Step 2: feed the labelled photos to a neural network built for images. Step 3: the network adjusts its weights until its guesses match most of the tags. Step 4: a new photo arrives, the network produces a score, and the system reports damaged or intact. Nobody wrote a rule about dents.

Common mistake: calling any automated logic AI. A fixed if-then rule, such as flagging any photo with a dark corner, is ordinary code. It does not learn from data, so it is not machine learning, and it will not improve as the data changes.

Consequence in a running system: a deep learning model that scores well in testing can still fail on photos unlike its training set, such as new lighting or packaging. A live system therefore needs its outputs monitored over time, not just a one-time check before launch.

Deep learning is a tool inside machine learning, and machine learning is a tool inside AI; choosing the innermost tool that meets the need is the sound default.

questions.prompt: A streaming company wants to tag short audio clips as containing a siren or not. Step 1: a person listens to a set of past clips and labels each one as siren or no siren. Step 2: a neural network built for audio is trained on those labelled clips. Step 3: [missing]. Step 4: a new clip arrives and the system reports siren or no siren. Which sentence correctly fills the missing Step 3?
choices: The network adjusts its weights until its outputs match most of the labels.
The labels are deleted so the network cannot memorise the clips.
The engineer writes a rule that flags any clip louder than 80 decibels.
The network is deployed once and never checked again.
questions.why: During training, the network adjusts its adjustable numbers (weights) until its guesses agree with most of the human labels, which is the learning step that the other choices either replace with a fixed rule or skip entirely.

questions.prompt: Which statement best separates machine learning from ordinary code?
choices: Machine learning learns its behavior from example inputs with known answers, while ordinary code follows rules a person wrote.
Machine learning and ordinary code are the same thing, but machine learning is written in a different language.
Machine learning is only used for text, while ordinary code is only used for images.
Machine learning always needs a larger computer than ordinary code, and that is what makes it different.
questions.why: Machine learning adjusts its internal settings to fit examples with known answers, whereas ordinary code does exactly what its author's written rules say.

questions.prompt: A finance team has a rule that says: reject any invoice over 10,000 dollars. Nothing is learned from past invoices. Which description is accurate?
choices: It is deep learning, because it has a threshold.
It is a neural network with one layer.
It is ordinary rule-based logic, not machine learning, because the threshold is fixed and does not change from data.
It is machine learning, because the number 10,000 was chosen from data.
questions.why: A fixed if-then rule that a person wrote and that does not adjust from data is ordinary code, so it is not machine learning or deep learning.

questions.prompt: A computer vision model that sorts photos of produce scored very well on its test set when it was launched. Three months later, accuracy has dropped on photos taken under new store lighting. What does the teaching text say a live system needs in response?
choices: No further action, since a model that scored well once will keep scoring well on any photos.
A one-time retest on the original test set, which will show whether the model is still correct.
Monitoring of its outputs over time, because a strong test score at launch does not guarantee it will keep working on new kinds of input.
Removal of all neural network layers so the model becomes a simple rule, which never degrades.
questions.why: The teaching text says a model can score well in testing yet fail on inputs unlike its training data, so live outputs must be monitored over time.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate, in your own words, how AI, machine learning, deep learning, and computer vision relate to one another, and name one limit of deep learning that the team should weigh before adopting it.
lessons.modelAnswer: AI is the umbrella: any technique that makes a computer do something that normally needs human judgment. Machine learning sits inside it and means the program learns its behavior from labelled examples rather than from hand-written rules. Deep learning sits inside machine learning and uses neural networks with many layers, which can learn complicated patterns in images, audio and text. Computer vision and NLP are application areas rather than extra layers: computer vision works on images and video, NLP works on language, and each can be built with classic ML or deep learning. The main limit of deep learning is that it usually needs a lot of labelled data and computing power, and it is hard to explain why it made a particular decision. So before adopting it, a team should first check whether a simpler rule or a classic model already meets the need.
rubricPoints: AI is the broad umbrella term for machines doing tasks that normally need human judgment
Machine learning is a subset of AI that learns from data rather than fixed rules
Deep learning is a subset of machine learning that uses multi-layer neural networks
Computer vision and NLP are application areas, and either can use classic ML or deep learning
Deep learning needs lots of labelled data and compute and is hard to explain, so simpler options should be considered first

suggested.rationale: The core skill here is being able to explain how these terms nest and where each one stops, which a learner demonstrates best by explaining it back.

lessons.plain: When people say 'the AI learned something,' four separate things are hiding in that phrase. The algorithm is the method for learning, like a recipe. Training is the cooking: running that method over past examples. The model is what comes out, a saved result that holds what was learned. Inference is using that saved result on a new case to get an answer. Keeping these apart matters because each one happens at a different time, costs a different amount, and is changed by different people.
lessons.guessPrompt: When a fraud tool flags a card payment as suspicious, which of these is running at that moment: the learning method, the process of learning from past payments, the saved result of that learning, or the saved result being applied to this one payment?
lessons.teach:
An algorithm is a fixed procedure for learning patterns from data, such as linear regression, which finds the best straight line through past examples, or a decision tree, which asks a chain of yes-or-no questions. It is the recipe, and on its own it contains no knowledge about your data. Training is the act of running an algorithm over a set of historical examples so it can adjust its internal numbers, called parameters or weights, until they fit those examples. The output of training is a model: the learned artifact, meaning the algorithm's structure together with the fitted numbers, saved so it can be reused. Inferencing, also called inference, is using a finished model on new input it has never seen, to produce an output such as a prediction or a score.

Worked example: linear regression is given 1,000 past home sales. Training adjusts two numbers so that price is roughly 120 times square feet plus 15,000. Step one is training. Step two is saving the pair of numbers with the formula; that saved bundle is the model. Step three is inference: a buyer enters 1,500 square feet, the saved model computes 120 times 1,500 plus 15,000, and it returns about 195,000. The algorithm was never run again during that request.

Common mistake: calling the algorithm 'the model', or treating retraining as if it were inference. Retraining runs training again on fresh data and produces a new model version. Inference happens on every request after that.

Consequence in a running system: you can replace a model with a newer version without changing the algorithm, and inference is the part that runs continuously, so its latency and per-request cost are what users and budgets actually feel.

The four are distinct: the algorithm is the method, training builds the model, the model is the saved result, and inference uses that result.

questions.prompt: A regional bike-rental company wants to estimate how many bikes will be rented in each hour. Step one: the team chooses a decision tree, which is a chain of yes-or-no questions about the input, as the algorithm. Step two: they run training on three years of hourly rental records, which sets the split points the tree uses. Step three: they save the trained tree as a model file. Step four is missing from the plan. Which choice correctly fills it?
choices: Delete the training records so the model cannot leak information about past customers.
Retrain the tree on the same records to confirm the split points have not changed.
Feed the saved model the conditions for a new hour, such as weather and day of week, and let it return an estimated rental count.
Rewrite the decision tree algorithm so that it contains the historical rental numbers directly.
questions.why: Step four is inference: using the finished saved model on new input it has never seen to produce an estimate, and the algorithm and training are not run again for that request.

questions.prompt: A card-fraud service loads a saved file that holds a tree's structure and learned thresholds, then scores each card transaction in under 50 milliseconds. Which term names what the service is doing on each transaction?
choices: Training, because the service adjusts the tree's thresholds for every transaction it sees.
Retraining, because the saved file is being refreshed with each new transaction.
Inference, because the finished model is applied to new input to produce a score.
The algorithm, because the decision tree procedure is being executed on each transaction.
questions.why: Applying a finished model to new input to produce an output is inference, while training changes the numbers and the algorithm is only the procedure, not the thing running per request.

questions.prompt: A weather-app team says they already have a model because they have chosen a linear regression algorithm and written the code for it, but they have never run it on historical data. What is the most accurate description of their current state?
choices: They have an inference service, since the code is ready to answer requests.
They have an algorithm but no model yet, because no training has produced fitted numbers to save.
They have a trained model whose parameters are set to zero until deployment.
They have a model, since the algorithm and code together are the learned artifact.
questions.why: The algorithm is only a fixed procedure with no knowledge of the data, and a model exists only after training has fitted its numbers and the result is saved.

questions.prompt: A subscription company retrains its customer-churn model at the start of each month on the latest customer records, producing a new numbered version. Each time a customer account is checked, the current version returns a churn risk score. Which statement is correct?
choices: Both the monthly run and each account check are inference, since both use the model.
The monthly retraining run is training and each account check is inference, and the algorithm is not what changes each month.
The monthly retraining run is inference, because it uses the newest customer records.
Each account check is training, because the model's view of that customer is being updated.
questions.why: Retraining runs the training process again on fresh data to produce a new model version, while each request to score a customer uses that finished model and so is inference.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate, in your own words, how the algorithm, training, the model, and inferencing differ, and name one limit or tradeoff that comes from keeping them separate in production.
lessons.modelAnswer: Think of it as four separate parts. The algorithm is the learning method, such as a decision tree; it is a procedure and holds no knowledge yet. Training runs that procedure over historical data and produces the model, which is the saved result containing the fitted numbers. Inference is calling that saved model with new input to get a prediction. The tradeoff to name is cost and timing: training is heavy and occasional, while inference runs on every request and has to meet latency targets. A limit is that a model is only as current as its training data, so it needs retraining and monitoring as the world changes. A newly retrained model is not automatically better, so it should be checked before it replaces the old one.
rubricPoints: The algorithm is the learning method and contains no learned knowledge by itself.
Training runs the algorithm on historical data to fit parameters.
The model is the saved, reusable result of training.
Inference applies the saved model to new input, and it runs on every request.

suggested.rationale: Being able to explain these four distinct parts back to a teammate, including their tradeoffs, is the core skill here, and no listed mission or planned engine covers it directly.

lessons.plain: A model can look accurate overall and still treat people unfairly or fail where it is actually used. Bias here means a systematic tilt in results, such as a model that errs more often for one group of customers. Fairness is a measurable standard for comparing outcomes across groups, not a feeling. Fit asks whether the model suits the real situation, meaning the data it learned from still resembles the data it sees today. All three can be checked with numbers by comparing results across groups and over time.
lessons.guessPrompt: A resume-screening model has 92 percent overall accuracy. Why might that single number still hide a fairness problem?
lessons.teach:
Bias, in this context, is a systematic skew in a model's results, usually traced to its training data, its labels, or how the problem was framed. Fairness is a measurable standard: you choose a split such as region or customer segment, then compare outcomes or error rates across the groups. Fit asks whether the model matches the situation it runs in, meaning the training data resembles the data arriving now. Each of these can be checked with numbers rather than intuition.

Why it works: an overall score is an average, so a small group with many mistakes barely moves it. Worked example: a screening model reviews 1,000 applicants, 800 from group A and 200 from group B. It is right for 90 percent of group A (720 correct, 80 wrong) and 60 percent of group B (120 correct, 80 wrong). The overall score is 840 out of 1,000, or 84 percent, which looks respectable. Splitting the results shows that group B is wrong four times as often as group A, a gap the total hides.

Common mistake: reporting one aggregate accuracy and calling the model fair, or picking a fairness measure only after seeing which one looks good.

Consequence in a running system: the applicant mix shifts over time, so the gap can widen without any code change. Per-group metrics must be tracked after deployment, not only before launch. Bias, fairness and fit are properties you measure per group and over time.

questions.prompt: A grocery chain uses a model to predict delivery times. In a test month it handled 500 orders: 400 from Zone North and 100 from Zone South. The model was off by more than the allowed margin on 40 of the North orders and 30 of the South orders. Step 1: North error rate is 40 out of 400, which is 10 percent. Step 2: South error rate is 30 out of 100, which is 30 percent. Step 3 is missing. Which statement completes the check?
choices: North's error rate is 20 points higher than South's, so North needs more work.
Average the two error rates to get 20 percent, which is the fair figure to report.
Overall accuracy is 86 percent, so the model treats both zones fairly.
South's error rate is three times North's, a gap that the overall 86 percent accuracy hides.
questions.why: Comparing the per-group error rates shows South is wrong three times as often as North, and the aggregate accuracy conceals that difference.

questions.prompt: In plain terms, what does the fit of a model measure?
choices: Whether the model's training data resembles the data it is seeing now in production.
How many features the model uses to make each prediction.
The share of predictions that a human reviewer later agrees with.
How quickly the model returns an answer under heavy request load.
questions.why: Fit asks whether the situation the model runs in matches its training data, which the teaching text defines directly.

questions.prompt: A fraud-detection model on a payments platform reports 92 percent accuracy across 2,000 transactions. A team lead says the model is fair because the number is high. Which response best describes the failure in that reasoning?
choices: The team should have reported precision instead of accuracy, since accuracy is never useful.
A single aggregate score can hide a small group with many errors, so results must be split by group before calling it fair.
The 2,000 transactions are too few to measure anything, so the model cannot be evaluated at all.
Fairness only applies to hiring and lending, so a payments model is outside the concept.
questions.why: An average is dominated by the large group, so a small group with many mistakes can be invisible in the single figure; fairness requires per-group comparison.

questions.prompt: A support-ticket classifier was checked before launch and showed similar error rates for all customer segments. Six months later, a growing share of tickets come from a segment that wrote few tickets during training. No code has changed. What is the most accurate description of what happened?
choices: The classifier automatically retrained itself on the new tickets, so its errors must have dropped.
The pre-launch check was invalid because fairness can only be measured on live traffic.
The applicant mix shifted, so the error gap can widen even without code changes, and per-group metrics must be tracked after deployment.
The model's fairness was fixed permanently at launch and cannot change afterward.
questions.why: The teaching text notes that shifting input mix can widen per-group gaps with no code change, so bias and fit must be measured per group and over time.

lessons.explainPrompt: A teammate says our model is 95 percent accurate, so it is fair to all customers. Explain to them, in your own words, what that claim leaves out, and name one limit of the fairness check you would run instead.
lessons.modelAnswer: Overall accuracy is an average across everyone, so it can hide a group where the model performs much worse. I would split the results by the groups that matter, such as region or customer type, and compare the error rate and the rate of positive decisions for each one. Those per-group numbers show whether one group is treated differently. The limit is that fairness has more than one definition, so the team has to agree which one applies before looking at the numbers. Also, if the groups are small or the labels are missing, the figures are noisy and can mislead. A model can pass on today's data and drift later as the customer mix changes, so the same comparison has to run again after launch. So 95 percent is a starting point, not proof of fairness.
rubricPoints: An overall accuracy figure averages over groups and can hide a weak group.
Fairness is checked by comparing error rates and decision rates across defined groups.
Fit means the training data must still resemble the data the model sees in use.
Fairness has more than one definition, and the chosen one must be agreed in advance.
Results must be re-measured after launch because the data can drift over time.

suggested.rationale: The core skill is reasoning about what a metric hides and explaining it to a teammate, which no listed mission or planned engine practises directly.

lessons.plain: Some computer programs can write an email, summarise a long report, or answer a question in ordinary sentences. The engine behind many of these is a large language model, a program trained on vast amounts of text to predict which words should come next. That simple habit produces surprisingly useful language skills. Generative AI is the wider family of systems that create new content such as text, images, or code, rather than only sorting or scoring existing things. Agentic AI goes a step further: the system plans several steps, uses tools such as search or a ticketing system, checks the results, and keeps working toward a goal.
lessons.guessPrompt: If a chatbot answers a question about yesterday's news fluently and confidently, what would you check before trusting it, and why might it sound sure even when it is wrong?
lessons.teach: Definitions first. A large language model (LLM) is a neural network, a kind of model built from many numerical weights that are adjusted during training, trained on very large amounts of text. Its training task is to predict the next token, a small piece of text such as a word or part of a word. Repeated over enormous data, this gives it grammar, broad knowledge from its training data, and a sense of style. Generative AI is the category of systems that produce new content such as text, images, audio, or code. An LLM is one important kind of generative AI. Agentic AI describes a system built around a model that works in a loop: it reads a goal, chooses a next action, calls a tool such as a search API or a database query, observes the result, and repeats until the goal is met or it stops. Why it works: the model generates one token at a time, each conditioned on everything before it, so a long answer is a chain of likely continuations. It does not look facts up unless a tool or a document supplied in the prompt provides them. Worked example: a customer asks where their parcel is. A generative system drafts a reply from tracking text pasted into the prompt, and takes no action. An agentic system does more. Step 1: it reads the question. Step 2: it calls a tracking tool with the order number. Step 3: the tool returns held at depot. Step 4: it drafts an apology and proposes a refund for a person to approve. Step 5: it stops and reports what it did. Each step is a model decision followed by a real tool call. Common mistake: treating a fluent answer as a verified one. An LLM can state a wrong fact confidently; this is called hallucination. Consequence in a running system: if an agent has permission to change orders and acts on a hallucinated status, it writes wrong data to production. Limit tool permissions, require approval for writes, and log every step. An agent is a loop wrapped around a model, not a smarter model.

questions.prompt: Harbor Pantry runs an agent that restocks its shops. Step 1: the agent reads a message that oat milk at the Riverside shop is low. Step 2: it calls the stock-count tool with item code 4471 and gets back 6 units on hand. Step 3: it compares 6 against the reorder threshold of 20 and decides to reorder. Step 4 is missing from this description. Step 5: it stops and reports what it did. Which choice correctly fills in Step 4?
choices: It drafts a 40-unit purchase order and routes it to a manager for approval.
It answers the original message from memory and makes no further tool call.
It replaces the count of 6 with the threshold of 20 so the stock record looks complete.
It submits the purchase order to the supplier directly because the count came from a tool.
questions.why: A write action such as placing an order should go through an approval step, so the agent drafts the order and a person approves it before anything is sent, while the other choices skip the approval, falsify data, or drop the tool use the loop depends on.

questions.prompt: Which description best matches agentic AI as defined in this course?
choices: A model in a loop that picks actions, calls tools, and repeats until the goal is met or it stops.
A database that stores past answers so the system can repeat them without a model.
A model that generates images from text prompts and has no ability to call tools.
A neural network with many adjustable weights, trained to predict the next token in text.
questions.why: Agentic AI is defined as a loop wrapped around a model that chooses actions, calls tools, observes results, and repeats, whereas the other options describe image generation, storage, or the basic next-token training of an LLM.

questions.prompt: A county library's assistant reads a catalogue record that staff pasted into the prompt and drafts a reply to a patron. It does not look anything up or change any record. Which category does this belong to?
choices: Generative AI but not agentic, since it calls no tool.
Agentic AI, because the model reads a goal and writes a reply.
Hallucination, because the reply sounds fluent.
A managed database, because the catalogue record is stored.
questions.why: The system produces new text, which makes it generative AI, but because it takes no action through a tool it is not agentic, and fluency alone does not make it hallucination or a storage system.

questions.prompt: A utility's assistant states a meter reading of 4,210 kWh from memory, with no tool call, and the reading is wrong. What is this failure called and what is the most direct control?
choices: Tokenisation; cap the tokens in each reply.
Agency loop; remove the goal from the prompt.
Weight drift; retrain the model every week.
Hallucination; require the reading to come from a meter-data tool call.
questions.why: A confident but unsupported fact is hallucination, and the direct control is to make the model obtain facts from a tool or supplied document rather than from memory, which the other options do not address.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate who has heard these terms in meetings but never seen them defined the difference between a large language model, generative AI, and agentic AI. Then name one limit or tradeoff that matters when you put an agent in front of a live system.
lessons.modelAnswer: A large language model is a model trained on huge amounts of text to predict the next small piece of text, which lets it write and reason in language. Generative AI is the broader group of systems that create new content such as text, images, or code, and an LLM is one of the main ways to do that. Agentic AI means a model wrapped in a loop: it picks a next step toward a goal, calls a tool like a search or an order system, reads the result, and continues until it finishes or stops. The main limit is reliability. An LLM can produce confident wrong answers, so its output is a claim to check, not a fact. When an agent can change real data, a wrong plan becomes a wrong write. So I would give it read-only access first, require human approval for changes, and log each tool call so we can see what it did.
rubricPoints: Defines an LLM as a model trained on large text data to predict the next token
Explains generative AI as the broader category that creates new content, with LLMs as one example
Describes agentic AI as a model in a loop that calls tools toward a goal
Names a real limit such as hallucination or the risk of acting on wrong output, with a practical safeguard

suggested.rationale: The core skill is explaining these three terms and their limits in your own words, which the explain format trains directly.

lessons.plain: AI is the broad goal of getting computers to do things that seem to need human judgment, such as recognising a face or answering a question. Machine learning is one way to do that: instead of writing every rule yourself, you show the computer many examples and it finds the patterns. Deep learning is a kind of machine learning that uses large layered networks of simple math units, which works well on messy data like photos and speech. Generative AI uses these models to produce new content such as text or images. Agentic AI goes a step further by letting a model plan steps and take actions through tools. Each layer is a narrower part of the one before it, and each has limits you should know before you choose it.
lessons.guessPrompt: A bank wants software that flags card transactions likely to be fraud, learning from past transactions. Is a system that writes a fluent paragraph of text the same kind of thing as that fraud flagger? Explain your reasoning in a few sentences.
lessons.teach:
Definitions first. Artificial intelligence (AI) is any technique that makes a computer perform a task that normally needs human judgment. Machine learning (ML) is a subset of AI in which the program's behaviour is learned from data rather than written as explicit rules. Deep learning is a subset of ML that trains neural networks, which are layered stacks of simple numeric units with adjustable weights. Generative AI is a subset of deep learning, usually built on large language models (LLMs, models trained on huge amounts of text), that produces new content such as text, images or code. Agentic AI is a system in which a model decides on a sequence of steps and calls tools to act toward a goal, rather than only producing one output.

Why the nesting matters: each inner circle is a more specialised technique. A problem that needs only a rule or a simple statistical model does not need deep learning, and a model that generates text does not automatically act in the world.

Worked example: a parcel sorter must decide whether a label is readable. Step 1, a fixed rule (if the barcode scans, pass it) is automated but learns nothing, so it is not machine learning. Step 2, a classifier trained on thousands of labelled label photos is machine learning. Step 3, if it uses a deep neural network to read messy handwriting, it is deep learning. Step 4, if it also drafts a reply to the customer, it is generative AI. Step 5, if it reorders the warehouse queue and books a redelivery on its own, it is agentic AI.

Common mistake: treating 'AI' as a synonym for the newest, largest model. Often a rule or a simple model is cheaper, more predictable and easier to explain.

Consequence: an agentic system that takes actions without limits can repeat a costly action many times. Where the system stops suggesting and starts doing is a design decision you must make on purpose.

So the layers are a map of what each technique can do, and a signal for when to choose a simpler one.

questions.prompt: A hotel group wants to schedule room cleaning. Work through the layers with its system. Step 1: when a guest checks out, a fixed rule marks the room as needing cleaning. This is automated but learns nothing from data, so it is not machine learning. Step 2: a model trained on two years of occupancy records predicts which rooms will be empty tomorrow. This is machine learning. Step 3: ____ (the missing step) The model also reads noisy corridor camera images with a multi-layer neural network to estimate foot traffic. Step 4: the system writes a friendly shift summary for the housekeeping staff in full sentences. This is generative AI. Step 5: the system assigns cleaners to rooms and orders extra linen without a person approving it. This is agentic AI. Which label fits Step 3?
choices: It is generative AI, because it classifies images.
It is still just machine learning, because any trained model is machine learning with no neural layers.
It is deep learning, because the image model is a layered neural network with adjustable weights.
It is agentic AI, because it reads the scene and then acts on it.
questions.why: Deep learning is the subset of machine learning that trains layered neural networks with adjustable weights, which is exactly what the corridor image model uses.

questions.prompt: A small accounting firm flags any invoice above 10,000 pounds for manager approval using a threshold written into its software. Which description fits this best?
choices: Agentic AI, because it acts on invoices without a person.
Deep learning, because it runs automatically on every invoice.
Rule-based automation, not machine learning, because the threshold is written in explicitly and nothing is learned from data.
Generative AI, because it decides which invoices to approve.
questions.why: A fixed, explicitly written rule is automation without learning, so it sits outside machine learning and the deeper layers.

questions.prompt: A dental practice wants to send patients a reminder text before each appointment. A consultant suggests a deep learning model trained on patient histories to pick the best reminder time. What is the most honest recommendation for this business problem?
choices: Use a generative model to write a different reminder message for every patient.
Send a fixed reminder 24 hours before each appointment, because the rule is predictable, cheap and easy to explain, and nothing needs learning.
Train a deep network on patient histories to choose a personal reminder time for each patient.
Use an agent that books and rebooks appointments on its own to reduce no-shows.
questions.why: Where a simple rule meets the need predictably and cheaply, the nesting map signals that a rule beats a prediction and deep learning is unnecessary.

questions.prompt: A support assistant drafts replies for customers and can also call a refund tool in a loop until a ticket is closed, with no cap on refunds per ticket. What makes this system agentic, and what is the main risk?
choices: It is agentic only because it writes text, so the risk is poor grammar in replies.
It is agentic because it chooses its own sequence of steps and calls tools toward a goal; the risk is that an action such as a refund can repeat many times and become costly unless limits are set.
It is agentic because it is built on a large model, so the risk is that the model becomes too large to run.
It is not agentic because a refund tool is a rule, so there is no risk.
questions.why: The system decides a sequence of steps and calls tools to act, and without limits a costly action can be repeated many times, which is the consequence the teaching text warns about.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how AI, machine learning, deep learning, generative AI and agentic AI relate to each other, and name one place where the more advanced layer is the wrong choice.
lessons.modelAnswer: Think of them as nested circles. AI is the widest: any technique that makes a machine do something that needs judgment. Machine learning sits inside it and learns patterns from examples rather than having rules written out. Deep learning sits inside machine learning and uses many-layered neural networks, which suit images, audio and free text. Generative AI sits inside deep learning and produces new content, usually from large language models. Agentic AI is not a deeper layer of the same kind; it wraps a model in a loop where it plans steps and calls tools to reach a goal. The limit I would raise: a deep or generative model is the wrong choice when the output must be exact and auditable, such as a fixed eligibility rule or a tax calculation. A plain rule or a simple trained model is cheaper, more predictable and easier to explain there. The same caution applies to agents, which need a clear boundary on what they may do without a human approving it.
rubricPoints: AI is the outermost category, and machine learning, deep learning and generative AI each sit inside the one before.
Agentic AI is a system pattern built around a model, not simply a bigger model.
Deep learning suits messy unstructured data but needs more data, compute and explanation effort.
Names a concrete case where a rule or simple model beats the advanced layer.
Notes that autonomous action needs explicit limits and human approval points.

suggested.rationale: The core skill is explaining how the layers relate and where each one stops, which is best checked by explaining it back, and no listed mission or planned engine covers this.

lessons.plain: Inferencing is when a trained model is actually used to produce an answer for new input, such as scoring a payment or summarizing a document. Training is the earlier step where the model learns from data. Inference modes describe how requests reach the model and when answers come back. There are four common patterns. Batch processes many inputs together on a schedule. Real-time gives one request an immediate answer. Asynchronous accepts a request into a queue and delivers the answer later. Serverless provides capacity on demand, so you pay per use and do not keep servers running while idle. Choosing among them mostly depends on how quickly the answer is needed, how much data arrives at once, and how much idle capacity you are willing to pay for.
lessons.guessPrompt: A retailer wants a fraud score on every card payment as it happens, and also wants risk scores for all of last month's customers every night. Without any prior study, which inference mode would you guess fits each job, and why?
lessons.teach:
Inferencing means running a trained model on new input to get a prediction. The place where a model is hosted and receives requests is often called an endpoint. Latency is the time between sending a request and getting the answer. Throughput is how much work the system completes over a period. Idle capacity is computing resources you pay for while they do nothing.

Batch inference collects many inputs and processes them together, usually on a schedule. It suits work where nobody waits on a single answer. Real-time inference answers each request immediately, which suits a user waiting at a screen. Asynchronous inference accepts a request, queues it, and returns the result later, which suits large or slow inputs such as long documents. Serverless inference scales capacity from zero up to demand and bills per request, which suits spiky or low traffic, though the first request after an idle period can be slower.

Worked example: a bank scores 2 million transactions each night for a risk report. Step 1: the transactions are written to a file at the end of the day. Step 2: a scheduled job loads the file and runs the model on every row. Step 3: the scores are written out before 6 am, when analysts arrive. Nobody waits on any single score, so batch fits. Now a card terminal needs approval within a second. That is real-time, because one request must get one fast answer.

Common mistake: choosing real-time for work that could wait. An always-on real-time endpoint costs money every hour, even at 3 am when nothing is being sent to it.

Consequence in a running system: a batch job that overruns its window delays every downstream report, so batch sizing must be planned against the deadline.

questions.prompt: A public library wants to find patrons who are likely to lose a borrowing card. On Friday evening, 90,000 patron records are exported to a file. Step 1 is that export. Step 2 is missing. Step 3 is that reminder letters are printed and mailed on Monday at 8 am, before the branches open. Which choice correctly fills the missing Step 2?
choices: The model is kept running on a dedicated server all weekend so that it can answer requests on demand.
Each patron's phone is called the moment their record is entered into the library system.
Each patron is asked to wait on the library website while their own risk score is calculated.
A scheduled job loads the Friday export and runs the model on every record, writing one score per patron before Monday.
questions.why: Because nobody waits on any single score and the scores are needed by Monday morning, the missing step is a scheduled job that processes all records together, which is the batch pattern.

questions.prompt: Which description best defines asynchronous inference?
choices: The model answers each request the instant it arrives, so the caller always waits on the connection.
The system gathers many inputs into one group and processes the whole group on a fixed timetable.
The system scales its capacity down to zero and bills only for each request that arrives.
The system accepts a request, places it in a queue, and returns the result later, which suits large or slow inputs.
questions.why: Asynchronous inference is defined by accepting a request, queuing it, and returning the result later, which is what the second choice describes.

questions.prompt: A law firm lets staff upload scanned contracts of around 300 pages each. Staff do not need the summary on screen; they can come back to it within an hour. Which inference type fits best, and why?
choices: Batch, because the firm must process all contracts in one nightly run.
Serverless, because the firm only pays for the uploads it makes.
Asynchronous, because the inputs are large and the caller can accept the result later.
Real-time, because every upload must be answered within a second.
questions.why: Large, slow inputs where the caller can collect the result later match asynchronous inference, so the fourth choice is the best fit.

questions.prompt: A small company runs a real-time endpoint 24 hours a day for an internal tool that staff use only from 9 am to 5 pm on weekdays, about 20 people in total. What is the main problem with this setup?
choices: It pays for idle capacity overnight and at weekends, when no requests are arriving.
It cannot be used for batch work at any time of the day.
Its latency is too low, so answers come back before staff are ready to read them.
It scales up to demand, so it will run out of capacity during the working day.
questions.why: An always-on real-time endpoint bills for every hour it runs, so paying for hours with no traffic is the core waste, which the first choice names.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would choose between batch, real-time, asynchronous, and serverless inference for a new feature. Name one limit or tradeoff of the option you would be most tempted to pick by default.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would start with two questions: how soon does someone need the answer, and how much data arrives at once. If a person is waiting on a single result, like an approval at checkout, I need real-time, and I accept that the endpoint has to stay running, so I pay for idle time. If the input is large but the caller can wait minutes, asynchronous fits, because requests queue and results come back later. If work runs on a schedule over a big dataset, batch is cheaper and simpler. Serverless suits low or unpredictable traffic, because it scales to zero and bills per request. The tradeoff I would watch for is serverless cold starts. The first request after a quiet period can be slow, so it is a poor choice for a strict latency target. My default instinct toward real-time is the thing to check, because it is often more capacity than the feature needs.
rubricPoints: Distinguishes batch, real-time, asynchronous, and serverless by when the answer is needed and how requests arrive
Explains that real-time endpoints incur cost while idle
Names the cold-start delay as the main tradeoff of serverless inference
Recommends matching the mode to latency needs rather than defaulting to real-time

suggested.rationale: Choosing an inference mode from a scenario with latency and volume constraints is best practised by reasoning through exam-style situations.

lessons.plain: AI models learn from data, and that data comes in different shapes. Some examples come with the correct answer attached, like a photo tagged cat, and some do not. Some data sits neatly in rows and columns, like a spreadsheet, while other data is free-form, like emails, audio, or pictures. Some data is ordered by time, like sensor readings taken every minute. Knowing which shape your data has tells you what kind of model can learn from it and what preparation it needs before anyone trusts the result.
lessons.guessPrompt: A company has ten years of customer purchase records in a spreadsheet, with a column showing whether each customer later cancelled. It also has a folder of raw customer support emails with no tags. Which dataset is labeled and which is unstructured, and why might that difference change how you would use each one?
lessons.teach:
A label is the known correct answer attached to an example. Labeled data pairs each input with that answer, and unlabeled data has inputs only. Structured data has fixed fields in a predefined layout, such as rows and columns with named types. Unstructured data has no predefined fields, such as free text, images, audio, or video. Tabular data is structured data arranged as a table, where each row is one record and each column is one feature. Time-series data is a sequence of values indexed by time, where the order of the values carries meaning. Image data is a grid of pixel values, and text data is a sequence of words or characters.

Why this matters: a model learns a mapping from inputs to outputs. Labels supply the target to learn against, so labeled data is what makes supervised learning possible. Structured data is easy to query and compare, while unstructured data usually needs a preprocessing step to turn it into numbers before a model can use it.

Worked example: a delivery company has a table of trips with distance, departure hour, weather, and a column marked late or on time. Step 1: each row is one trip, so this is tabular, structured data. Step 2: the late column is the label, so the data is labeled. Step 3: GPS pings every 30 seconds form a time-series, and the order of those pings must be preserved. Step 4: driver notes written in free text are unstructured text, and they stay unlabeled unless someone tags them.

Common mistake: randomly shuffling time-series rows into training and test sets. The model then sees future readings while learning to predict the past, so test scores look better than production results. In a running system this shows up as a forecast that looks accurate in review and then misses badly once live data arrives.

The data shape decides the technique and the preparation, so identify it before you choose a model.

questions.prompt: A greenhouse operator keeps three datasets. The first is a log of soil moisture readings taken every 10 minutes for one bed, in the order they were recorded. The second is a spreadsheet with one row per crop batch, showing seed variety, water used, and yield in kg, plus a column marked grade A or grade B. The third is a folder of photos of tomato leaves, with no tag or note attached to any photo. Step 1: the soil moisture log is time-series data, because the order of the readings carries meaning. Step 2: the batch spreadsheet is tabular, structured data, because each row is one batch and each column is one feature, and the grade column is the label, so it is labeled. Step 3: [missing; work this out yourself]. Step 4: the leaf photos are the only remaining dataset, so the operator must decide how to store and prepare them before a model can use them.
choices: Structured and labeled, because each photo sits in a fixed folder with a file name
Unstructured image data that is unlabeled, because the photos carry no tag giving a known correct answer
Tabular, because each photo can be treated as one row in a photo log with one column per pixel
Time-series, because the photos were taken on different days and so are ordered by time
questions.why: The leaf photos are image data, which is unstructured because they have no predefined fields, and they are unlabeled because nothing attaches a known correct answer to them.

questions.prompt: A support team has 5,000 customer emails stored as plain text. Nobody has assigned each email a category. How should the data be described?
choices: Structured tabular data with labels
Image data with labels
Unstructured text data with no labels
Time-series data with labels
questions.why: Free-text emails have no predefined fields, so they are unstructured text, and with no assigned category they carry no label.

questions.prompt: A bank has three years of daily account balances for each customer, stored in date order. It wants a model that forecasts next month's balance. Which handling is correct?
choices: Shuffle all rows randomly, then split them 80/20 into training and test sets, since every row has the same shape
Treat each customer's rows as independent of time and shuffle them within each customer
Remove the date column first so the data becomes plain tabular data, then split it
Keep the months in order, train on the earlier months, and test on the later ones
questions.why: Balances over time form a time-series where order carries meaning, so the split must respect time, with training on the past and testing on the future.

questions.prompt: A logistics firm has a box of paper delivery receipts that were photographed one by one. The receipts have no agreed layout, and the handwriting varies from one receipt to the next. Which statement about this data is correct?
choices: The receipts are unstructured image data, so they must be converted into numbers before a model can use them
The receipts are tabular data because each receipt is one row and needs no preparation
The receipts are time-series data because each one is dated
The receipts are structured data because each one has a total printed near the bottom
questions.why: Photographed receipts with no predefined layout are unstructured image data, and the text says unstructured data usually needs a preprocessing step to turn it into numbers first.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate who is new to machine learning how you would tell whether a dataset is labeled, what the data's shape (tabular, time-series, image, or text) implies for the model you could train, and name one limit or tradeoff of depending on labels.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would start by checking whether each example has a known correct answer attached. If a column holds that answer, such as whether an order was returned, the data is labeled and supervised learning is possible. If there is no such column, the data is unlabeled, and we would need someone to label examples, which costs time and money. Next I would look at the shape. Rows and columns with fixed fields mean structured, tabular data. Free text, images, and audio are unstructured and need conversion into numbers first. If the records are ordered by time, the data is a time-series, and I would split it by time rather than randomly, so the test set only contains later data. The main tradeoff of relying on labels is that labels are expensive to produce and can be wrong or inconsistent, which limits how much the model can learn and how far we should trust its scores.
rubricPoints: Labeled data has a known correct answer per example; unlabeled data does not
Structured data has fixed fields, while unstructured data such as text, images, or audio does not
Time-series data needs order-preserving splits to avoid leaking future information
Labels are costly or error-prone, which limits supervised learning

suggested.rationale: Telling data types apart from a realistic business scenario is best practised by reasoning through a mixed dataset, which no current mission covers directly.

lessons.plain: Machine learning lets software find patterns in examples instead of following rules a person wrote by hand. The learning type describes what feedback the software gets while it learns. If every example comes with the right answer attached, the software learns to predict that answer. If there are no answers and it must find structure in the data itself, it groups things on its own. If it learns by trying actions and getting a score afterward, it learns from reward. Knowing which type applies tells you which tool fits and what data you need before you start.
lessons.guessPrompt: A bank has ten years of loan applications, each marked as repaid or defaulted, and a second project has a million customer records with no outcome attached. Which project could you train to predict defaults directly, and what is the one thing the other project is missing?
lessons.teach:
Supervised learning means training on examples that already carry the correct answer, called a label. You show the model inputs paired with their labels, it adjusts itself until its guesses match the labels on examples it has seen, and then you use it on new inputs. Predicting a number is called regression; predicting a category is called classification. Spam filtering and house-price estimation are typical cases.

Unsupervised learning works on unlabeled data, where no correct answer exists. The algorithm looks for structure by itself, such as grouping similar customers together. This grouping is called clustering. The groups are only as meaningful as the features you supplied, and nobody can say they are right or wrong, only useful or not.

Reinforcement learning involves an agent that takes actions in an environment and receives a reward signal afterward. It is not told the correct move at each step. It learns which sequences of actions earn the most reward over time. Game-playing and robot control are examples.

Worked example: a parcel company wants to flag late deliveries. It has past shipments, each marked on time or late. Step one: the late-or-on-time column is the label, so this is supervised classification. Step two: the model learns from the route, weight and weather columns. Step three: it scores tomorrow's shipments before they leave.

Common mistake: choosing supervised learning because it sounds more powerful when no trustworthy labels exist. Labels cost money and can be wrong, and a model learns whatever the labels say, including their errors.

In a running system, a supervised model trained on last year's labels keeps predicting as if last year still holds, so its accuracy falls when behaviour changes. You need to monitor it and retrain it on fresh labelled data.

questions.prompt: A kitchen-appliance retailer has 4,000 past orders, each marked yes or no for whether it was returned within 30 days. It wants to predict which new orders will be returned. Step one: the yes/no column is the label, so the task is supervised classification. Step two: the model learns from order value, delivery days and product category. Step three: [missing]. What belongs in the missing step?
choices: Cluster the new orders into unlabeled groups first, since classification cannot run on data with a known outcome.
Ask the model to generate its own return labels for the new orders, so the labels match its predictions.
Hold back some past orders the model never trained on, and compare its predictions with their known outcomes before trusting it.
Skip any checking, because a model that has seen the labels will be correct on new orders by default.
questions.why: Checking predictions against held-back labelled examples is how you find out whether the model has learned something that generalises, and the other choices either skip that test or misuse the labels.

questions.prompt: A school district has student records with attendance and study-hour figures but no outcome column. It wants to find groups of students who behave similarly. Which learning type fits, and why?
choices: Reinforcement learning, because students take actions and the district can give them rewards.
Unsupervised learning, because the data has no correct answer and the goal is to find groups by structure.
Supervised regression, because the district wants a number for each student.
Supervised classification, because the district wants each student put into a category.
questions.why: With no labels, the algorithm must find structure itself, which is unsupervised learning and typically produces clusters.

questions.prompt: A warehouse robot picks items from shelves. It is not shown the correct movement at each step. It tries different movements and gets a reward signal after each completed pickup, gradually learning which sequences earn the most reward. Which learning type is this?
choices: Reinforcement learning, because an agent acts in an environment and learns from the reward it receives afterward.
Unsupervised learning, because the robot receives no labels.
Supervised regression, because the robot is predicting how long each pickup takes.
Supervised classification, because each movement is labelled good or bad in advance.
questions.why: The defining feature is an agent learning sequences of actions from a reward signal rather than from correct answers shown in advance.

questions.prompt: A county office has three years of permit decisions marked approved or rejected, but a different clerk applied the rules inconsistently each year. A team trains a model on these decisions and expects it to be accurate. What is the most accurate assessment?
choices: Once enough rows exist, the model will average out the clerks' inconsistencies and recover the correct rules.
A model learns whatever the labels say, so inconsistent labels will teach it that inconsistency and its accuracy will suffer.
Clustering the permits first would fix it, because unsupervised learning ignores errors in the labels.
Switching to reinforcement learning removes the problem, because the reward signal replaces the need for labels.
questions.why: Supervised models copy the patterns in their labels, errors included, so unreliable labels cap how well the model can perform.

lessons.explainPrompt: You are talking to a teammate who wants two features: one that groups users by their behaviour, and one that recommends the next action for each user. Explain the difference between supervised and unsupervised learning, say which one you would use for each feature and why, and name one limit or tradeoff of the approach you chose for the grouping feature.
lessons.modelAnswer: Supervised learning trains on examples that already have the correct answer attached, so the model learns to predict that answer for new inputs. Unsupervised learning gets no answers and finds structure, such as groups of similar users, on its own. For grouping users by behaviour, I would use unsupervised clustering, because we have no labelled right group for each user. The main tradeoff is that the clusters have no ground truth. Someone has to decide whether they are useful, and changing the features or the number of groups can change the result completely, so we should check with the product team that the groups mean something. The next-action recommendation is different: if we have logs of what users did next, that becomes a supervised problem with those logs as labels.
rubricPoints: Supervised learning uses labelled examples with known correct answers to predict outcomes.
Unsupervised learning finds structure such as clusters in unlabeled data, with no correct answer to check against.
The grouping feature suits unsupervised clustering because no labels exist for the groups.
The chosen approach has a tradeoff: clusters need human judgement about whether they are useful, and results depend on features and group count.

suggested.rationale: Being able to explain which learning type fits a problem and why is the core skill here, and no listed mission or planned engine practises it directly.

lessons.plain: This lesson is about spotting the situations where a learned prediction actually helps, as opposed to a plain set of rules or a person doing the job. Artificial intelligence is software that performs tasks we normally associate with human judgment. Machine learning is one way to build it: instead of writing the rules by hand, you show the software many past examples and it finds patterns it can apply to new cases. Those patterns usually pay off in three ways. They help a person make a better decision, they let one good solution handle far more cases than a team could, or they take a repetitive step off people's hands entirely. Knowing which of these you are buying is the first step in deciding whether AI is worth using at all.
lessons.guessPrompt: A support team receives 4,000 emails a day, and about 80 percent are one of ten routine questions. Before reading anything else, would you guess the best first use of an AI tool here is to have it reply to every routine email on its own, to help each agent answer faster, or to do something else? Give your reason in a sentence.
lessons.teach:
Three kinds of value show up again and again. Decision support means a model produces a score or suggestion and a person makes the final call; a fraud score that flags a card transaction for an analyst is one example. Scaling means the same learned behaviour is applied to volumes no team could review by hand, such as checking millions of product photos for damage. Automation means the system acts on each case without a person checking it, such as routing an email to the right queue. Each one earns its cost in a different way, so name which one you are buying before choosing a technique.

Why it works: a model learns statistical patterns from past examples and then applies them to new inputs. That is useful when the rules are too many or too fuzzy to write down, and when a wrong answer is tolerable or a person can check it.

Worked example: a bank reviews 50,000 card transactions a day with 40 analysts. Step one: the model gives each transaction a fraud risk score. Step two: transactions above a threshold go into a human queue, ordered by score. Step three: analysts confirm or clear each one. The model is decision support: it makes the analysts faster, and no card is blocked without a person. If volume grows tenfold, the scoring step runs unchanged, so the benefit of scaling is that the team does not have to grow tenfold.

Common mistake: calling something automation when a person still checks every output, or assuming a model is needed at all. If a fixed rule such as 'block any transaction over 10,000 from a country the card has never used' does the job and anyone can explain it, a rule beats a prediction.

Consequence: when automation runs unchecked, one bad model fails the same way across every case at once. The speed that makes scaling valuable is also what multiplies the damage.

questions.prompt: An insurer receives 8,000 motor claims a month and has 12 adjusters. Step one: a model reads each claim and produces a score from 0 to 1 for how likely the claim is to be legitimate. Step two: claims scoring under 0.2 are paid straight away with no adjuster looking at them, and the rest go into an adjuster queue. Step three is missing. Which completion correctly names the kind of value the insurer has bought and the cost that comes with it?
choices: Automation: low-score claims are paid with no person checking them, so one wrong threshold repeats across every such claim.
Scaling only: the same score now covers more claims, so the insurer no longer needs its adjusters.
Decision support: the score is only advice, so adjusters remain in charge of every payment.
A rule, not a model: the cutoff of 0.2 is fixed, so no model is involved at all.
questions.why: Paying claims without a person checking each one is automation, and because the same threshold applies to every case, one bad model or cutoff fails the same way across all of them at once.

questions.prompt: A retailer uses a model to read 2 million customer reviews a week and tag each one with a product topic, so a small team can spot trends. Which kind of value is this mainly buying?
choices: Scaling, because the same learned behaviour is applied to a volume no team could read by hand.
None, because tagging text is always a rule and never needs a model.
Automation, because the tags are applied with no person involved at any point.
Decision support, because a person reads the tags before acting on them.
questions.why: The model applies one learned behaviour to a volume too large for manual review, which is the defining feature of scaling, even though a person later reads the results.

questions.prompt: A warehouse uses a model to label each incoming parcel with a loading dock number, and parcels are sent to that dock with no staff check. A manager says this is decision support because a model is involved. What is the best response?
choices: The manager is right, because any system that uses a model is decision support.
The manager is right, because the staff can still correct a parcel after it has been sent.
The manager is wrong, but only because loading docks are never a valid use for AI.
The manager is wrong: this is automation, since no person checks each output, and a wrong label misroutes many parcels at once.
questions.why: Decision support requires a person to make the final call, and here nobody checks each routing, so it is automation; the presence of a model does not decide the category.

questions.prompt: A small clinic wants to flag any patient who has missed three visits in a row so a receptionist can call them. Which approach fits best?
choices: A prediction model trained on past visits, because any flagging task needs learning from examples.
Automated cancellation of the patient's future bookings, because the flag is certain to be correct.
A plain rule that counts consecutive missed visits, because the condition is explicit and anyone can check it.
A scaling model that reviews every visit record, because the clinic has many patients.
questions.why: When the condition is clear and can be written as a rule that anyone can explain, a rule beats a prediction, and the other options add learning or action that the problem does not need.

lessons.explainPrompt: A colleague wants to put an AI model in charge of approving refunds with no human review, because it would save the team many hours each week. Explain to them, in your own words, where AI/ML adds value in a case like this and what limit or tradeoff they should weigh before deciding.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would separate the three kinds of value first. Refund approval with no review is automation, so the model's mistakes reach customers directly and repeat at the same speed as its correct decisions. The hours saved are real, but I would ask whether most refunds are routine enough that a simple fixed rule would capture much of the gain. A middle option is decision support: the model scores each refund and sends only the uncertain or large ones to a person. Before going fully automatic, I would want measured accuracy on past refunds, a clear rule for cases the model is unsure about, and a way to catch it going wrong after launch. The core limit is that a model makes predictions, not guarantees, and it is only as fair as the examples it learned from.
rubricPoints: Distinguishes decision support, scaling, and automation.
Notes that automation removes the human check, so errors repeat at scale.
Says a fixed rule may beat a prediction when the logic is simple and explainable.
Names a tradeoff or limit: predictions are imperfect and depend on the training data.
Suggests a safeguard such as human review of uncertain cases or monitoring after launch.

suggested.rationale: Deciding whether AI adds value in a messy business situation is best practised by reasoning through an exam-style scenario, and no listed mission or planned engine covers this objective directly.

lessons.plain: Sometimes the right answer to a business problem is not a machine learning model at all. A model makes a prediction, which is a best guess that can be wrong. When you need an exact, fixed result every time, such as checking whether a customer is old enough or applying a refund rule written into policy, a plain set of rules written by a person is usually better. A model also costs money to build, needs data, and needs ongoing care. Before reaching for AI, ask two questions: does the answer need to be certain, and do the benefits outweigh the full cost of building and running the model? Using a neural network to add two numbers is like hiring a weather forecaster to tell you what 2 plus 2 equals.
lessons.guessPrompt: A small company wants to decide whether an order qualifies for free shipping, which happens when the order total is at least 50 dollars. Would you build a machine learning model for this, and why or why not?
lessons.teach: A prediction is an output that estimates something uncertain, such as the chance a customer will leave or whether a transaction is fraud. Every prediction has some error rate. A specific outcome is a result that must be right in every case, such as a tax calculation or an eligibility check, and it is usually produced by explicit rules. Cost-benefit means comparing what a solution is worth against its total cost over time. For machine learning that total includes collecting and labeling data, training, hosting the model, monitoring it, and retraining it when the world changes. Those costs recur, while a rule usually costs a few hours to write and test. Worked example: a bank must confirm an applicant is at least 18. Step 1: subtract the birth date from today's date to get an age in whole years. Step 2: compare the age with 18. Step 3: the result is always correct and easy to audit. A model estimating age from a photo would be wrong sometimes, cost far more to run, and could create legal risk, so the rule wins. Common mistake: choosing machine learning because it sounds modern, then judging it only by accuracy on a test set without asking what each wrong answer costs. Consequence in a running system: a model that is 97 percent accurate still gets 3 in 100 requests wrong, and if those requests are refunds or eligibility decisions, that error rate becomes an incident and its monitoring and retraining costs continue every month. A rule that is correct by construction avoids both problems.

questions.prompt: A parcel firm adds a 15 currency-unit oversize surcharge when a parcel's longest side is over 120 cm. Every surcharge must be right, so this is a specific outcome rather than a prediction. Worked steps: Step 1: read the longest side from the scanner's dimension record, in cm. Step 2: compare that number with 120. Step 3: [missing]. Which choice correctly completes step 3?
choices: If the number is greater than 120, add the 15 unit surcharge; otherwise charge the standard rate, and record the decision for audit.
Round every measurement to the nearest 10 cm before comparing, so small scanner noise does not matter.
Train a model on past parcel photos to estimate whether each parcel is oversize, and accept its 95 percent accuracy.
Compare the parcel's weight instead, since heavy parcels are usually oversize.
questions.why: Step 3 applies the explicit rule to the result, which is deterministic and auditable, so it is correct for every parcel by construction.

questions.prompt: Which statement best describes a specific outcome as this unit uses the term?
choices: A dashboard number that updates each week as new data arrives.
A result that must be right in every case, usually produced by explicit rules.
Any output that a neural network produces, regardless of how it is used.
A result estimated from patterns in past data, with a known error rate.
questions.why: A specific outcome is defined by the requirement that it be right in every case, and such results are usually produced by explicit rules rather than predictions.

questions.prompt: A café wants to predict which of its 40 daily pastries will sell out by noon so it can bake fewer leftovers. A wrong guess wastes a few pastries, and the forecast runs on a spreadsheet the owner already maintains. Which conclusion is best supported by cost-benefit thinking?
choices: A prediction is never appropriate for anything involving food.
A dedicated machine learning model is always required, because predictions are always more accurate than rules.
A prediction can be worth it here because each error is cheap, but its total cost over time should still be compared with the benefit.
The café should judge the forecast only by its accuracy on last month's data.
questions.why: Cost-benefit compares the value of a solution against its total cost, and here cheap errors and near-zero added cost make a prediction reasonable if that comparison is actually done.

questions.prompt: A team reports their model is 99 percent accurate on a held-out test set and wants to ship it to check loan documents, where each check must be exact. What is the most important gap in their reasoning?
choices: They should have used more test data, since 99 percent accuracy is suspiciously high.
Test set accuracy is irrelevant, so they should ship without any further checking.
They have not compared what each wrong answer costs, or the recurring costs of hosting, monitoring and retraining the model.
They should replace the model with a neural network because neural networks are more accurate.
questions.why: Judging a model only by test accuracy ignores what each error costs and the ongoing costs of running it, which is the common mistake this objective warns about.

lessons.explainPrompt: A teammate proposes using a machine learning model to decide which invoices automatically get a late-fee waiver. Explain to them when a fixed rule would be the better choice here, and name one limit or tradeoff of the approach you recommend.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would first ask whether the decision needs a guess or a certain answer. A late-fee waiver usually follows a written policy, such as paid within 5 days of a due date or the customer has a waiver code, so a rule can check it exactly every time and anyone can audit why an invoice was waived. A model would produce a probability, meaning some waivers would be wrong, and we would need data labeling, training, hosting, and monitoring that keep costing money. The tradeoff of the rule is that it is rigid: if the policy changes or has exceptions, someone must update it by hand and the rule cannot notice patterns on its own. So I would start with the rule and only consider a model later if the exceptions become too numerous to write down and the cost of occasional wrong waivers is acceptable.
rubricPoints: States that a rule gives certain, repeatable results while a model gives probabilistic predictions with some errors
Compares the one-time cost of writing a rule with the recurring costs of data, hosting, monitoring, and retraining a model
Explains that the cost of each wrong answer should be weighed against the benefit
Names a real limit of the rule, such as rigidity when policies change or exceptions multiply

suggested.rationale: Choosing between a rule and a model in an exam-style business scenario requires weighing costs and outcomes, which is best practised by reasoning through situations.

lessons.plain: Most prediction problems fall into one of three shapes of question. Regression answers how much or how many: a number on a sliding scale, like next week's sales in pounds. Classification answers which one: pick a label from a fixed list, like whether an email is spam. Clustering finds groups nobody labelled in advance: you hand over customer records and the system proposes segments that look alike. Choosing the right shape comes before choosing any tool, and sometimes the honest answer is that a simple rule or a lookup table does the job better than any of them.
lessons.guessPrompt: A subscription business wants to know, for each customer, whether that customer will cancel next month, yes or no. Before reading on, which of the three shapes (regression, classification, or clustering) would you pick for this, and why?
lessons.teach:
Regression predicts a number on a continuous scale, such as a delivery time in minutes or a monthly energy bill. Classification predicts which category an item belongs to from a fixed set of labels, such as spam or not spam. Clustering groups items by similarity when no labels exist; the system finds the groups, and a person names them afterwards. Whether training data comes with the right answers matters too. Regression and classification are supervised learning, meaning past examples carry known outcomes. Clustering is unsupervised learning, meaning the data has no outcomes attached.

Why it works: each technique learns a mapping from inputs to an output of a particular shape. A regression model fits a line or curve through past examples and reads off a value. A classifier learns boundaries that separate categories. A clustering algorithm measures how close records are to one another and places near ones together.

Worked example: a fleet operator wants to predict fuel used per trip. Step 1: the output is kilometres per litre, a number, so the task is regression. Step 2: the operator also wants to flag each trip as efficient or wasteful. That output is one of two labels, so the task is classification, trained on past trips marked with the label. Step 3: to discover driver behaviour types without predefined categories, the operator runs clustering on the trip records and then names the groups. One dataset, three questions, three techniques.

Common mistake: choosing a technique because it sounds sophisticated instead of because of the output you need. Treating a yes-or-no question as a number, or using clustering when the business needs a named answer, produces results nobody can act on. In a running system, a classifier left on a threshold it was never tuned for will quietly misroute customers, and the problem often surfaces only through complaints.

Sometimes no technique is right. If the policy is refund any damaged item under 10 pounds, a plain rule is cheaper, testable and easy to explain.
