questions.prompt: A dental clinic wants three things from its booking records. Step 1: predict how many minutes each patient will wait in the lobby, which is a number on a continuous scale, so the task is regression. Step 2: decide whether a booked patient will fail to attend, which is a yes-or-no label taken from past bookings marked attended or missed, so the task is classification. Step 3: the clinic wants to find groups of patients with similar visit habits, but the records have no outcome attached to them and nobody has defined the groups in advance. Which technique fits Step 3, and why?
choices: Clustering, because the records have no outcomes attached and the system finds the groups by similarity, after which a person names them
Classification, because the clinic will eventually label each group with a category
A fixed rule, because grouping patients is always a simple threshold on visit count
Regression, because the groups are a number of visits per patient
questions.why: Clustering is unsupervised, so it suits records with no known outcomes, where the algorithm places similar records together and people name the groups afterwards.

questions.prompt: A coating lab has ten years of oven logs, each recording the oven temperature and the measured coating thickness in microns for that batch. The lab wants to estimate the thickness for a planned temperature setting. Which technique matches this output?
choices: Clustering, because the batches can be grouped by similar temperature
Regression, because the output is a number on a continuous scale
Classification, because thickness falls into acceptable and unacceptable bands
Clustering, because the logs have no labels to learn from
questions.why: The output is a continuous number (microns), so regression is the fit, and the logs carry known outcomes, so the data is supervised.

questions.prompt: A finance team has past invoices, each already marked by an auditor as fraudulent or legitimate. The team asks a clustering tool to decide whether each new invoice is fraudulent, and then wants to name the groups it finds. What is the main problem with this choice?
choices: Nothing is wrong, because clustering is the most accurate technique for fraud
Clustering cannot process invoice amounts because they are numbers
The team needs a yes-or-no answer for data that already has known outcomes, so classification is the matching technique and clustering discards the labels
Clustering always produces too many groups to be useful for auditing
questions.why: Labelled past examples and a required yes-or-no output point to classification; clustering ignores the known outcomes and the groups it forms do not answer the question asked.

questions.prompt: A retailer's policy says any item returned within 30 days with a valid receipt is refunded in full. A manager proposes training a model to predict refund eligibility from past returns. Given the policy as written, what is the best answer?
choices: Train a classifier, because any policy involving customers needs a learned model
Use a plain rule, because the policy is explicit, testable and cheap to explain, so no prediction is needed
Use clustering to discover the refund rules from return records
Train a regression model, because refund amounts are numbers
questions.why: When the decision is fully specified by a clear rule, a prediction adds cost and unpredictability without adding value, so the plain rule is the honest choice.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate who has only worked with spreadsheets how you would decide between regression, classification, and clustering for a new request, and name one limit or tradeoff of the approach you would choose.
lessons.modelAnswer: I start with the output the business needs. If the answer is a quantity on a scale, such as hours to repair or expected revenue, that is regression. If the answer is one label from a fixed list, such as approve, review, or reject, that is classification. If there are no answers to learn from and we want to discover natural groups, such as customer segments, that is clustering. I also check whether we have labelled history, because regression and classification need past examples with known outcomes. The tradeoff I would name is that a classifier only knows the categories it was trained on, so when the business adds a new category, the model needs retraining. Clustering has a similar limit: the groups it finds may not match business meaning, so a person must check and name them before anyone relies on them.
rubricPoints: Chooses the technique from the shape of the output: number, fixed label, or unlabelled groups
Notes that regression and classification need labelled historical examples while clustering does not
Names a concrete limit, such as classifiers being bounded by their trained categories
Mentions that a simple rule may beat a model when the logic is clear

suggested.rationale: Choosing a technique from a business question and defending the choice in plain words is the core skill here, and no listed mission or planned engine practises it directly.

lessons.plain: Real-world AI shows up as a handful of recurring jobs. Computer vision means a system reads images or video, such as spotting a damaged part on a production line. Natural language processing (NLP) means a system works with written text, such as sorting support tickets by topic. Speech recognition turns spoken audio into text. Recommendation suggests items a person might want, forecasting estimates a future number such as next month's demand, and fraud detection flags transactions that look unusual. A knowledge base lets a system answer questions from your own documents, and agentic AI describes systems that plan and take several steps toward a goal. Matching the business problem to the right job is the core skill.
lessons.guessPrompt: A retailer wants to know, each week, roughly how many units of each product it will sell next month so it can order stock. Which application type in this lesson fits best, and what in the problem makes you think so?
lessons.teach:
Each application type is a way of pointing a model at a particular kind of input to get a particular kind of output. A model is the learned pattern produced by training, and using it on new input is called inferencing. Computer vision takes images or video and produces labels, locations, or measurements. Natural language processing takes text and produces meaning, such as a category, a sentiment, or extracted names. Speech recognition takes audio and produces a transcript. Recommendation ranks items for a user based on past behaviour. Forecasting predicts a number over future time periods from a history of values, which makes it a time-series problem. Fraud detection scores events, such as card payments, for how unusual they are, and the positive cases are usually very rare. A knowledge base is a store of your own documents that a system searches before answering, so answers rest on current facts. Agentic AI describes a system that breaks a goal into steps, calls tools, checks results, and decides what to do next.

Worked example: a support team receives emails. Step 1: the input is text, so the family is NLP. Step 2: the output needed is a category such as billing or outage. Step 3: the team has past emails already labelled with categories, so a classifier can learn from them. Step 4: if the team instead wants answers drawn from its policy manual, a knowledge base is the better fit.

Common mistake: choosing a technique because it sounds impressive rather than because the input and output match. An agent is not needed to sort emails into three folders, and a forecast does not check a single payment for fraud.

Consequence: a fraud model that flags too many legitimate payments blocks real customers, while one that misses fraud loses money. The application you pick determines which kind of error matters most.

The right application starts with the input, the output, and the cost of being wrong.

questions.prompt: A logistics firm receives photos of parcels from drivers and wants each photo labelled as damaged or intact. Step 1: the input is photos, so the family is computer vision. Step 2: the output needed is a label of damaged or intact. Step 3: [missing]. Step 4: the firm decides that missing a damaged parcel costs more than a false alarm, so the model should be tuned to catch more damage. Which statement correctly fills the missing Step 3?
choices: Forecast next month's parcel volumes from the past twelve months of delivery counts.
Load the courier handbook into a knowledge base so the system answers from it.
Check whether the firm already has past photos labelled damaged or intact, since a classifier learns from labelled examples.
Build an agent that emails drivers and decides refunds on its own.
questions.why: A classifier learns from labelled examples, so checking for past labelled photos is the step that decides whether this approach can work.

questions.prompt: A retailer wants to estimate its revenue for each of the next four quarters using the last three years of quarterly revenue figures. Which application family fits best?
choices: Forecasting
Computer vision
Speech recognition
Recommendation
questions.why: Forecasting predicts a number over future time periods from a history of values, which matches a quarterly revenue series.

questions.prompt: A travel app receives a request to rebook a traveller's flight. The system must look up alternative flights, check seat availability, book the best option, and then confirm with the traveller. Which application family describes this best?
choices: Natural language processing, because the request is written in text
Fraud detection, because the booking involves payment
Agentic AI, because the system breaks the goal into steps, calls tools, checks results, and decides the next step
Forecasting, because flight prices change over time
questions.why: Agentic AI describes a system that breaks a goal into steps, calls tools, checks results, and decides what to do next, which is exactly what the rebooking requires.

questions.prompt: A clinic deploys a chatbot that answers patients' questions about opening hours. The bot sometimes gives last year's hours because it relied on what it learned during training. Which change best addresses this failure?
choices: Retrain the bot on a larger set of general internet text
Use a forecasting model to predict the hours patients will ask about
Store the current hours document in a knowledge base that the system searches before answering
Replace the chatbot with a speech recognition model that transcribes calls
questions.why: A knowledge base is a store of your own documents that the system searches before answering, so answers rest on current facts rather than on what the model remembered from training.

lessons.explainPrompt: A product manager asks whether we can use AI to decide which customer complaints to escalate to a manager. Explain to a teammate which application type fits, what its limit is, and one tradeoff we should raise before building anything.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would frame this as a text classification problem, which belongs to natural language processing, because the input is the complaint text and the output is a category such as escalate or not. We would need past complaints labelled with whether they were escalated, so the model has history to learn from. The limit is that it predicts escalation from patterns and cannot fully judge how serious a complaint is in context, so it should assist a human decision rather than make it. The tradeoff to raise is the cost of errors: if the model misses a serious complaint, a customer may leave, and if it escalates too many, managers get overloaded. Before building, we should agree on an acceptable error rate and check whether a simple keyword rule would already do most of the job.
rubricPoints: Names natural language processing or text classification as the fit, based on text input and category output.
Notes that the approach needs labelled past examples to learn from.
States a limit: the model predicts patterns and does not fully understand context or seriousness.
Raises a tradeoff about the cost of missed escalations versus excess escalations.
Considers whether a simple rule would be enough before building a model.

suggested.rationale: Mapping a business problem to the right application type is best practised by reasoning through an exam-style situation, and no listed mission or engine covers this choice.

lessons.plain: AWS offers ready-made AI services that you call like any other cloud service, so you do not have to build the model yourself. Amazon Transcribe turns speech into text. Amazon Translate converts text between languages. Amazon Comprehend reads text and finds things such as sentiment, names, and key phrases. Amazon Lex runs chatbots that work out what a user wants. Amazon Polly turns text into spoken audio. Amazon SageMaker AI is different: it is a workspace for building, training, and hosting your own machine learning models when the ready-made options do not fit. Think of the first five as finished tools on a shelf and SageMaker AI as the workshop.
lessons.guessPrompt: A call centre wants every recorded phone call turned into searchable text. Before reading further, which of these would you guess fits best: Amazon Transcribe, Amazon Polly, or Amazon SageMaker AI? Say why in one sentence.
lessons.teach:
A managed service is one where AWS runs the servers, software, and scaling, and you send inputs and receive outputs. Five of the services are pretrained, meaning the models already exist and you only call them. Transcribe converts recorded speech into text. Translate converts text from one language into another. Comprehend analyzes text and returns structured findings: the language, the sentiment (whether the tone is positive, negative, or mixed), named entities such as people, places, and organizations, and key phrases. Lex builds conversational interfaces. You define intents, which are things a user wants to do, and slots, which are details the bot must collect, such as a date. Polly, a text-to-speech service, turns written text into natural-sounding audio. SageMaker AI is a different kind of offering: a platform where you prepare data, train your own model, and host it behind an endpoint, which is a network address your application calls to get predictions.

Worked example: a customer leaves a voicemail in Spanish. Step 1, Transcribe converts the audio into Spanish text. Step 2, Translate converts that text into English. Step 3, Comprehend reads the English text and returns a negative sentiment and the product name it mentions. Your application routes the case to a priority queue. At no point did you train a model.

Common mistake: reaching for SageMaker AI first. Training and hosting your own model adds data preparation, monitoring, and retraining work. If a pretrained service covers the task, that work is avoidable.

In a running system, these services give probabilistic answers. Comprehend's sentiment result is a best guess, so a routing rule built on it will sometimes misfile a case, and the design should expect that.

questions.prompt: A parts supplier, Harwick Tools, receives a French voicemail from a customer about a late pallet. The team wants to flag negative messages for priority handling and will use only pretrained services. Step 1: Transcribe converts the recording into French text. Step 2: Translate converts that French text into English. Step 3: (missing). Step 4: Your application flags the message for the priority queue when the sentiment is negative. Which step fills the gap?
choices: Comprehend reads the English text and returns the sentiment and named entities such as the product or supplier name
Lex collects the customer's preferred callback date as a slot
SageMaker AI trains a custom sentiment model on the French transcript before any other step runs
Polly converts the English text into audio so a human can listen to it
questions.why: Comprehend is the pretrained service that analyzes English text for sentiment and entities, and its sentiment output is what the flagging step needs.

questions.prompt: A small law firm wants to train its own contract-classification model on its documents and host it behind a network address that its intake app can call. Which offering from this objective fits that need?
choices: Amazon Translate
Amazon SageMaker AI
Amazon Lex
Amazon Polly
questions.why: SageMaker AI is the platform for preparing data, training your own model, and hosting it at an endpoint, while the other named services are pretrained and you only call them.

questions.prompt: A logistics company routes support emails with a rule that sends any email Comprehend labels as negative to a manager. Last month about one in ten emails was sent to the wrong queue. What is the most sensible design response?
choices: Remove the sentiment step and send every email to the manager so nothing is ever misfiled
Accept that Comprehend's sentiment result is a best guess, and design the routing so errors can be caught and corrected, such as with a review path
Switch to SageMaker AI and train a model before routing, since pretrained services never misfire
Treat the misrouting as a fault in AWS and wait for a fix before changing anything
questions.why: Comprehend returns probabilistic answers, so the design should expect some misfiled cases and include a way to catch and fix them.

questions.prompt: A travel firm builds a Lex bot that books train seats. The customer says, 'Book a seat to Leeds on Friday.' Which description correctly separates the intent from the slots?
choices: Intent is Leeds; the slot is booking a seat
Both the intent and the slot are the single word Friday
The phrase has no intent, because only the bot can have one
Intent: book a seat. Slots: Leeds and Friday
questions.why: An intent is what the user wants to do, and slots are the details the bot must collect, such as the destination and the day.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate, in your own words, how you would choose between a pretrained AWS AI service and Amazon SageMaker AI for a new feature, and name one limit of the pretrained option that you would check before committing.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would start by asking whether a pretrained service already does the job. If the need is speech to text, text translation, text analysis, a chatbot, or spoken audio, Transcribe, Translate, Comprehend, Lex, or Polly is usually the fastest route, because AWS runs the model and we only call it. I would move to SageMaker AI only if the task is specific to our own data, such as classifying our own product defects, and the pretrained tools miss it. The limit I would check on a pretrained option is accuracy on our real inputs. A transcript of noisy call audio or a sentiment score on industry jargon may be wrong often enough to matter. So before committing I would test the service on a sample of our own data, decide what error rate is acceptable, and plan how the feature handles its mistakes.
rubricPoints: Pretrained managed services are the first choice when they cover the task, because AWS runs the model.
SageMaker AI fits when the task needs a custom model trained on your own data.
A pretrained option can be wrong on your specific inputs, so test accuracy on real samples.
Plan how the product handles errors, since the outputs are predictions, not guarantees.

suggested.rationale: This objective is mostly product catalogue facts about what each named service does, which is best learned by reading rather than by a current OpsForge mission or planned engine.

lessons.plain: Sometimes a business problem needs a model built for one narrow job, trained on the company's own data, such as a table of past loan decisions. Other times it needs a very large general-purpose model that already learned language and images from huge amounts of public material and can be pointed at many tasks by describing what you want. This lesson is about choosing between the two. The choice is not mainly about which one is more impressive. It depends on three pressures: rules set by regulators, whether you must explain each individual decision, and what your team can realistically run and keep running.
lessons.guessPrompt: A bank wants software that approves or declines loan applications, and every decision must be explained to the applicant in writing. Would you reach first for a small model trained on the bank's past decisions or a large general-purpose text model, and what single fact would make you change your choice?
lessons.teach:
A traditional machine learning model is a model trained on your own labeled data for one specific prediction, such as a risk score or a yes or no answer. Its inputs and outputs are narrow and known in advance. A foundation model is a very large model pre-trained on broad data so it can handle many tasks, and it is usually adapted or prompted rather than built from scratch. Three words matter here. Regulation means the legal rules that govern how a decision must be made and documented. Explainability means being able to say which inputs drove a particular output. Operational constraints means the practical limits of latency, cost per request, staffing, data location and uptime.

Why this choice works the way it does: a narrow model can be tested on known cases, its behavior can be audited, and the same input gives the same output. A foundation model covers far more ground, which makes it flexible, but its reasoning is hard to trace and its outputs can vary between calls.

Worked example. Step 1: the loan decision must come with reasons for each applicant, under a fairness rule. That points to a traditional model whose features can be inspected. Step 2: a friendly summary letter that restates the decision in plain language is low stakes and text-heavy, so a foundation model fits there. Step 3: the team has two engineers and no ML operations staff, which favors a managed service over hosting either model yourself.

Common mistake: choosing the foundation model because it is newest, then assuming its written explanation is a faithful account of how it reached the answer. Fluent explanations are not proof.

Consequence in a running system: each foundation model call adds latency and per-request cost. A high-volume single score served that way can break the budget and the response time target, and variable output can make audits fail.

The decision is driven by the rules, the need for reasons, and what your team can operate, not by which model is larger.

questions.prompt: A county tax office wants to sort incoming property appeals into likely valid and likely invalid, so staff review the likely valid ones first. Step 1: state law requires the office to give each appellant the specific reasons their appeal was ranked low, so the ranking must rest on inputs that can be inspected. Step 2: the ranking must cover about 400,000 appeals every night and finish before staff arrive at 6 a.m. Step 3 is left for you: state what that nightly volume implies for choosing between a traditional model and a foundation model.
choices: Step 3: high nightly volume makes per-request cost and latency the deciding factors, favoring the narrow traditional model.
Step 3: a foundation model is cheaper per request, so the nightly run favors it over the narrow model.
Step 3: the volume does not matter because a batch job has no response time target at all.
Step 3: once the office buys a managed service, the number of calls stops affecting which model type fits.
questions.why: Each foundation model call adds latency and cost, so running 400,000 of them every night pushes against the time window and budget, which favors the narrow model.

questions.prompt: Which description best defines a traditional machine learning model as the teaching text uses the term?
choices: A model trained on an organisation's own labeled data for one specific prediction, with narrow inputs and outputs known in advance.
Any software that follows a fixed list of if-then rules written by a developer to reach a decision.
A model whose outputs are guaranteed identical across calls because it has no randomness anywhere in its design.
A very large model pre-trained on broad internet data that can be prompted for many unrelated tasks without any further adaptation.
questions.why: The teaching text defines a traditional model as trained on your own labeled data for one specific prediction with narrow, known inputs and outputs.

questions.prompt: A retailer wants a draft reply to each customer email about delivery delays. A human agent reviews every draft before it is sent. No law requires the reasons behind each draft to be recorded, and volume is a few thousand emails a day. Which choice best fits the objective's factors?
choices: A traditional model trained on the retailer's past emails, because the output must be identical every time for audit.
Hosting a self-built foundation model on the retailer's own servers, because managed services are not allowed for customer data.
A foundation model reached through a managed service, because the drafts are text-heavy, low stakes, and the volume is modest.
A rule-based template system, because a foundation model can never be used where a human reviews the output.
questions.why: Low-stakes text drafting with no explanation requirement and moderate volume fits a foundation model, and a managed service suits a small team.

questions.prompt: An operations lead argues that a foundation model used for loan decisions is acceptable because it writes a clear paragraph explaining each decision. What is the main flaw in this reasoning?
choices: The lead should have chosen a larger foundation model, since larger models always produce more accurate written reasons.
Loan decisions can never use a foundation model under any circumstances, so the paragraph is irrelevant.
The paragraph is too long, and the rules require explanations to be under fifty words.
A paragraph written in fluent language is not proof of which inputs actually drove the output, so the explanation may not be faithful.
questions.why: The teaching text warns that a foundation model's reasoning is hard to trace and fluent explanations are not proof, so explainability needs inspectable inputs.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would decide between a traditional ML model and a foundation model for a new use case. Name one limit or tradeoff of the option you would not pick first.
lessons.modelAnswer: I start with three questions. First, does a regulator or policy require a per-decision reason that a person can check? If yes, a traditional model trained on our own labeled data is the safer default, because I can test it on known cases and inspect which inputs mattered. Second, is the task a single prediction with a measurable right answer, or open-ended language work? Narrow predictions usually suit a traditional model; drafting or summarizing suits a foundation model. Third, can we run it? A foundation model adds latency and per-request cost, so at high volume it may not fit the budget. The tradeoff of the foundation model is that its written explanation is not a reliable record of its reasoning and its output can vary between calls, so I would not rely on it alone for a decision that must be justified.
rubricPoints: States that regulation or a need for per-decision explanation favors a traditional, inspectable model.
Explains that a foundation model is flexible for open-ended tasks but harder to audit and explain.
Names an operational constraint such as latency, per-request cost, or staffing that affects the choice.
Names a concrete limit of the option not chosen, such as cost at volume or unreliable self-explanation.

suggested.rationale: Choosing between these two model types is best practiced by reasoning through an exam-style scenario with competing regulatory, explainability and operational pressures, which no current mission covers.

lessons.plain: An AI or machine learning pipeline is the chain of steps that turns raw data into a model that makes predictions for a real user. Think of a kitchen line: ingredients arrive, get cleaned and cut, a recipe is tested, the dish is served, and someone checks whether customers still like it. Each station has one job, and a problem at one station shows up as a bad result at the end. Knowing what each station contributes lets you say where a project is stuck and what to fix first.
lessons.guessPrompt: A team's model scores 97 percent on the examples it learned from, but it performs badly on new customer records. Before reading further, which stage of the project do you suspect first, and why?
lessons.teach: A pipeline is the ordered set of stages a machine learning project moves through, from collecting data to running a model in production. Each stage makes a distinct contribution, and a weak stage degrades everything after it. Data ingestion gathers raw records from sources such as logs, databases, or files. Data preparation cleans those records, removes duplicates, handles missing values, and builds features, which are the measurable inputs the model learns from. If the data is labeled, each example carries its correct answer. Training runs an algorithm, the procedure that finds patterns, over the prepared data to produce a model, the saved result of that learning. Evaluation tests the model on held-out data, examples set aside and never shown during training, using metrics such as accuracy (the share of predictions that are correct), precision (the share of flagged cases that were truly positive), and recall (the share of real positives the model found). Deployment makes the model available so applications can send inputs and receive predictions, a step called inferencing. Monitoring watches live inputs and predictions for drift, meaning the real world has moved away from the training data, and triggers retraining when needed. Worked example: a fleet company wants to flag vehicles likely to need repair. Ingestion pulls engine telemetry and service records. Preparation joins them per vehicle and creates a feature such as hours since last service. Training fits a classifier on past vehicles labeled as needing or not needing repair. Evaluation shows 90 percent accuracy overall but only 40 percent recall on the rare failures, so the team returns to preparation to rebalance the data. Deployment serves nightly predictions. Monitoring later shows a new vehicle model whose sensors report differently, and that drift triggers retraining. Common mistake: treating the score on training data as the final result. A model can look excellent there and fail on new inputs. Consequence: without monitoring, a model can keep returning confident answers long after its inputs have shifted, and nobody notices until customers complain. Each stage is a place where a fault can start, so a pipeline is only as trustworthy as its weakest stage.

questions.prompt: A grocery distributor wants to flag warehouses likely to run short of a product next week. Ingestion pulls weekly sales and stock counts from 12 warehouses. Preparation removes duplicate shipment rows and builds a feature called days of stock on hand. Training fits a classifier on past weeks labeled short or not short. Evaluation shows 92 percent accuracy overall but only 22 percent recall on the short weeks. The team then has to decide what happens next. Deployment and monitoring come after that decision. Which stage does the team return to, and why?
choices: Preparation, because the weak recall on the rare short weeks points to the data and features needing rebalancing before retraining
Ingestion, because the distributor must first collect more warehouses before anything else
Monitoring, because 92 percent accuracy shows the live inputs have already drifted
Deployment, because the model should serve predictions before its accuracy is judged
questions.why: Low recall on the rare class means the model misses real short weeks, and the teaching text says the fix for that kind of evaluation result is to return to preparation and rebalance the data.

questions.prompt: A dental clinic's reminder model flags 50 patients as likely to miss their appointment. Afterward, 40 of those 50 actually missed. What does precision measure here, and what is its value?
choices: 40 percent, because it divides true positives by all patients in the clinic
The model's accuracy, which cannot be worked out from this information
80 percent, the share of flagged patients who truly missed their appointment
100 percent, because every flagged patient is counted as a correct flag
questions.why: Precision is the share of flagged cases that were truly positive, so 40 of 50 flagged patients gives 80 percent.

questions.prompt: A regional airline builds a model that scores 99 percent on the data it trained on and is deployed straight away. Within a month, its predictions on new flights are poor. Which mistake most directly explains this?
choices: The team used too many features, which always makes a model fail on unseen flights
The team skipped deployment, so the model had no chance to see new data
The team treated the score on training data as the final result, when a model can look excellent there and still fail on new inputs
The team deployed without first labeling the flights, which means the model cannot make any predictions
questions.why: The teaching text warns that a high score on training data does not guarantee performance on new inputs, which is why evaluation uses held-out data.

questions.prompt: A customer support center wants a model that routes incoming tickets to the right team. Which pipeline stage is responsible for turning cleaned records into the measurable inputs the model learns from?
choices: Ingestion, which gathers raw ticket records from the helpdesk system
Evaluation, which tests the model on held-out tickets
Data preparation, which builds the features the model learns from
Training, which runs the algorithm to produce the saved model
questions.why: The teaching text defines data preparation as the stage that cleans records and builds features, which are the measurable inputs for learning.

lessons.explainPrompt: A teammate asks why a model that scored 95 percent in a notebook is failing in production. Explain the pipeline stages to them in your own words, say which stage most likely caused the gap, and name one limit of your explanation.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would walk them through the stages in order. Data is ingested and prepared, the model is trained with an algorithm, and then it is evaluated on held-out data the training never saw. A 95 percent score in a notebook is usually measured on data that overlaps or resembles the training set, so the first suspect is evaluation, or preparation that let test examples leak into training. Production then exposes the model to inputs that differ from what it learned, so the second suspect is drift that monitoring should have caught. I would check whether the evaluation split was truly separate and compare production inputs against the training data. The limit of my explanation is that I have not inspected the data yet. A high accuracy on imbalanced data can also hide poor recall on the rare cases that matter, so I would check that metric too.
rubricPoints: Describes the pipeline stages in order from data ingestion through monitoring
Explains that evaluation must use held-out data separate from training
Identifies drift or input mismatch as a cause of production failure
Names a limit or tradeoff, such as accuracy hiding poor recall on rare cases

suggested.rationale: Being able to explain how the stages connect and where each can fail is the core skill here, and no listed mission or planned engine covers pipeline stages directly.

lessons.plain: A foundation model is a very large AI model that someone has already trained on a huge pile of general data, such as text or images. You can start from one and use it for many jobs rather than building your own from nothing. Some are released openly so anyone can download and run them, and others are offered by a company through a service you call over the internet. The real choice is whether to reuse a ready-made model or to pay the cost of training one of your own on your own data.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your team needs a tool that summarizes support tickets. Would you train a language model from scratch on your own tickets, or start from an existing general model? Which would you try first, and why?
lessons.teach:
A pre-trained model is a model whose parameters, the numbers inside it that were adjusted during training, have already been set by someone else. Training is the expensive step where a model is shown large amounts of example data and its parameters are nudged until its outputs improve. A foundation model is a large pre-trained model built to be useful across many tasks, so the same base can summarize, answer questions, or classify with only light guidance. Foundation models come from two broad sources. Open-source or openly released pre-trained models publish their model weights, which are the saved parameters, so you can download them and run them on infrastructure you control. You must read the license, though, because it sets what you may do commercially. The other route is training a custom model. You can train from scratch on your own data, or fine-tune, which means continuing training of an existing model on a smaller set of your examples so it learns your domain.

Why does reuse work? A model that has already learned grammar, facts and patterns from a broad body of text gives you a head start, so you need far less of your own data and compute. Training from scratch demands large, curated datasets, specialist skill, and significant compute time, which is why it is usually reserved for cases where no existing model can meet the need.

Worked example: a support team wants ticket summaries. Step one, check whether an existing foundation model handles summarization at acceptable quality. Step two, test it on fifty real tickets and score the outputs. Step three, if quality falls short on company jargon, fine-tune with a few hundred approved summaries. Step four, check the license and data terms before deployment.

Common mistake: assuming an open model is free to use in any way, or that its training data is safe to trust. Licenses differ, and a model can carry biases from the data it learned from.

Consequence: once a custom or self-hosted model is in production, your team owns hosting, scaling, monitoring and updates. That operating cost continues long after training is finished.

questions.prompt: A dental practice wants to sort incoming patient emails into three groups: reschedule, cancel, or new booking. Its team followed these steps. Step 1: they tested an openly released pre-trained model on 40 real emails and scored its answers, reaching 88 percent against a target of 95 percent. Step 2: they fine-tuned that model on 300 emails the staff had already labelled by hand. Step 3: they tested the fine-tuned model on 60 new emails and reached 96 percent. Step 4 is missing. Which step belongs in the blank before the model starts handling real patient emails?
choices: Check the model's license and the practice's data terms, since these decide what the model may legally be used for.
Rename the model so staff can tell it apart from the original release.
Train a new model from scratch on all patient emails so the fine-tuned version is no longer needed.
Skip any further checks, because the model already passed testing on new emails.
questions.why: A license sets what you may do with an openly released model, and passing a quality test does not replace checking those terms before deployment.

questions.prompt: A fintech startup downloads the saved parameters of an openly released model so it can run the model on its own servers. Which description of those downloaded parameters is accurate?
choices: They are the original training dataset, which the startup must keep private and cannot use for any purpose.
They are the licensing contract itself, which the model reads and enforces automatically while it runs.
They are the numbers inside the model that were adjusted during training, and running them on infrastructure you control is what the release allows.
They are a list of example prompts the vendor used for testing, and they do not affect how the model answers.
questions.why: Model weights are the saved parameters adjusted during training, and an open release lets you run them on your own infrastructure, subject to the license.

questions.prompt: A regional newspaper wants a tool that suggests headlines in its house style. It has 2,000 approved headlines and a small budget for compute. Which approach fits best?
choices: Train a new model from scratch on the 2,000 headlines, because a model trained only on the paper's own material will match its style most closely.
Deploy an existing foundation model unchanged and skip testing, because its general language skill is enough for any house style.
Write a fixed list of if-then rules from the headlines and use no model at all, because a rule can never be improved by a prediction.
Fine-tune an existing foundation model on the approved headlines, since the base model already knows language and needs only domain learning.
questions.why: Fine-tuning reuses a model's general language learning and adds the newspaper's style with far less data and compute than training from scratch.

questions.prompt: A team says: We downloaded an open model whose license says it is free, and its training data was collected widely, so it is safe to trust. We will skip our own evaluation and go straight to production. What is the main problem with this reasoning?
choices: Open models cannot be run on a company's own servers, so the team must use a vendor-hosted version instead.
Once the model is in production the team has no ongoing costs, so skipping evaluation saves money with no downside.
The license may restrict some uses, such as commercial deployment, and the model can carry biases from its training data, so it still needs testing on your own cases.
Nothing is wrong, because a free license permits any use and widely collected training data is always safe.
questions.why: Open models come with license limits and can inherit biases from their training data, so the team must check the license and test the model on its own use case before relying on it.

lessons.explainPrompt: A product manager asks why we should not just train our own model for the new feature. Explain to a teammate when reusing a pre-trained foundation model is the better choice, when a custom model is worth its cost, and one limit or tradeoff of each.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would start by reusing a pre-trained foundation model, because it already has broad language ability and we only need to show it our task. That is cheap and fast to test. Training from scratch needs large curated datasets, specialist skills and compute, so it only makes sense when no existing model reaches the quality we need, or when data rules prevent sending data to outside services. The limit of reuse is that we inherit the model's training biases and license terms, and we cannot change its core behavior much. The limit of custom training is cost and ongoing ownership: we must keep the data, retrain as things change, and run and monitor the model ourselves. Fine-tuning is a middle path, but it still needs a good set of approved examples. So I would test the reuse option first and let measured quality and cost decide.
rubricPoints: Defines a foundation model as a large pre-trained model reusable across many tasks
Distinguishes open or released pre-trained models from training or fine-tuning a custom model
States the tradeoff of custom training: data, expertise, compute and ongoing operating cost
Names a limit of reuse, such as license terms or inherited bias

suggested.rationale: The core skill is articulating the reuse-versus-custom tradeoff in your own words, which no listed mission or engine directly practices.

lessons.plain: When a team wants a trained AI model to answer questions or make predictions for a real product, the model has to be running somewhere that other software can reach. That running form is called an endpoint: a web address your application sends a request to and gets an answer back. You have two broad choices. You can use a provider who runs the model and handles the machines, or you can run the model yourself on servers you manage. The first saves effort and upkeep. The second gives more control over the model, the data path, and the cost curve. Choosing well is mostly about who carries the work of keeping it running.
lessons.guessPrompt: A small team has a model that works in a notebook and now needs to answer requests from their app. Would you rather have someone else run the servers and keep the model available, or run them yourselves? What facts would make you change your mind?
lessons.teach:
Definitions first. A managed API service is a model that a provider hosts and operates. You send requests over the network and pay per use or per unit of capacity, and the provider handles the machines, scaling, patching, and uptime of the serving layer. A self-hosted API is a model you package and run yourself, on virtual machines or a container platform you control, exposing an endpoint you designed. Inferencing, the step where a trained model turns new input into an answer, is the work both options perform for you.

Why this is a real decision: every production model carries the same chores. These include capacity planning, health checks, rolling out new model versions, logging, security patches, and responding to alerts. A managed service moves those chores to the provider, so your team spends its time on the product. Self-hosting keeps those chores with you, but it buys control. You choose the exact model build, pin its version, keep traffic inside your network, tune the hardware, and can run models a provider does not offer.

Worked example. A team needs sentiment scores for 2 million support messages a day. Step 1: the managed option charges per request, with no servers to watch. Step 2: the self-hosted option needs a fleet of accelerator machines sized for peak load, mostly idle at night, plus a deployment pipeline. Step 3: the team compares monthly cost and staffing hours, then checks its data rules before choosing.

Common mistake: choosing self-hosting because it feels more professional, then finding the team spends weeks on scaling and patching instead of the feature. The reverse mistake is assuming a managed service removes responsibility. You still own the data you send, the quality of the outputs, monitoring, and the bill.

Consequence in a running system: a self-hosted endpoint that falls over at peak takes the feature down with it, and nobody outside your team can fix it at 3 a.m. A managed endpoint can be limited by the provider's rate quotas, so the application must plan for throttling, retries, and fallbacks. The right choice depends on who carries the operations load and how much control the business needs.

questions.prompt: A logistics firm wants to tag 40,000 delivery-delay emails a week as refund, reroute, or other. Traffic is steady across the week with no quiet night period. The team is weighing a managed API service, where a provider hosts and operates the model, against a self-hosted API, where the firm runs the model on machines it controls. Step 1: the team estimates the weekly volume at 40,000 emails and confirms the load is steady. Step 2 is blank in the team's notes and must be filled in. Step 3: the team compares the monthly cost of each option and the staff hours each would consume. Which completion correctly fills the blank at Step 2?
choices: Step 2: the team assumes that choosing a managed service transfers responsibility for the email content and its outputs to the provider.
Step 2: the team signs a contract guaranteeing the provider will never throttle requests, so no retry logic is needed.
Step 2: the team decides the model must be retrained from scratch before either option can serve any email.
Step 2: the team estimates the peak-hour volume and sizes a self-hosted fleet for it, noting the fleet would sit mostly idle between peaks.
questions.why: Sizing a self-hosted fleet for peak load, and noticing the machines sit mostly idle otherwise, is the capacity-planning step the comparison needs before cost and staffing can be weighed.

questions.prompt: Which description best fits a managed API service?
choices: A model you package and run on machines you control, with an endpoint (the address your application sends requests to) that you designed yourself.
A dashboard that reports model accuracy after the model has been deployed to production.
A process that trains a new model from your own data so that the model can later be run anywhere.
A model that a provider hosts and operates, billed per use or per unit of capacity, with the provider handling the serving layer's machines, scaling, and uptime.
questions.why: A managed API service is defined by the provider hosting and operating the model while you send requests over the network and pay per use or capacity.

questions.prompt: A small insurer processes about 3,000 claim notes a month. It has no staff who patch or scale servers, and its data rules do not restrict where the notes are processed. Which option fits best, and why?
choices: A managed API service, because the volume is low and the team has no operations staff to carry patching and scaling.
A managed API service with no retry or fallback logic, because the provider guarantees uptime and throttling never happens.
A self-hosted endpoint, because self-hosting always costs less than a managed service at any volume.
A self-hosted fleet, because a team that owns its machines cannot be throttled by anyone and that is the deciding factor.
questions.why: Low volume, no operations staff, and no restrictions on data location point toward the managed option, since the provider carries the chores that self-hosting would leave with the team.

questions.prompt: A team uses a managed API service for a chat feature. During a sudden burst of traffic, the provider's rate quota is exceeded, and some users see failed replies. Which change best addresses this failure?
choices: Increase the size of each request so that the provider processes the traffic in fewer, larger calls.
Remove all monitoring, because the provider already watches the endpoint and the application does not need its own alerts.
Switch to self-hosting immediately, because throttling proves the provider is at fault and no application design can prevent it.
Add retries, fallbacks, and handling for throttling in the application, because rate quotas are a known limit of managed endpoints that the application must plan for.
questions.why: Managed endpoints can be limited by provider quotas, so the application itself must plan for throttling with retries and fallbacks rather than assuming the provider absorbs every spike.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would decide between calling a managed model API and hosting the model yourself. Name one limit or tradeoff of each option.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would start with who will run the thing day to day. A managed API means the provider keeps the machines up, handles scaling and patching of the serving layer, and bills per use, so our team can focus on the application. The tradeoffs are that we inherit the provider's model versions and rate quotas, our data leaves our network under their terms, and cost rises with volume. Self-hosting gives us control: we pin the exact model, keep traffic inside our network, and tune hardware for cost at steady high volume. The price is that we own capacity planning, on-call response, security patches, rollouts, and monitoring. So for a new feature with uncertain or spiky volume and no dedicated ops team, I would choose managed. For steady very high volume, strict data residency rules, or a custom model the provider cannot serve, I would look at self-hosting and budget the staffing cost honestly.
rubricPoints: Defines managed API as provider-run and self-hosted as team-run endpoints
Names operations burden (scaling, patching, monitoring, on-call) as the main difference
Gives one limit of managed services, such as rate quotas, data leaving your network, or cost at volume
Gives one tradeoff of self-hosting, such as control over versions and data path versus staffing cost

suggested.rationale: Choosing between managed and self-hosted depends on the scenario's volume, data rules, and staffing, so reasoning through an exam-style situation adds the most.

lessons.plain: An AI/ML pipeline is the chain of steps an AI project moves through: gathering data, preparing it, training a model, putting that model where people or systems can call it, and watching it afterward. AWS offers different managed services for different stages. Some let you build and train your own model, some let you call a model someone else already trained, and some are finished assistants you use directly. This objective is about knowing which tool belongs to which stage, so you can choose one for a real problem instead of guessing from product names.
lessons.guessPrompt: A small firm wants a tool that drafts short replies to customer emails, and it has no history of labeled reply examples to learn from. Would you start by training a custom model from scratch, or by calling an existing foundation model, and which stage of the pipeline would you spend most of your effort on?
lessons.teach:
A pipeline is the ordered set of stages an AI or machine learning project moves through. Data preparation cleans raw information and attaches labels where needed. Training is the process of showing a learning algorithm examples so it adjusts its internal settings; the result is a model. Inferencing means using a trained model on new input to get an output. Monitoring watches the model's behaviour after release, because real inputs drift away from training data over time.

On AWS, the build-your-own path centres on Amazon SageMaker AI, a managed environment for preparing data, training, tuning and deploying custom models, with labeling support, managed training jobs, hosted endpoints and monitoring each sitting at a specific stage. The other path is Amazon Bedrock, which gives managed API access to foundation models, large models pretrained on broad data, from several providers. You skip training; the work moves to choosing a model, writing prompts, grounding answers in your own documents through a knowledge base, and adding guardrails. Amazon Quick is a finished workplace assistant you use rather than build, and Kiro is an AI coding environment that helps engineers write software. Neither is a stage of your model pipeline.

Worked example: a retailer wants product descriptions drafted from supplier spec sheets. Data preparation is light because no custom labels exist. Model choice: a foundation model on Amazon Bedrock. Inferencing: the hosted model is called per request. Monitoring: outputs are checked through guardrails and sampled human review. No training happens at all.

Common mistake: training a custom SageMaker AI model when a hosted foundation model would do, which adds data collection, compute cost and maintenance.

A hosted model's behaviour can change when its provider updates it, so output quality must be monitored in production, not only checked at launch.

questions.prompt: A city transit agency wants the route number pulled from scanned paper complaint forms. It has no labeled examples and does not want a custom model. Its plan so far: (1) Choose a foundation model on Amazon Bedrock and write a prompt that asks for the route number. (2) During inferencing, call the model once per scanned form. (3) Monitoring stage: [missing]. Which completion fits the missing stage?
choices: Nothing is needed, because no training happened, so the model's behaviour stays fixed after launch.
Sample extracted route numbers each month and compare them with human-checked forms, since the hosted model can change when its provider updates it.
Train a custom SageMaker AI model on the forms so the agency can monitor it through its own training runs.
Delete the outputs after launch and rely on the test results from launch day.
questions.why: Monitoring means watching behaviour after release, and a hosted model can change when its provider updates it, so periodic sampled checks against human-verified answers are the right stage step.

questions.prompt: A logistics firm runs a demand-forecast model in production. Every week it compares the model's predictions with actual shipments and checks whether the incoming input patterns have moved away from the data the model was trained on. Which pipeline stage is this?
choices: Training
Inferencing
Monitoring
Data preparation
questions.why: Checking behaviour after release for drift away from training data is the monitoring stage, not preparation, training, or the per-request use of the model.

questions.prompt: A small accounting firm has 12,000 past invoices already sorted by its staff into six custom categories, and it wants a model that learns those exact categories. Which AWS service path fits best?
choices: Amazon Quick, because it is a finished workplace assistant that staff can open each day
Amazon Bedrock with no data, because a foundation model always beats custom training
Kiro, because it helps engineers write the sorting code
Amazon SageMaker AI, because labeled data and custom categories call for a custom trained model
questions.why: Labeled examples of the firm's own categories point to building a custom model with managed training on SageMaker AI, while Quick and Kiro are not pipeline stages and a foundation model cannot learn the firm's private labels without that data.

questions.prompt: A team builds a support-reply drafter on Amazon Bedrock and argues it needs no monitoring after launch because it never trained a model. What is the flaw in that reasoning?
choices: Monitoring only applies to models trained on SageMaker AI, so the team's reasoning is correct
Hosted model behaviour can change when the provider updates the model, so outputs still need checking in production
Guardrails replace monitoring entirely, so no further checks are needed after launch
Monitoring is only needed for training data, which the team does not have, so the team's reasoning is correct
questions.why: Monitoring covers behaviour after release, and a hosted foundation model's outputs can shift when its provider updates it, so skipping training does not remove the need to monitor.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate who is new to AWS how you would map a customer-support triage project onto the AI/ML pipeline stages, naming which AWS service you would use at each stage and one limit or tradeoff of building a custom model versus calling a foundation model.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would split the project into stages first: data preparation, model choice, training if needed, inferencing, and monitoring. If we have thousands of past tickets already labeled by category and need a fixed set of categories with predictable results, I would prepare that labeled data and train a custom classifier on Amazon SageMaker AI, then host it on an endpoint. If we have no labels and only need draft replies, I would call a foundation model through Amazon Bedrock, add a knowledge base over our help articles so answers stay grounded, and apply guardrails. The main tradeoff is that the custom model costs time and data work to build and maintain, but its behaviour is stable and cheap per request, while a hosted foundation model needs no training yet can change when the provider updates it, so we would monitor its outputs either way.
rubricPoints: Breaks the project into pipeline stages such as data preparation, training, inferencing and monitoring
Maps Amazon SageMaker AI to building and hosting custom models and Amazon Bedrock to calling foundation models
Explains that labeled data and a fixed outcome favour a custom model, while no labels favours a foundation model
States a real tradeoff between build effort and stability versus hosted convenience and provider-driven change
Notes that monitoring applies whichever path is chosen

suggested.rationale: This objective is mostly a product map of which AWS service serves which stage, and no listed mission or planned engine practises that directly.

lessons.plain: MLOps stands for machine learning operations. It is the set of habits and tools that keep a model working reliably after someone builds it. Building a model once in a notebook is the easy part. The hard part is running it for months while the data changes, other systems depend on its answers, and you still need to update it safely. MLOps borrows ideas from software operations: record every experiment, automate the steps so they can be rerun, watch the model in production, and replace it when it starts to drift. Think of it as the difference between a recipe that worked once in your kitchen and a repeatable process that feeds a restaurant every night.
lessons.guessPrompt: A fraud-scoring model was 94 percent accurate when a data scientist tested it last spring, but this autumn it is missing more fraud than before. Before reading on, what would you check first, and what would you change so this kind of decline gets noticed early next time?
lessons.teach:
MLOps means machine learning operations: the practices that let a model run in production the way any dependable service does. Its main parts are experimentation, repeatable processes, scalable systems, monitoring and retraining. An experiment is one training attempt with its inputs, settings and results recorded, so you can later say which run produced which model. A repeatable process is a pipeline, meaning the steps from raw data to a deployed model written down and automated so anyone can rerun them. Technical debt is the cost of shortcuts, such as a notebook nobody can rerun or a feature calculated by hand, which slows every later change. Production readiness asks whether the model handles real traffic, has a rollback path, and has someone watching it.

Why this matters: a model's quality depends on data that keeps changing, so the job is never finished at deployment. Monitoring compares live inputs and outcomes against what the model saw during training. Data drift means the inputs have shifted. Concept drift means the relationship between inputs and the correct answer has shifted. Retraining fits a new model on fresh data, and a model registry keeps each version so you can roll back.

Worked example: a fraud model was trained in spring on card sizes and merchant types. By autumn a new payment method changes typical amounts. Step 1: monitoring shows the average transaction amount has moved well outside the training range. Step 2: the team checks labelled recent cases and finds precision has dropped from 0.9 to 0.6. Step 3: they retrain the pipeline on recent data, record the run, compare it with the live model on a holdout set, and promote the new version only if it wins.

Common mistake: treating the accuracy reported on launch day as the model's permanent quality. The consequence is that the service keeps returning confident scores, logs show no errors, and losses grow quietly until someone checks the outcomes.

A model that is not monitored and retrained is a model whose quality is unknown.

questions.prompt: A parcel company trained a model in March to flag parcels likely to arrive late. It uses the sorting depot, route length and weather. In September the company opens a new depot that uses different sorting machines, so parcel volumes and sorting times change sharply. Step 1: monitoring shows the share of parcels passing through the new depot is far outside anything in the training data. Step 2: the team checks labelled recent deliveries and finds precision (the share of flagged parcels that really were late) has dropped from 0.85 to 0.55. Step 3: [missing]. Step 4: the new version is promoted to live only if it beats the current live model on a holdout set (a set of recent cases kept back and not used for training).
choices: Write a note that the March accuracy still applies, since the model was correct when it was launched.
Retrain the pipeline on recent delivery data and record the run so it can be traced later.
Raise the flagging threshold so fewer parcels are flagged, and leave the model unchanged.
Delete the old model from the registry so only one version remains, which keeps the system simple.
questions.why: Step 3 is the retraining: a new version is fitted on fresh data via the repeatable pipeline and recorded, which is what allows the comparison in step 4.

questions.prompt: A clinic's no-show predictor was trained on appointment history. The clinic then launches a new booking app that records appointment times in a different format, so the inputs look different even though patients behave the same way. Which description best fits this change?
choices: Concept drift, because the relationship between inputs and no-shows has changed.
Data drift, because the inputs the model receives have shifted from what it saw in training.
Technical debt, because the booking app was built with shortcuts.
A rollback failure, because the old model cannot be restored.
questions.why: The inputs have shifted while the underlying link between inputs and no-shows is unchanged, which is data drift rather than concept drift.

questions.prompt: A logistics team's cost-forecast model was built in a notebook. A key feature, fuel surcharge, is calculated by an analyst copying numbers into a spreadsheet each week. Nobody else can rerun the steps, and each new model change takes longer. What best describes this situation?
choices: Concept drift, because the surcharge changes over time.
Production readiness, because the model has a working forecast.
A scalable system, because the spreadsheet handles large volumes.
Technical debt, because the hand-made feature and unrepeatable notebook slow down every later change.
questions.why: Shortcuts such as a hand-calculated feature and a notebook nobody can rerun are the textbook form of technical debt, and they slow later work.

questions.prompt: A call-centre routing model is about to go live. It has passed a load test with realistic traffic and the team has kept the previous version so they can switch back. However, no one has been assigned to watch its outputs after launch. Which statement about production readiness is correct?
choices: The model is not yet ready, because it needs a new training run before any launch.
The model is ready, because accuracy measured at launch stays valid indefinitely.
The model is ready, because a load test and a rollback path are the only requirements.
The model is not yet ready, because someone must be watching it, and that gap is a readiness problem.
questions.why: Production readiness asks whether the model handles real traffic, has a rollback path and has someone watching it, so a missing monitor owner means it is not yet ready.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate who has only built models in a notebook why a model that scored well at launch still needs MLOps work afterwards. Name one limit or tradeoff of retraining on a fixed schedule compared with retraining when monitoring raises an alert.
lessons.modelAnswer: A launch score only describes the data the model was tested on at one moment. After launch, the live data keeps changing, so the model can get worse while the code and infrastructure look healthy. MLOps is the set of practices that catches this: every training run is recorded so we know what produced the live model, the training steps are a pipeline anyone can rerun, and monitoring compares live inputs and labelled outcomes against training data. Retraining on a fixed schedule is simple and predictable, but it can waste effort when nothing has changed and can still be late when something suddenly shifts. Retraining on an alert reacts to real change, but it depends on monitoring being accurate and on enough labelled outcomes arriving to judge quality. Before a new model replaces the old one, it should be compared on a holdout set and be ready to roll back.
rubricPoints: A launch score reflects only the data at test time, so quality can decline as live data changes.
Experiments and pipelines make training runs recorded and repeatable.
Monitoring must watch inputs and outcomes to detect data or concept drift.
Scheduled retraining is predictable but may be wasteful or late; alert-driven retraining depends on monitoring quality.
A new model should be compared against the current one and kept rollback-ready before promotion.

suggested.rationale: The core skill is explaining why a launched model degrades and which operational habits prevent it, which is best practised by articulating it to a teammate.

lessons.plain: A model can be scored on how often its guesses are right, but the business cares about cost, money made, and whether customers are happy. This lesson is about telling those two kinds of score apart and knowing which one to chase. Imagine a spam filter that is 99 percent accurate but still hides a real customer's order confirmation. Technical scores tell you how a model behaves on test data. Business scores tell you whether the running system is worth keeping. A good engineer watches both and does not mistake a high score for a successful product.
lessons.guessPrompt: A fraud model flags payments as fraud. Of its flags, 99 percent are real fraud, but it misses half of all the fraud that actually happens. Which number would you check first to decide whether the model helps the business, and why?
lessons.teach:
Accuracy is the share of all predictions that are correct. Precision is, of the cases the model flagged as positive, the share that really were positive. Recall is, of all the real positive cases, the share the model found. F1 is one number that combines precision and recall, and it drops sharply when either one is weak. Business metrics sit outside the model: cost per user is what the running system costs divided by active users, development cost is the money and time spent building it, ROI (return on investment) is the gain minus the cost, divided by the cost, and customer feedback is what people report about the result. Why the split matters: the model metrics come from a labelled test set, so they describe behaviour in a lab, while business metrics describe whether anyone benefits after deployment.

Worked example. Suppose a fraud model reviews 10,000 payments, 100 of which are truly fraud. It flags 70 payments, 60 of them real fraud. Step one, accuracy: 9,950 of 10,000 answers are right, so 99.5 percent. Step two, precision: 60 of 70 flags are real, so about 85.7 percent. Step three, recall: 60 of 100 frauds were caught, so 60 percent. Step four, F1: 2 times 0.857 times 0.6, divided by the sum 1.457, gives about 70.6 percent. Step five, money: each missed fraud costs 200, so 40 misses cost 8,000, and each wrong flag costs 20 in support time, so 10 wrong flags cost 200.

Common mistake: reporting the 99.5 percent accuracy as the success story. Most payments are legitimate, so a model that never flags anything would score almost as well. Consequence in a running system: a fraud model tuned for accuracy looks healthy on the dashboard while the 40 missed frauds drain money, and if precision drops, support queues and customer complaints grow, pushing cost per user and ROI the wrong way.

Model metrics tell you whether the predictions are good; business metrics tell you whether the predictions are worth running.

questions.prompt: A parcel-scanning model checks 2,000 parcels, 50 of which are truly damaged, and flags 80 parcels, 40 of them truly damaged. Steps one to three are done: accuracy is 97.5 percent, precision is 50 percent, and recall is 80 percent. The missing step four is to compute F1 from the precision and recall values. Which result is correct for F1?
choices: 97.5 percent, the same as accuracy
61.5 percent, from 2 times precision times recall divided by their sum
80.0 percent, which is equal to recall alone
65.0 percent, the simple average of precision and recall
questions.why: F1 combines precision and recall as 2 times precision times recall divided by their sum, which gives 0.8 divided by 1.3, about 61.5 percent, and it stays low when either input is weak.

questions.prompt: A help-desk assistant costs 4,200 dollars a month to run and has 1,400 active users. What is its cost per user?
choices: 2.00 dollars per user
4.20 dollars per user
3.00 dollars per user
5,600 dollars per user
questions.why: Cost per user is the running cost divided by active users, so 4,200 divided by 1,400 is 3 dollars per user.

questions.prompt: A subscription service's churn model is 97 percent accurate on a test set where only 3 percent of customers cancel. Which statement best describes what that accuracy tells you?
choices: The model is catching most of the customers who will cancel
A model that never predicts cancellation would also score about 97 percent, so accuracy alone does not show it works
The high accuracy guarantees the model will raise ROI
The model's precision is 97 percent
questions.why: When positives are rare, a model that always predicts the majority class scores almost as well on accuracy, so accuracy alone cannot show the model finds the real cancellations.

questions.prompt: A retention email campaign costs 5,000 dollars and brings in 8,000 dollars of extra revenue. What is its ROI?
choices: 8,000 percent
60 percent
3,000 percent
160 percent
questions.why: ROI is the gain minus the cost, divided by the cost, so (8,000 minus 5,000) divided by 5,000 equals 0.6, or 60 percent.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate why a model with 99 percent accuracy on a rare-event problem can still be a bad business decision, and name one limit of the metric you would use instead.
lessons.modelAnswer: Accuracy counts every correct answer equally, and on a rare-event problem like fraud most cases are the easy negative ones. A model that rarely flags anything can reach 99 percent accuracy while missing most of the events that cost money. So I would look at recall, which tells us what share of the real fraud we caught, and precision, which tells us how many flags were real. Those two together show the trade-off. The limit of recall is that it says nothing about how many legitimate customers we annoyed, so I would pair it with precision and a cost estimate per missed case and per false alarm before deciding whether the model earns its running cost.
rubricPoints: Explains that accuracy can look high simply because the common class dominates
Defines recall and precision in plain words
Names a limit of the chosen metric, such as ignoring false alarms or missed-case cost
Connects the technical score to a business cost or benefit

suggested.rationale: Deciding which score matters for a business goal is a judgment call that is best practised by reasoning through a realistic scenario.

lessons.plain: Computers that generate text do not read letters and words the way you do. They break input into small pieces called tokens, which might be a whole short word, part of a longer word, or a punctuation mark. Each piece is counted, and that count decides how much the system can handle in one request and how much you pay. Chunking means cutting long documents into smaller pieces so they fit and can be searched. An embedding turns a piece of text into a list of numbers that captures its meaning, so texts with similar meaning get similar lists. Those lists are called vectors. Together these ideas let an application find the right passage first, then ask a model to answer using only that passage.
lessons.guessPrompt: Suppose a model charges you for every piece of text it reads, and you paste a 50-page manual into a chat each time someone asks a question. What do you think happens to the cost, and to the answer quality, if you paste only the one relevant section instead?
lessons.teach:
A token is the unit a language model reads and writes. It is usually a fragment of a word, a whole short word, or a punctuation mark, produced by a fixed splitting rule called a tokenizer. Tokens matter for two reasons. First, a model has a context window, the maximum number of tokens it can handle in one request, counting both what you send and what it replies. Second, most generative AI services bill per token, input and output separately, so every extra token has a price and adds time to the response.

Chunking means splitting long material into smaller pieces, such as paragraphs of a few hundred tokens, so each piece fits comfortably and can be searched on its own. An embedding is a list of numbers, also called a vector, produced by an embedding model that represents the meaning of a piece of text. Texts with similar meaning produce vectors that point in similar directions, so the system can compare them by a measure of closeness called similarity.

Worked example: a 1,000-word manual is roughly 1,300 tokens. Step 1, split it into chunks of about 300 tokens. Step 2, embed each chunk once and store the vectors. Step 3, when a user asks a question, embed the question. Step 4, find the three stored vectors closest to it. Step 5, send only those three chunks and the question to the model, roughly 900 tokens plus the question, instead of the full 1,300 tokens on every query.

The common mistake is treating a word as a token, using chunks so large they dilute meaning, or so small they lose context. Another is comparing vectors produced by two different embedding models, since their numbers are not comparable. In a running system, a request that exceeds the context window fails or gets cut off, and a design that sends whole documents multiplies the bill with every user question.

Chunking and embeddings let an application send the model only what it needs, so token count is a design decision, not just a line on an invoice.

questions.prompt: A support team at a regional utility has a 6,000-token billing FAQ. They split it into 15 chunks of about 400 tokens each, embed each chunk once, and store the vectors. When a customer asks a question, they embed the question and find the 4 stored vectors closest to it. They then send those 4 chunks plus the question to the model, about 1,600 tokens plus the question. One step is missing from their plan: before they can find the closest vectors, they must ______.
choices: Embed the customer's question using the same embedding model that produced the stored chunk vectors
Store the customer's question as a new chunk so future searches can find it
Send the full 6,000-token FAQ with the question so the model cannot miss any relevant text
Count the question's characters and divide by four to estimate its token count before splitting it
questions.why: The question must be turned into a vector by the same embedding model used for the stored chunks, because vectors from different models cannot be compared for closeness.

questions.prompt: Which description best defines a token in a language model?
choices: A fragment of a word, a whole short word, or a punctuation mark, produced by the tokenizer's fixed splitting rule
A numeric vector that records how similar two sentences are in meaning
