Always one complete English word, separated from its neighbours by a space character
A fixed block of 100 characters that the user chooses when sending a request to the model
questions.why: A token is the unit the model reads and writes, and the tokenizer produces it as a word fragment, short word, or punctuation mark rather than always a whole word.

questions.prompt: A legal-research app sends a 40,000-token case file with every question and is billed per input token. Which change most directly reduces cost while keeping the relevant text available to the model?
choices: Remove all punctuation from the case file before sending it, since punctuation adds extra tokens to every request
Re-embed the entire case file on every question so that the search results are always as fresh as possible
Raise the model's output limit so that its answers become longer and more complete for the lawyers
Split the case file into chunks, embed each chunk once, and send only the closest matching chunks with each question
questions.why: Sending only the closest chunks reduces the input tokens billed per request, whereas the other options either increase output, rely on a misconception about punctuation, or add embedding work without reducing what is sent to the model.

questions.prompt: A team stores vectors from embedding model A and vectors from embedding model B in the same index. They then embed a new query with model A and compare it against every stored vector, including those produced by model B. What is the main risk of this design?
choices: The index will run out of storage space sooner than planned because each vector is stored twice across the two models
The query will grow too large to fit inside the context window, so the model will cut off the answer part way through
Every request will be billed twice for input tokens, once for each embedding model that the index happens to contain
The similarity scores are not meaningful for the model B vectors, because vectors from different embedding models are not comparable
questions.why: Vectors from two different embedding models are produced on different scales and meanings, so their closeness scores cannot be compared, which makes the search results unreliable.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate, in your own words, why a team would chunk and embed its documents instead of pasting whole documents into every model request, and name one limit or tradeoff of this approach.
lessons.modelAnswer: Pasting whole documents into every request costs a lot, because the model charges per token and every question re-sends the same text. It also risks hitting the context window, so the request fails or gets cut off. Chunking splits the documents into smaller pieces, and an embedding model turns each piece into a vector that captures its meaning. When a question comes in, we embed it too and pull back only the closest chunks, so the model sees a short, relevant context. The tradeoff is retrieval quality: if the search misses the right chunk, the model answers without the facts it needs, and a chunk boundary can split a sentence or idea in half. We also have to keep the vectors in sync when documents change, and we must use the same embedding model for both storing and querying.
rubricPoints: Explains that cost and context limits are driven by token count, so sending only relevant chunks reduces both.
Describes chunking and embeddings as turning text into searchable vectors that capture meaning.
Names a real limit, such as missed retrieval or chunks that split ideas.
Notes that the same embedding model must be used for storing and querying.

suggested.rationale: An exam-style scenario asking which design fits a document question app and why it fails under long documents adds the most reasoning practice for this objective.

lessons.plain: Prompt engineering is the practice of designing the text you send to a generative AI model so that the answer you get is useful, consistent, and checkable. The word prompt means the input you give the model: an instruction, some background, maybe examples. Treating it as a discipline means you write prompts deliberately, test them against real cases, change one thing at a time, and measure the results, rather than hunting for a magic phrase that happens to work once. Think of it like writing a clear work order for a capable but literal new colleague who has never seen your system.
lessons.guessPrompt: Suppose you ask a chatbot to summarise a support ticket and it sometimes returns a paragraph, sometimes a bulleted list, and sometimes invents a customer name. Without any teaching, what would you change in the request first, and why do you think that would help?
lessons.teach: A prompt is everything you send to a foundation model in one request: the instruction, any background material, examples of the output you want, and the question itself. A foundation model is a large model trained on broad data that can be pointed at many tasks. A generative model produces new content such as text. A token is a small chunk of text, roughly a word or part of one, and models read and write in tokens. Prompt engineering is the design work of shaping that input so the output is more predictable. It works because the model continues the text it is given, guided by patterns it learned from training. Vague input leaves many continuations open, so the output varies. A disciplined prompt usually states the task, supplies the facts the model should rely on, shows one or two examples of the desired format (this is called few-shot prompting, meaning you give a few worked examples), sets explicit constraints such as 'use only the ticket text' or 'reply in one sentence', and says what to do when information is missing. Worked example: your goal is a one-line summary of a ticket. Step 1: draft 'Summarise this ticket.' Step 2: add 'Use only the ticket below. Reply with one sentence under 25 words. If the customer name is absent, write unknown.' Step 3: add one example ticket and its correct summary. Step 4: run both versions on twenty real tickets and count how many outputs have the right shape and no invented names. The discipline lives in step 4: you change one element, re-test, and keep what measurably improves. Common mistake: treating a prompt that worked once as proven. Models are nondeterministic, meaning the same input can produce different outputs on different runs, so a single good answer proves little. Consequence: prompts also cost money. Every token in the prompt, including long pasted documents and examples, is billed under token-based pricing and adds response time, so a bloated prompt makes a system slower and more expensive. A prompt also cannot give the model facts it was never given; supplying those is a separate context design problem, covered elsewhere.

questions.prompt: A hotel chain wants a prompt that turns one guest review into a single neutral sentence under 20 words. The team has done three steps. Step 1: they wrote 'Summarise this review.' Step 2: they changed it to 'Use only the review text below. Reply with one sentence under 20 words. If the room number is not mentioned, write none.' Step 3: they added one sample review and its correct one-sentence summary. Their plan has a fourth step that is missing. That step is what tells them whether the changes actually helped. Which step belongs there?
choices: Ship the version with the sample review, since the sample makes the output look clearly better.
Add the full hotel policy manual to the prompt so the model knows every room type.
Run both prompt versions on a fixed set of real reviews, count outputs with the right shape and no invented details, and keep only the change that measurably improves the count.
Switch to a larger model and skip testing, since bigger models do not need prompt changes.
questions.why: The missing step is the re-test: the team must run each version on the same real reviews, count results, and keep only changes that measurably help, because a single good output proves little.

questions.prompt: What does the word 'prompt' refer to in a single request to a foundation model?
choices: The model's training data, which is attached to every request automatically by the provider.
Only the output format, since the question is implied by the instruction and does not need to be written out.
Only the instruction, because examples and background are stored by the model during training and not sent again.
Everything sent in one request: the instruction, any background material, examples of the wanted output, and the question itself.
questions.why: A prompt is defined as everything you send in one request, which includes the instruction, background, examples, and the question.

questions.prompt: A support team tests a new prompt on one ticket, gets a clean summary, and approves it for a tool that will process 50,000 tickets a day. What is the main flaw in this decision?
choices: Models are nondeterministic, so one good output is weak evidence that the prompt works across repeated runs and varied tickets.
The team should have set a larger token limit before running any test at all.
The summary is probably too short for support staff to read quickly, so the length should be increased first.
The model will always produce the same output for the same ticket, so one good run is enough evidence.
questions.why: Because the same input can produce different outputs on different runs, a single good result does not show the prompt works reliably across many tickets.

questions.prompt: A team pastes a 30-page policy document into every request so the model can answer one-line questions. Which consequence should they expect?
choices: The model stores the policy after the first call, so every later call is free of charge.
Only the output tokens are billed, so the pasted policy adds no cost to each call.
Every token in the prompt is billed and adds response time, so each call becomes slower and more expensive.
Pasted text is free to send but reduces how many examples can fit, so cost is unaffected.
questions.why: Each prompt token is billed under token-based pricing and adds to response time, so a bloated prompt makes the system slower and costlier on every request.

lessons.explainPrompt: A teammate says prompt engineering is just finding the right magic words. Explain to them, in your own words, what a disciplined prompt approach involves, and name one limit that better prompts alone cannot fix.
lessons.modelAnswer: I'd tell them it's closer to writing a specification than hunting for magic words. A disciplined approach states the task clearly, gives the model the material it should rely on, includes a couple of examples of the output format, and sets explicit rules such as what to do when information is missing. Then you test that prompt against a set of real cases, change one thing at a time, and keep changes only when the measured results improve, because the model is nondeterministic and a single good answer proves nothing. The main limit is that a prompt cannot supply knowledge the model was never given. If the answer depends on your company's current policies, the prompt needs that material delivered as context, or the system needs a retrieval step; wording alone won't make the model know it. Long prompts also cost tokens and time, so every addition has to earn its place.
rubricPoints: Describes prompt engineering as a repeatable design and testing process, not a single trick phrase
Names concrete prompt elements such as task, context, examples, and output constraints
Explains that outputs are nondeterministic, so prompts must be tested across many cases
States a real limit, such as prompts being unable to add facts the model lacks, or token cost of long prompts

suggested.rationale: The core skill here is articulating a design discipline and its limits in your own words, which an explanation exercise tests directly.

lessons.plain: A foundation model is a large AI model trained once on very broad data, so it can be reused for many tasks such as writing, summarizing, answering questions, or describing a picture. Most text foundation models are transformers, a design that reads a whole passage at once and learns which words matter to which other words. Multi-modal models handle more than one kind of input, such as text and images together. Diffusion models make images or audio by starting from random noise and gradually cleaning it up until it matches a description. Think of a foundation model as a general-purpose engine that you adapt to a job, rather than a tool built for one job.
lessons.guessPrompt: Why do you think a model trained on public internet text would struggle to answer a question about your company's internal handbook, even if it writes very fluently?
lessons.teach:
A foundation model is a large model trained once on very broad data, so that it can then be adapted to many tasks rather than built for one. Most text foundation models are large language models (LLMs), and most of those are built on the transformer, a neural network design that uses attention: for each piece of input, the model learns how strongly every other piece should influence it. Transformers read a whole passage at once rather than strictly word by word, which is a large part of why they scale well. Text is split into tokens, chunks that are often parts of words, and the core training task is next-token prediction: given the tokens so far, guess the next one. Doing this across enormous data forces the model to pick up grammar, facts, and reasoning patterns as a side effect. A multi-modal model accepts or produces more than one kind of data, such as text plus images. A diffusion model generates images by learning to reverse a process that adds noise to pictures; at generation time it starts from pure noise and removes it step by step, steered by your prompt.

Worked example: the prompt is 'The cat sat on the'. The model splits it into tokens, attention links 'cat' and 'sat' to shape the context, and it outputs a probability for each possible next token, say 'mat' at 0.6 and 'sofa' at 0.2. It picks 'mat', appends it, and repeats the whole process for the next token until the reply ends.

Common mistake: treating fluent output as checked fact. The model optimises for plausible continuation, not truth, so it can state invented details with confident wording. This is called hallucination.

Consequence: a customer-support assistant that answers from general training alone may invent a refund policy your company does not have. The fix is to supply the real policy in the input, not to trust the model's memory. The model generates one plausible token at a time, so its quality depends on what it is given as much as on what it was trained on.

questions.prompt: A seed company's assistant receives the prompt 'Plant the tulip bulb in the'. Step 1: the prompt is split into tokens. Step 2: attention links 'tulip' and 'bulb' to set the context. Step 3: the model assigns probabilities to candidate next tokens: 'soil' at 0.7, 'pot' at 0.2, 'sky' at 0.01. It picks 'soil' and appends it to the text. Step 4 is missing. Which action completes the process for the rest of the reply?
choices: It checks 'soil' against a catalogue of tulip facts before appending it.
It re-runs the next-token prediction with 'soil' included in the input, choosing the next token each time, until the reply ends.
It discards 'pot' and 'sky' and retrains the model on the prompt before continuing.
It returns 'soil' as the whole answer and stops, because the reply is now complete.
questions.why: The model generates text one token at a time, so after each token is appended it repeats the prediction on the extended input until the reply finishes.

questions.prompt: A design studio asks an image model for a poster. Which description best matches how a diffusion model produces the image?
choices: It starts from random noise and removes it step by step, with the prompt steering each step.
It reads the prompt word by word from left to right and paints each region in that order.
It assembles the poster by copying the closest stored photo that matches the prompt's keywords.
It searches a large catalogue of designs and blends the top three into a single image.
questions.why: A diffusion model is described as starting from pure noise and removing it step by step, guided by the prompt, rather than copying, reading in order, or searching.

questions.prompt: A law firm feeds an LLM only its question, with no contract text in the input. The model gives a confident clause number and wording that does not exist in any of the firm's contracts. What best explains this?
choices: The model optimises for plausible continuation rather than checked fact, so it can invent details, and the fix is to supply the real text in the input.
The model searched the firm's contracts, misread them, and reported the wrong clause with confidence.
The transformer's attention was too weak to understand the question, so it fell back on a default answer.
The fluent wording shows the model checked its answer against the contracts before replying.
questions.why: The text explains that the model optimises for plausible output rather than truth, so invented details can sound confident, and that supplying the real source in the input is the remedy.

questions.prompt: A team is told that a language model reads its input as tokens. A staff member asks how a long, rare word such as 'ultrasonography' is handled. Which answer is correct?
choices: It is always exactly one token, because every word is one token.
It is treated as one full sentence token, because tokens always match whole sentences.
It is always one token per character, so the word becomes many tokens of one letter each.
It may be split into several smaller chunks, each of which is a token.
questions.why: The text says tokens are chunks that are often parts of words, so a long or rare word may be split into several tokens rather than being one token per word.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate, in your own words, how a large language model produces a reply, and name one limit that follows from how it was trained.
lessons.modelAnswer: A large language model is a transformer trained to predict the next token from the text before it. It breaks the prompt into tokens, uses attention to work out which earlier tokens matter for each position, scores every possible next token, picks one, appends it, and repeats until the reply is finished. The main limit follows from that training objective: the model is rewarded for plausible continuation, not for being true. So it can produce confident wrong answers, called hallucinations, especially about facts outside its training data or about private information it has never seen. For a feature that needs accurate answers about our own documents, I would supply the relevant source text in the request and treat the output as a draft that needs checking, rather than trusting the model's memory.
rubricPoints: Explains the transformer's attention and next-token prediction in plain words
Describes generation as repeated one-token-at-a-time choice from probabilities
Names hallucination or inaccuracy as a limit that follows from the training objective
Suggests supplying trusted source text or checking output rather than trusting memory

suggested.rationale: The core skill is explaining how these models work and where they fail to a teammate, which is best practised by articulating it back.

lessons.plain: A generative AI use case is a specific job you point a generative model at, such as drafting a summary, answering a customer, or making a picture. The jobs in this lesson are making images, video and audio; summarizing long text; running assistants; translating; writing code; handling customer service chats; searching by meaning; and suggesting items a person might like. Each job has a different input and output shape, and each has a typical way it goes wrong. Knowing the shape helps you decide whether a generative model fits the job at all, and what to check before trusting its answer.
lessons.guessPrompt: A company wants an AI to read 300 support tickets a day and write a one-paragraph summary of each for a manager. Which part of that job do you think is most likely to go wrong, and why?
lessons.teach:
A use case is the job you ask a generative model to do. Generative AI means models that produce new content, such as text, images, audio or code, based on patterns learned from large amounts of example data. A foundation model is a large model trained once on broad data and then used for many different jobs. The model reads its input as tokens, which are small pieces of text or media that it processes one at a time. The number of tokens going in and coming out largely sets the cost and speed of a job.

Each use case maps to a common input and output. Summarization takes long text and returns shorter text, so the risk is leaving out facts or inventing new ones. Translation takes text in one language and returns it in another. Code generation returns source code that must be run and tested before anyone relies on it. Image, video and audio generation take a description and return media. Search and recommendation often use embeddings, which are numeric representations of meaning, to find or rank items, and a generative model may only write the final answer on top. Assistants and customer service chat handle back-and-forth messages, usually with company information supplied when the question is asked.

Worked example: a support team wants a summary of a 2,000-token chat transcript. Step 1: the transcript goes in as input tokens. Step 2: the model produces a summary of about 150 output tokens. Step 3: the team pays for both input and output tokens, and the reply takes longer as the output grows. Step 4: a person checks that the refund amount in the summary matches the transcript.

Common mistake: treating the output as a finished fact because it reads fluently. Generative models can produce confident but wrong content, which is called hallucination, and the same prompt can produce different wording on different runs.

In a running system, a customer service bot that answers from memory without checking current company policy can promise refunds that do not exist. The design therefore needs the company's own documents supplied to the model at question time and a route to a human agent.

questions.prompt: A regional hospital's communications team uses a model to translate a 900-token patient leaflet from English into Spanish. Step 1: the 900 English tokens go in as input. Step 2: the model returns a Spanish version of about 1,050 output tokens. Step 3: [missing]. Step 4: the team is billed for the 1,950 tokens of input and output together, and the reply takes longer because 1,050 tokens were generated.
choices: The team asks the model to shorten the Spanish output so the job costs less, since translation adds no cost.
The Spanish text is printed immediately because fluent wording in a translation is reliable.
A bilingual staff member checks that drug names and dosage figures came through the translation unchanged.
The leaflet is sent back through the model a second time to be translated into French for comparison.
questions.why: Translation can silently alter facts such as drug names and dosages, so a person who reads both languages must verify them before the text is relied on.

questions.prompt: In generative AI, what is a token?
choices: A small piece of text or media that the model processes one piece at a time.
A numeric list that represents the meaning of a sentence for ranking search results.
A complete finished document the model stores and later retrieves by its name.
A fixed monthly coupon that unlocks a model for a single cloud account.
questions.why: A token is a small piece of text or media that a model reads and processes one at a time, and the number of tokens largely sets cost and speed.

questions.prompt: A music streaming app wants a Songs you may like list with a short written blurb for each pick. Which design is most sound?
choices: Have a generative model invent a fresh set of songs for each listener and present them as the recommendations, since that avoids the catalogue entirely.
Put the complete listening history for every user into one prompt and let the model pick songs from memory each time, without any search step at all.
Match listener and song embeddings to rank candidates, then have a generative model write the blurb for the top picks.
Let a generative model rank the whole catalogue alone, because it has already learned the popularity of every song and needs no separate lookup.
questions.why: Embeddings find and rank real candidates from the catalogue, and the generative model is only used to write the final text on top of that ranking.

questions.prompt: An airline's chatbot answers baggage fee questions from what the model learned during training, with no company documents supplied at question time. Which fix best addresses the risk?
choices: Increase the output length so every answer includes more background on fees.
Supply current fee policy documents with each question and route unclear cases to a human agent.
Ask the model to add a disclaimer saying it might be wrong, then keep answering from what it remembers about fees and policies.
Raise the temperature setting so the model varies its wording and sounds less certain.
questions.why: Answering from memory can produce outdated or invented policy, so the current documents must be supplied at question time and a human route must exist for cases the documents do not settle.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate why a customer service chatbot and a product recommendation feature can both use generative AI but need very different checks before launch. Name one limit or tradeoff for each.
lessons.modelAnswer: Both features use a generative model, but they fail in different ways. A customer service chatbot writes free-form answers, so its main risk is a confident wrong statement, such as an invented refund policy. Before launch we would test it against real questions, supply it with the current policy documents, and make sure a human can take over. Its limit is that it can only be as accurate as the documents it is given, and each conversation costs tokens. A recommendation feature mostly ranks items that already exist in our catalogue. Its main risk is poor suggestions or bias toward popular items, so we would measure click-through and check for odd patterns. Its limit is that it needs enough interaction data to work well, and new products have little history. The checks differ because one produces open-ended text and the other mostly chooses from a known list.
rubricPoints: Chatbot risk is confident but wrong free-form answers, such as invented policy.
Chatbot checks include grounding in current documents and a human fallback.
Recommendation risk is poor or biased suggestions, checked with usage measures.
Recommendation limit includes weak results for new items with little data.

suggested.rationale: This objective is a catalogue of use cases that no current mission or planned engine directly exercises, so reading and recall fit best.

lessons.plain: Building a foundation model is a long chain of steps, not a single button press. First you choose and clean the data the model will learn from. Then you pick a model design and train it on a huge pile of general text or images so it learns broad patterns; that first big run is pre-training. Optionally you train it further on a smaller set of your own examples to specialise it, which is fine-tuning. Next you test it against measurements, put it into service where applications can reach it, and gather feedback from real use that feeds into the next round. Knowing where each step sits tells you who controls what, and where your problems will come from.
lessons.guessPrompt: A company wants a chatbot that answers questions about its own internal HR policies. Before any training happens, which lifecycle stage do you expect needs the most care, and why?
lessons.teach:
The foundation-model lifecycle is the sequence of stages a large generative model goes through, from raw material to a running service and back again. A foundation model is a large model trained on broad data so it can be adapted to many tasks. The stages are: data selection (choosing and cleaning the material the model learns from), model selection (choosing a model design, and whether to build one or reuse an existing one), pre-training (the first, very large training run on general data, which teaches broad language or image patterns), fine-tuning (a smaller extra training run on your own labelled examples to shape behaviour for one task), evaluation (measuring output quality against defined tests), deployment (making the model reachable by an application, with capacity and access controls), and feedback (collecting real-world results and errors to guide the next round).

Why it works: each stage narrows what the model does. Late changes are cheap and early changes are expensive. Pre-training takes large compute and data budgets, so most teams start from a pre-trained model and work on fine-tuning, evaluation and deployment.

Worked example: a team wants short summaries of support tickets. Data selection: they pull 2,000 past tickets and strip personal details. Model selection: they pick a pre-trained model that summarises English well and fits their cost limit. Fine-tuning: they train it on 1,000 ticket and summary pairs written by agents. Evaluation: they score 200 held-back tickets for accuracy and missing facts. Deployment: they release it inside the ticket tool with rate limits. Feedback: agents rate summaries, and low-rated cases join the next training set.

Common mistake: treating evaluation as a one-time gate. Quality can drift as inputs change, so the same test set must be rerun after every change.

Consequence: if training data holds sensitive or outdated records, no later stage removes them, so the model keeps producing them in production. The lifecycle does not really end; each release should feed its results back into data selection.

questions.prompt:
A regional bank wants an internal assistant that drafts reply templates for branch staff. Each stage is shown below, with one stage left for you to fill in.

Data selection: they gather 3,000 approved reply templates and remove customer account numbers and names.
Model selection: they reuse an existing pre-trained model rather than building one, because training from nothing is too costly for them.
Fine-tuning: they train that model on 600 draft-and-approved-reply pairs written by senior staff.
MISSING STAGE: ?
Deployment: they release the model behind a staff login with a cap on requests per hour.
Feedback: staff rate each draft, and low-rated drafts go into the next training set.

Which choice correctly fills the missing stage?
choices: Delete the account numbers from the model after deployment so that it forgets any it saw during training.
Pre-train a new model from scratch on the 3,000 templates so it learns bank language before anything else happens.
Skip testing and rely on staff ratings after launch, since those already reveal quality problems.
Score the fine-tuned model on 120 held-back drafts against defined accuracy and compliance checks before release.
questions.why: Evaluation, measuring output quality against defined tests on held-back examples, belongs between fine-tuning and deployment, and the other three choices either repeat pre-training, skip evaluation, or wrongly assume a model can unlearn data after training.

questions.prompt: A small insurance firm receives a model that its vendor says has already been trained on broad general text. The firm plans to train it further on 500 of its own labelled claim letters so it writes claim responses in the firm's house style. Which lifecycle stage is the firm working in?
choices: Pre-training, because the firm is teaching the model general language patterns for the first time.
Model selection, because the firm is choosing between two existing designs.
Feedback, because the firm is collecting results from claim letters to guide future work.
Fine-tuning, because the firm is running a smaller extra training pass on its own labelled examples to shape behaviour for one task.
questions.why: Fine-tuning is the smaller extra training run on your own labelled examples after a pre-trained model already exists, which matches the firm's plan, while the other choices describe different stages.

questions.prompt: A travel company evaluated its trip-question model once, in March, against a fixed set of 150 test questions, and then never tested it again. By September, customers were writing questions with new place names and booking terms, and complaints rose sharply even though the model had not been changed. Which lesson from the lifecycle best explains this?
choices: The model needed more pre-training, because a larger general run would have covered the new place names.
Deployment failed, because a model that is reachable by the application cannot produce wrong answers.
Evaluation is not a one-time gate; quality can drift as inputs change, so the same tests should be rerun after changes in the inputs.
Evaluation should happen before pre-training, so the test set can shape the general training data.
questions.why: The lesson is that quality can drift as real inputs change, so the same test set must be rerun over time, which the one-time March evaluation missed; the other choices invent causes the scenario does not support.

questions.prompt: A retailer's training data for a returns assistant included a set of store addresses and return rules copied from a 2019 archive. The rules were changed in 2023 and the assistant now quotes the 2019 policy to customers. The team's later evaluation and deployment steps ran without errors. Which statement best explains why the wrong policy still reaches customers?
choices: Outdated records in the training data are not removed by later stages, so the model keeps producing them in production.
The evaluation step was too strict, so it wrongly marked correct 2023 answers as failures.
Deployment should have removed the outdated rules by filtering the output at the access layer.
Fine-tuning always overwrites older facts, so the model must have been left on pre-training data.
questions.why: The consequence of this lifecycle is that stale or sensitive records in training data are not cleaned up by any later stage, so the model keeps producing them, which is the only choice consistent with the teaching text.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate who is new to AI why the lifecycle has separate fine-tuning and feedback stages, and name one limit or tradeoff of fine-tuning a pre-trained model compared with building a model from scratch.
lessons.modelAnswer: Fine-tuning and feedback do different jobs. Fine-tuning is a targeted training run that reshapes a pre-trained model for one task, such as summarising our support tickets in our house style. Feedback is the ongoing loop where real users and reviewers rate outputs, and those ratings decide what goes into the next training set and what gets re-tested. One is a training action; the other is an information source that keeps the training honest. The main tradeoff of fine-tuning a pre-trained model is that you inherit its base behaviour and its gaps, so if the base model handles our domain poorly, a modest set of examples may not fully fix it. Building from scratch avoids that inheritance but needs far more data and compute than most teams have. So we start from a pre-trained model, measure carefully, and fine-tune only where evaluation shows a real gap.
rubricPoints: Fine-tuning is a targeted extra training run on task-specific examples
Feedback is ongoing real-world input that guides the next data and training round
Fine-tuning inherits the base model's strengths and weaknesses
Building from scratch needs far more data and compute than most teams have

suggested.rationale: Explaining how the stages connect and what tradeoffs they carry is the core skill here, and no listed mission or planned engine covers this lifecycle.

lessons.plain: When you use a generative AI model that runs as a managed service, you usually pay based on how much text it reads and writes, measured in tokens. A token is a small chunk of text, often a short word or part of a longer word, that the model handles one piece at a time. Think of it like paying a print shop by the word rather than by the whole job: longer prompts and longer answers cost more, and they also take longer to produce. Knowing this lets you predict a bill and shape a feature so it stays affordable and responsive.
lessons.guessPrompt: Suppose two chatbot features answer the same question. One returns a three-sentence reply and the other returns a five-page essay. Before any teaching, which one would you expect to cost more to run, and what would you look at to explain the difference?
lessons.teach:
A token is the unit a language model reads and writes. It is usually a fragment of a word, a whole short word, or a punctuation mark, and how text splits into tokens depends on the model. Providers typically price usage per thousand tokens, and they often charge separately for input tokens (what you send, including instructions and any documents you attach) and output tokens (what the model generates). Output tokens are usually priced higher. Why this works: the model does computation for every token it reads, and it generates the answer one token at a time, so both length and speed follow token counts.

Worked example with fictional rates of 0.5 credits per 1,000 input tokens and 1.5 credits per 1,000 output tokens. Step one: the request carries 800 input tokens, costing 800 divided by 1,000 times 0.5, which is 0.40 credits. Step two: the reply is 200 output tokens, costing 200 divided by 1,000 times 1.5, which is 0.30 credits. Step three: add them for a total of 0.70 credits per call.

Common mistake: estimating cost from the visible answer alone. The system instructions and retrieved documents resent with every call are input tokens too, and they often outweigh the answer.

Consequence in a running system: at 50,000 calls a day, 0.70 credits per call is 35,000 credits daily. Trimming the input from 800 to 400 tokens saves 0.20 credits per call, or 10,000 credits daily, and it also shortens the time before the first word appears.

questions.prompt: A law firm's contract-review tool sends a 3,000-token contract plus instructions to a model and gets back a 600-token summary. Input is priced at 0.3 credits per 1,000 tokens and output at 1.2 credits per 1,000 tokens. Step one: input cost is 3,000 divided by 1,000 times 0.3, which is 0.90 credits. Step two: output cost is 600 divided by 1,000 times 1.2, which is 0.72 credits. Step three, which is missing: state the total cost of one call.
choices: 0.18 credits, the difference between the input and output costs
0.72 credits, since only output tokens are billed
1.62 credits, the sum of the input and output costs
0.90 credits, since the input cost already covers the whole call
questions.why: A call's total cost is its input cost plus its output cost, so 0.90 plus 0.72 gives 1.62 credits.

questions.prompt: A product-description tool sends a 2,500-token brand style guide with every request and receives about 150-token descriptions. Which change would most reduce the cost per call?
choices: Remove the output length limit, because output is usually the cheaper side of the bill
Shorten the style guide that is resent with every request, since those input tokens are billed on every call
Switch to a faster model only, because price depends only on speed
Ask for longer descriptions, since output is what the customer sees
questions.why: The resent style guide is a large share of billed input on every call, so shortening it cuts cost on each request.

questions.prompt: A team estimates its monthly spend by counting the words in the visible reply and multiplying by a rate. What is the main flaw in this method?
choices: Output tokens are free, so the reply should not be counted at all
Input tokens are billed only on the first call of a session
Input tokens, such as instructions and retrieved documents, are resent and billed on every call, and the visible reply hides them
Visible reply length equals token count, so the method has no flaw
questions.why: Input tokens resent with each call are billed and often outweigh the answer, so estimating from the visible reply understates cost.

questions.prompt: A chat feature reduces the input sent per call from 1,600 tokens to 800 tokens. Which statement about the effect is correct?
choices: It lowers cost only if the output also shrinks by the same amount
It lowers the input cost per call and tends to shorten the wait before the first word appears, because the model has fewer input tokens to process
It has no effect on speed, because speed depends only on output length
It raises output cost, because the model must compress more text
questions.why: Fewer input tokens means less computation before generation starts, so both the per-call input cost and the time to the first word fall.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate why a feature that returns long answers can become both expensive and slow even when the model is working correctly. Name one tradeoff you would accept or refuse when shortening prompts or answers.
lessons.modelAnswer: The bill for a generative AI feature is driven by tokens, not by how many requests we think we are making. Every request is billed for the tokens it sends in and the tokens it gets back, and output tokens usually cost more. A long answer therefore costs more per call, and it also takes longer, because the model generates it one token at a time, so users wait longer. Multiply that by call volume and the cost grows quickly. The same applies to large system instructions or documents we attach to every call, since those are resent and billed each time. To reduce cost, we can shorten instructions, retrieve less text, or cap answer length. The tradeoff is quality: if we cut context too hard, answers may miss details the user needed, so I would accept shorter answers only after testing that accuracy holds on a representative set of questions.
rubricPoints: Tokens are the unit of billing, with input and output usually priced separately.
Output tokens are generated one at a time, so long answers add latency as well as cost.
Repeated instructions or documents in every call are billed each time.
Shortening prompts or answers trades cost and speed against possible loss of accuracy, which must be tested.

suggested.rationale: A cost model in fictional credits lets the learner change input and output token counts and watch the per-call and daily totals move, which is the core skill of this objective.

lessons.plain: Context engineering is the work of deciding what goes into the text a language model reads before it writes its reply. A model only knows what sits in front of it at that moment: its instructions, the conversation so far, any documents you paste in, and the results of tools it has called. Someone building an app chooses, orders, trims, and refreshes that material. Good context makes answers relevant and grounded. Careless context makes them vague, wrong, or expensive. Think of it as packing a briefing folder for a contractor who has no memory of anything else.
lessons.guessPrompt: A customer-support chatbot gives a confident answer about a refund policy that changed last week. The model itself was not retrained. What is the most likely reason the answer is outdated, and what would you change to fix it without retraining the model?
lessons.teach: A context window is the fixed maximum amount of text a model can read in one request. The amount is measured in tokens, which are the small pieces of text a model splits its input into. Context engineering is the design of what fills that window: standing instructions (often called a system prompt, the instructions the app sends with every request), the conversation history, documents fetched at question time, tool outputs, and examples. It works because a model continues the text it sees. It has no live view of your database or policy pages unless you place those facts into the window. Worked example: a customer asks whether a sale item can be returned. Step 1: the app searches its policy store for passages about returns. Step 2: it finds the passage updated last week. Step 3: it places that passage, the question, and the instruction answer only from the passages provided and say so if they do not cover the question into the window. Step 4: the model answers from the new text. Without step 2, the model falls back on older knowledge from training, which is stale. A common mistake is stuffing everything into the window. Long context costs more tokens, slows responses, and can bury the one rule that matters, which the model may then miss. In a running system, every extra token adds cost and latency to every request, so a bloated context can make a feature expensive at scale. Good context is selected, not merely large.

questions.prompt: A parts supplier runs an assistant that answers warranty questions for its trade customers. The app works in four steps. Step 1: it sends a standing instruction telling the model to answer only from the warranty clauses supplied and to say so if they do not cover the question. Step 2: it searches the warranty clause store and retrieves the clauses that match the customer's question. Step 3: this step is missing from the list and must be filled in. Step 4: the model writes its answer using only the clauses that are now in the window. Which action correctly fills Step 3?
choices: Enlarge the window to hold all 40,000 product manuals, since bigger is always safer.
Ask the customer to repeat the question so the model's training data is refreshed.
Place the matching clauses and the customer's question into the window, next to the standing instruction.
Fine-tune the model on the full warranty manual so it memorises the clauses.
questions.why: The model can only use facts placed in its context window, so the matching clauses and the question must be put there alongside the standing instruction before the model answers.

questions.prompt: In plain terms, what is the context window of a model?
choices: The screen area where the user types questions to the model.
The permanent set of facts the model learned during its training run.
The fixed maximum amount of text the model can read in one request, measured in tokens.
The time limit the app allows before a request is cancelled.
questions.why: The teaching text defines the context window as the fixed maximum amount of text a model can read in one request, measured in tokens.

questions.prompt: A team adds an entire 300-page staff handbook to every request, even when users ask only about holiday dates. Which result is the most likely consequence, based on the teaching text?
choices: The model will update its training data with the handbook after each request.
The model will become more accurate because it has more reading material.
Each request costs more tokens and responses slow down, and the one rule that matters may be missed.
The answers will cost nothing extra because the handbook is only read, not stored.
questions.why: Long context adds tokens to every request, which raises cost and latency, and it can bury the key rule so the model misses it.

questions.prompt: Which of these is NOT something context engineering decides about what fills the window for a given request?
choices: Which earlier conversation turns are included in the window.
Which facts the model absorbed during its original training, which the app cannot change per request.
Which documents are fetched at question time and placed into the window.
Which standing instructions the app sends with every request.
questions.why: Context engineering governs what the app places into the window per request, whereas facts absorbed during training are fixed and are not chosen by the app at request time.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate who is planning a new feature what context engineering is, and name one limit or tradeoff the team must weigh when deciding how much material to put into the context.
lessons.modelAnswer: Context engineering means deciding what the model sees in its input for each request: the standing instructions, the conversation so far, any documents the app fetched, and tool results. The model has no memory beyond that window and no live access to our systems, so if a fact is not in the window, the model either guesses or falls back on stale training knowledge. The main tradeoff is size against focus. Adding more material can improve grounding, but every token costs money and adds latency on every request, and a crowded window can hide the key rule so the model misses it. So we should select and order the most relevant material, keep the instructions short, and measure whether the extra context actually improves answers before we keep it.
rubricPoints: Defines context as everything the model reads in one request, not its training knowledge.
Names the kinds of material that fill the context, such as instructions, history, retrieved documents, and tool results.
States a concrete limit: the window is finite and every token costs money and time.
Explains the tradeoff that more context can dilute or bury key facts, so selection matters more than volume.

suggested.rationale: Explaining what goes into a model's input and why is the core skill here, and no listed mission or planned engine practises it directly.

lessons.plain: An agentic AI system is a generative AI model that does more than produce text once. It runs in a loop: it reads a goal, decides on a next step, calls a tool such as a search or a calculator, looks at the result, and continues until the job is done or it gets stuck. Think of a capable assistant who can go and fetch things rather than only answering from memory. Several such assistants can also be arranged to split up work. The ideas here are how they divide tasks, what they remember between steps, how they use outside tools, and how a fixed workflow keeps them on track.
lessons.guessPrompt: A customer asks a chatbot to book a flight and email the itinerary. Without any teaching, what extra abilities beyond writing text would the system need, and what could go wrong if it simply guessed the flight price instead of looking it up?
lessons.teach:
An agent is a model wrapped in a loop. Each turn, the model receives the goal plus everything that has happened so far, chooses one action, and either gives an answer or requests a tool call. A tool is any external function the system is allowed to run, such as a search, a database lookup, or a calendar write. The surrounding program executes the tool, feeds the result back to the model, and repeats. This works because the model supplies judgment about what to do next, while tools supply current facts and side effects that the model cannot produce from its own training.

Memory means what the system carries from one step or session to the next. Short-term memory is the running conversation and tool results held in the prompt, and it is limited by the context window, which is the maximum amount of text the model can read at once. Long-term memory is stored outside the model, often in a database, and only the relevant pieces are retrieved when needed.

Orchestration is the control logic that decides the order of steps, the retries, and the stopping conditions. A multi-agent pattern splits work among several agents: a supervisor hands tasks to specialists, or agents pass results down a fixed pipeline. More agents means more coordination and more cost.

Worked example: a travel agent is asked to book a train under 80 pounds. Step 1, the model calls a search tool and gets three options. Step 2, it calls a price tool for the cheapest and sees 74. Step 3, it writes the booking request and stores the confirmation in long-term memory. Step 4, it stops and reports the result.

Common mistake: letting the loop run with no step limit and no confirmation before actions that change things, so a confused agent books, retries, and books again.

In a running system, every tool call is a real request with latency and cost, so an unbounded loop can run up a bill and create duplicate writes that a human must clean up. Bounded loops and guarded write actions are part of the design, not optional extras.

questions.prompt: A returns assistant at an online homeware shop runs as an agent. Step 1: the model calls the order lookup tool and gets back order 5517, delivered 3 days ago, total 42 pounds. Step 2: [missing step]. Step 3: after the reviewer approves, the model calls the refund tool once and gets refund ID R-903. Step 4: the model stops and reports the refund to the customer. Which action fills the missing step 2?
choices: The model calls the refund tool straight away to save a turn, and asks the reviewer to approve it afterwards.
The model stops and reports the refund as complete without calling any tool.
The model stores the 42 pound total in long-term memory and skips the refund step entirely.
The model pauses and requests human approval of the 42 pound refund before any write action runs.
questions.why: The teaching text says a guarded write action needs confirmation before it runs, so the pause for approval must come before the refund tool call, which is the only write in this flow.

questions.prompt: A dental clinic's booking assistant keeps the full history of each patient's past appointments in a database outside the model. When a patient asks a question, the system fetches only the relevant visits and places them in the prompt. Which kind of memory is this?
choices: Orchestration, because the system decides the order of the steps.
Short-term memory, because the visits are placed in the prompt for the current request.
Long-term memory, because it is stored outside the model and only relevant pieces are retrieved when needed.
Context window, because the model reads the whole history at once.
questions.why: Long-term memory is defined in the teaching text as storage outside the model from which only relevant pieces are retrieved, which matches the clinic's database and selective fetch.

questions.prompt: A logistics company's agent is allowed to call an invoice-sending tool. Its loop has no step limit and it sends invoices without any confirmation step. A network timeout occurs and the agent retries several times. What is the most likely consequence, and the design fix the teaching text points to?
choices: Nothing happens, because a timeout stops the loop automatically, so no fix is needed.
Duplicate invoices are sent and a human must clean them up, so the fix is a bounded loop plus guarded write actions.
The agent runs out of memory, so the fix is a larger context window.
The agent sends the invoices more slowly, so the fix is to add more specialist agents.
questions.why: The teaching text warns that an unbounded loop with unguarded writes can create duplicate writes that humans must clean up, and that bounded loops and guarded write actions are part of the design.

questions.prompt: A content firm uses one supervisor agent that receives a brief, hands the research to a search specialist and the drafting to a writing specialist, then combines their results. What does the teaching text say about this multi-agent pattern?
choices: It is a supervisor pattern where the supervisor hands tasks to specialists, and more agents bring more coordination and cost.
It is a single agent with several tools, so no coordination cost arises.
It removes the need for orchestration, because the agents coordinate themselves without control logic.
It is a fixed pipeline where each agent always passes results to the next one in the same order.
questions.why: The teaching text defines the supervisor pattern as a supervisor handing tasks to specialists and notes that more agents means more coordination and more cost, which the firm's design reflects.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate the difference between an agent's short-term and long-term memory, and name one limit or tradeoff of letting an agent call tools without a step limit or an approval gate.
lessons.modelAnswer: Short-term memory is what sits in the prompt during one task: the conversation so far and the results of recent tool calls. It is fast and needs no lookup, but it is bounded by the context window, so long tasks fill it and earlier details get crowded out. Long-term memory lives outside the model in a store such as a database, and the system fetches only the relevant pieces when needed. It survives across sessions, but retrieval can miss something or return stale facts, and it adds a lookup step. The tradeoff with tools is that each call can have real effects. Without a step limit, an agent that misreads a result can loop, spending money or duplicating bookings. An approval gate before writes trades some speed for safety. I would cap the number of steps, require confirmation for changes, and log every call.
rubricPoints: Short-term memory is the in-prompt working context, limited by the context window
Long-term memory is stored externally and retrieved selectively across sessions
Tool calls have real side effects, costs, and latency
An unbounded agent loop can repeat actions or run up costs
An approval gate or step limit trades speed for safety

suggested.rationale: A workflow state machine engine would let the learner see orchestration, step limits, and guarded transitions directly, which this objective depends on.

lessons.plain: Model Context Protocol, usually shortened to MCP, is a shared rulebook that lets an AI program ask outside systems for help. Without it, every AI tool needs its own custom wiring to every database, file store, or service it touches. With it, the outside system runs a small adapter that describes what it can do, and the AI program can discover and use those abilities in a standard way. An AI agent, which is a model that can take steps toward a goal, uses this to look up a record, check a status, or send a message. The idea is like a standard power socket: the shape is agreed once, so many devices can plug into many walls.
lessons.guessPrompt: A support chatbot needs to check the live status of a customer's order, which sits in a company database. Why can't the model simply read that database on its own, and what do you think must sit between them?
lessons.teach: Model Context Protocol (MCP) is an open standard describing how an AI application talks to outside systems. Think of it as a common plug shape: instead of writing a custom connector for every model and every tool, both sides agree on one way to offer and call capabilities. The parts have names. The host is the AI application a person uses, such as a chat assistant or an agent you build. Inside the host, a client keeps a connection open to one server. A server wraps an outside system, such as a ticketing database, a file store, or a calendar, and advertises what it offers: tools the model may invoke, resources it may read, and prompt templates it may reuse. An agent is a model that can decide to take actions in a loop, and tools are how those actions reach the world. Why it works: the model never touches the system directly. It produces a request to call a named tool with arguments; the client forwards that request to the server; the server runs the real operation under its own credentials and returns a result, which the model reads before it answers. Worked example. A support assistant is asked how many open tickets exist for route 7. Step 1: the client asks the ticketing server what it offers and receives a tool called count_open_tickets that takes a route parameter. Step 2: the model chooses that tool and fills in route equal to 7. Step 3: the server queries the ticketing system and returns 23. Step 4: the model writes its answer using that returned number. Common mistake: treating a connected server as harmless. Every tool description is text loaded into the model's context window, so many tools add tokens to every request, raising cost and latency. A server that exposes write actions with broad credentials also lets a model change real data, so access must be narrowly scoped. Consequence in a running system: when a server is slow or unavailable, the tool call fails or times out, and the agent has to handle that failure rather than guess at an answer.

questions.prompt: A freight company's staff assistant is asked how many pallets of part SKU-550 are in the north depot. The learner sees this trace of a tool call. Step 1: the client asks the depot server what it offers and receives a tool called check_stock that takes a location parameter. Step 2: the model chooses check_stock and fills in location equal to north. Step 3: [blank: the client forwards the call to the depot server, which runs the query under its own credentials and returns the count]. Step 4: the model writes its answer using the returned count of 412. Which sentence correctly fills the blank at step 3?
choices: The client forwards the model's request to the depot server, which runs the query under its own credentials and returns 412.
The server sends the tool list back to the model, which then picks the number to report.
The model connects straight to the stock database with the warehouse login and reads the count itself.
The model guesses the count from last week's conversation because the tool list is already loaded.
questions.why: The model never touches the system directly, so the client must forward the named tool request to the server, which performs the real operation under its own credentials and returns the result.

questions.prompt: In the Model Context Protocol, what is the role of a server?
choices: It is the AI application the person uses in a chat window.
It wraps an outside system and advertises the tools, resources, and prompt templates it offers.
It is the single connection kept open inside the host to one outside system.
It is the model that decides which actions to take in a loop.
questions.why: A server wraps an outside system such as a database or calendar and advertises what it offers; the host is the application, the agent is the deciding model, and the client is the connection inside the host.

questions.prompt: A team plans to connect an assistant to 40 tool servers so the model always has every capability available. Which concern from the teaching text matters most for this choice?
choices: Servers cannot return results to the model, so the assistant will never see any answer from the tools.
Tool descriptions are stored permanently in the model's weights, so adding them retrains the model each time.
The Model Context Protocol forbids more than five servers in one host, so the setup will fail to start.
Each tool description is text loaded into the context window, so many tools add tokens to every request and raise cost and latency.
questions.why: The teaching text says every tool description is loaded into the context window on each request, so a large number of tools increases token cost and latency.

questions.prompt: A warehouse assistant calls a stock-count tool on a server, but the server is down and the call times out. What should a well-built agent do?
choices: Handle the failure explicitly rather than guess at an answer, because the tool result never arrived.
Retry the call forever until the server answers, without limit.
Pick the most likely number from earlier turns and present it as the current count.
Ask the model to invent a plausible count and mark it as an estimate.
questions.why: When a server is slow or unavailable the tool call fails or times out, and the agent must handle that failure rather than guess, since no real result was returned.

lessons.explainPrompt: A teammate asks why we should not just give our chatbot a database password and let it query the database directly. Explain how MCP would sit between them, and name one limit or tradeoff of that setup.
lessons.modelAnswer: Giving the chatbot the raw password means the model can reach everything that account can reach, with no clear boundary. With MCP, the database is wrapped in a server that offers only specific tools, such as checking one order's status, and that server runs the query under its own tightly scoped credentials. The chatbot's client talks to that server using the shared protocol, so the model asks for a named action and gets a result back without ever seeing the connection details. The tradeoff is that every extra tool adds its description to the model's context on each request, which costs tokens and adds latency, so we should expose only the tools the assistant genuinely needs. A server also becomes a dependency: if it is down, the assistant has to report that and not invent an answer.
rubricPoints: MCP standardizes how a model-driven application discovers and calls outside tools or data through a server wrapper.
The model never gets raw credentials; the server holds access and can be scoped to specific actions.
Tool descriptions consume context tokens on every request, so exposing many tools raises cost and latency.
If a server is slow or down, the tool call fails and the agent must handle the failure instead of guessing.

suggested.rationale: Explaining how a host, client, and server divide the work, and what each exposed tool costs, is the core skill here and no listed mission or engine covers it directly.

lessons.plain: Generative AI is software that produces new content, such as text, images or code, in response to what you give it, instead of only sorting or scoring existing data. Its main strengths are that one system can be adapted to many tasks without being rebuilt, it replies quickly, it can hold a back-and-forth conversation, and it can draft content on demand. Think of a capable new colleague who can write a first draft of almost anything you ask, in seconds, and then take a follow-up request. That flexibility is why teams adopt it, though the strengths only pay off when the work suits them.
lessons.guessPrompt: Suppose you have one tool that can write a product description, answer a customer question in chat, and turn a bug report into a draft fix summary. Before reading further, what do you think makes that one tool more useful to a business than three separate narrow programs, and what might make it less useful?
lessons.teach:
Adaptability means one generative model can be pointed at many different jobs by changing the instruction it receives, rather than by writing new software for each job. Responsiveness means it returns an answer quickly enough to sit inside an interactive tool. Conversational ability means it can keep a back-and-forth exchange going, using earlier turns as context. Content generation means it creates new material such as text, images, code or audio, not only labels or scores on existing material. A prompt is the instruction plus any supplied material, and context is everything the model can see in a single request.

These strengths come from training on very large collections of examples, so the model learns patterns it can apply to inputs it has never seen. Because its behavior is set by a prompt rather than hard-coded rules, a team can change what the system does in minutes.

Worked example: a support team wants reply drafts. Step 1: the application sends a prompt containing the customer message and a short refund policy excerpt. Step 2: the model returns a draft in a few seconds. Step 3: the agent types 'shorter, and mention the 14-day window'; the earlier draft is still in context, so the model revises that draft rather than starting over. Step 4: the agent checks the wording and sends it.

Common mistake: assuming adaptability means no effort. Each new task still needs clear instructions, examples and checking, and fluent output is not the same as correct output.

Consequence: if nobody checks drafts, a confident reply quoting the wrong refund window reaches a customer. The speed gain only holds when review is built into the process.

questions.prompt: A bicycle repair shop uses one generative model to draft job quotes. Step 1: the app sends a prompt containing the customer's description of the fault and the shop's labour rate card with three tiers. Step 2: the model returns a draft quote in about three seconds. Step 3: a step is missing here. Step 4: the quote is sent to the customer. Which step fills the gap?
choices: The mechanic checks each labour rate in the draft against the rate card before the quote goes out.
The app sends the whole conversation history to a second model with no new instruction.
The shop switches to a larger model so the draft arrives faster.
The model is retrained on the shop's past quotes so the next draft is more accurate.
questions.why: The teaching text says every new task still needs clear instructions, examples and checking, and a fluent draft can still contain a wrong figure, so a person must compare the quoted rates with the source before sending.

questions.prompt: In the sense used in the teaching text, what does adaptability mean?
choices: The model is rewritten in new code each time a new task appears.
The model keeps a back-and-forth exchange going using earlier turns.
The model returns answers quickly enough to sit inside a live tool.
One model can be pointed at many different jobs by changing the instruction it receives.
questions.why: Adaptability means the same model is redirected to new jobs through the instruction it receives, rather than through new software written for each job.

questions.prompt: A bank uses one generative model to summarise call notes, draft fraud-alert wording and sort customer emails, changing only the instruction for each task. Which advantage of generative AI does this setup mainly show?
choices: Training scale, because the model learned from very large collections of examples.
Adaptability, because one model serves several jobs when the instruction changes.
Responsiveness, because each answer comes back within seconds.
Conversational ability, because the model keeps earlier turns in context.
questions.why: The defining feature of the setup is one model being redirected to several tasks by changing only the instruction, which is the adaptability advantage described in the teaching text.

questions.prompt: A team deploys a generative tool to write customer-facing policy summaries and removes the human review step because the outputs read smoothly. What is the main risk?
choices: The model will gradually lose its ability to handle new tasks.
The tool will stop holding a back-and-forth conversation once review is removed.
Smooth wording can hide a wrong figure, and nobody catches it before it reaches customers.
Responses will become slower because review has been removed from the model's pipeline.
questions.why: The teaching text warns that fluent output is not the same as correct output, and that without checking, a confident but wrong reply can reach a customer.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate who has only used traditional software why a generative AI feature can be quick to change and useful across many tasks, and name one limit or tradeoff that comes with that flexibility.
lessons.modelAnswer: The main point is that traditional software encodes behavior in code, so a new task usually means new development. A generative model's behavior is steered by the instruction and material in each request, so the same model can draft emails, summarize tickets or answer questions, and a team can change what it does by editing the prompt, often within minutes. It also replies fast enough to sit inside a chat window and can keep earlier turns in context, so follow-up requests make sense. The tradeoff is that the same flexibility makes output less predictable. Because the model generates text from patterns rather than checking facts, a fluent answer can be wrong, and the same prompt can produce different wording on different runs. So I would tell the team that the speed of change is real, but outputs need review or validation before they reach customers.
rubricPoints: Adaptability: one model serves many tasks by changing the prompt, not the code.
Responsiveness and conversation: fast replies and context from earlier turns enable interactive use.
Content generation: it produces new drafts, not only labels or scores.
Limit: fluent output can be wrong or vary between runs, so review is needed.

suggested.rationale: The core skill here is explaining the advantages and their limits in your own words, which a written explanation tests better than any listed mission.

lessons.plain: Generative AI systems, such as chatbots that write text or tools that make images, produce new content by predicting what should come next. That makes them useful, but it also gives them four weaknesses. They can invent facts that sound confident (hallucination), they are hard to explain step by step (poor interpretability), they can simply be wrong (inaccuracy), and asking the same question twice may get two different answers (nondeterminism). Knowing these in advance tells you where a system needs checks, human review, or a different design before anyone relies on its output.
lessons.guessPrompt: If a chatbot gives you a confident, specific answer you cannot verify, what could go wrong, and why might asking the same question again produce a different answer?
lessons.teach:
Each of the four disadvantages has a plain meaning. Hallucination means the model produces output that is fluent and confident but not supported by real facts or by the source material it was given. Inaccuracy is the broader problem that the output is simply wrong, whether or not it sounds plausible. Poor interpretability means you cannot easily trace why the model produced a particular answer, because its behaviour comes from billions of learned numerical weights rather than readable rules. Nondeterminism means the same input can produce different outputs on different runs, because generation involves sampling from probabilities. A setting called temperature controls how much randomness is allowed.

Why does this happen? A generative model is trained to predict a likely next token, a small piece of text such as a word or part of a word. Likely is not the same as true. When its training gives it no reliable answer, it fills the gap with the most plausible continuation, and that continuation can be invented.

Worked example: a support assistant is asked what the refund window is for plan B. The model has no policy document in front of it. Step 1: it recognises the question pattern. Step 2: it predicts a plausible number of days, such as 30, because that is common in its training text. Step 3: it writes the sentence in a confident tone. Step 4: asked again, sampling may choose 14 days instead. The first answer is a hallucination, and the change between runs is nondeterminism.

Common mistake: treating a fluent, confident answer as evidence it is correct, or assuming that setting temperature to zero makes the answer right. Lower randomness makes output more repeatable, not more true.

Consequence in a running system: if that refund figure reaches customers unchecked, the business has made a commitment it never agreed to. Mitigations include grounding answers in a checked source, logging inputs and outputs so you can investigate, and routing high-stakes answers to a person. A wrong answer that is repeated consistently is still wrong.

questions.prompt: A regional airline's booking assistant is asked how many kilograms of checked baggage a passenger on the economy fare gets. No fare rules are provided to the model. Step 1: it recognises the question as a baggage-allowance question. Step 2: it predicts a plausible figure, 23 kg, because that number is common in its training text. Step 3: it writes the sentence in a confident, friendly tone. Step 4: the same question is asked again, and sampling picks 20 kg on this run. Which statement correctly describes step 4?
choices: The model consults the airline's live fare table and returns the official allowance, so the two answers should match.
The second answer is more accurate because the model learned from its first reply during the conversation.
Sampling selects a different figure on this run, so the two answers disagree, which is nondeterminism rather than a sign the model is reasoning about fare rules.
The model detects that no fare rules are available and stops, returning an empty answer.
questions.why: Nondeterminism means the same input can produce different outputs because generation samples from probabilities, and the disagreement between runs shows that neither figure is backed by a checked source.

questions.prompt: Which description best defines a hallucination in a generative model?
choices: A reply that is wrong only because the user typed the question incorrectly.
A fluent, confident output that is not supported by real facts or by the source material the model was given.
A reply that changes each time the same question is asked, regardless of whether it is correct.
A deliberate error inserted by a developer to test whether the system is being monitored.
questions.why: The teaching text defines hallucination as output that is fluent and confident but unsupported by facts or the supplied source, which is the third choice.

questions.prompt: A hospital's scheduling assistant gives the same clinic opening hours on every run after its temperature setting is lowered to zero. A colleague says this proves the hours are correct. What is the best response?
choices: The temperature should be raised so the model explores more options and finds the correct hours.
The answer is only wrong if the model changes it, so no further check is needed.
The colleague is right, because a repeatable answer is a verified answer.
The hours should be checked against the clinic's published schedule, because lower randomness makes output more repeatable but not more true.
questions.why: Setting temperature to zero reduces randomness and makes output repeatable, but a consistently repeated answer can still be wrong, so it must be checked against a real source.},{

questions.prompt: A logistics firm asks why its generative model's answer about a delivery surcharge cannot be traced back to a readable rule the way a spreadsheet formula can. Which explanation is correct?
choices: The model simply has not been given enough training examples about surcharges to form a rule.
The surcharge is stored in a hidden table that the model queries, and the table is not accessible to the firm.
The behaviour comes from billions of learned numerical weights rather than readable rules, so the reasoning path is hard to trace; this is poor interpretability.
Generation involves sampling from probabilities, so each answer is random and has no cause at all.
questions.why: Poor interpretability means the model's behaviour is spread across billions of numerical weights rather than explicit rules, which makes it hard to trace why a particular answer was produced.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate, in your own words, why a generative AI answer can be confidently wrong, and name one limit or tradeoff of lowering the randomness setting as a fix.
lessons.modelAnswer: A generative model writes text by predicting likely next tokens, and likely is not the same as true.
