When it lacks a reliable fact, it can produce a plausible answer and state it confidently. That is hallucination, and the broader category is inaccuracy. We also cannot easily trace why it said what it did, which is poor interpretability, so we cannot audit one answer by reading its logic. On the tradeoff: lowering temperature makes outputs more repeatable, which helps testing and comparison, but repeatable is not correct. A wrong answer will now be wrong every time, and very low randomness can make creative or varied output bland. So the real fix is grounding answers in a checked source, validating them, and adding human review for high-stakes cases, not just turning one setting down.
rubricPoints: Defines hallucination or inaccuracy as plausible-sounding output that is not supported by fact
Explains that the model predicts likely text, which is not the same as true
Notes that nondeterminism means repeated runs can differ, and that low temperature reduces this
States the tradeoff: lower randomness gives repeatability but does not fix correctness, and can reduce variety
Names a practical mitigation such as grounding, validation, or human review

suggested.rationale: The core skill is reasoning about where generative output fails and explaining that limit to a teammate, which no listed mission or planned engine currently covers.

lessons.plain: Choosing a generative AI model means picking which pre-built AI system will power a feature that writes, summarizes, answers questions, or creates images. The options differ in what they produce (text, images, audio, or several at once), how well they perform on your task, what data they are allowed to handle, how much they cost to run, how fast they reply, and how hard they are to operate. Nobody should pick the strongest model by default. The right choice is the cheapest, fastest, and safest model that is good enough for the job, and you only learn that by weighing those factors against what the feature must do. It is like choosing a vehicle: a truck is not better than a bicycle, it depends on the load and the road.
lessons.guessPrompt: A team wants a chatbot that answers customer questions in under two seconds, handles sensitive account data, and runs on a tight budget. Before reading on, list which of these needs would push the choice toward a smaller, cheaper model and which would push it toward a larger, more capable one, and say which need you think matters most.
lessons.teach:
A model type is the kind of output a model was built to produce. A large language model, or LLM, is a text model trained on vast amounts of language, used for writing, summarizing, and answering questions. A diffusion model generates images by starting from noise and refining it step by step. A multi-modal model handles more than one kind of data, such as text plus images. A foundation model is a large model trained broadly once and then adapted to many tasks. Fine-tuning means further training an existing model on your own examples so it behaves differently; it adds cost and complexity.

The rest of the decision is a set of trade-offs. Performance is how often the output is right for your task, measured on examples you actually care about. Capability is what the model can do at all, such as reading images or following long instructions. Constraints are limits you cannot negotiate, such as input size, output length, supported languages, or where the model runs. Compliance covers rules about where data goes and who may process it. Cost is what you pay at your expected volume. Latency is the delay between sending a request and getting the answer. Complexity is the effort needed to build, evaluate, and operate the choice.

Worked example: a support tool must summarize 200-word tickets for agents, run on every ticket, and keep data in one country. First, the type: summarizing text calls for a text model. Second, constraints and compliance: remove any model not offered in that country or whose data handling fails policy. Third, performance: test the remaining candidates on 50 real tickets and score accuracy. Fourth, cost and latency: a large model may score best but be slow and expensive across thousands of tickets a day, so a smaller model that clears the accuracy bar wins.

The common mistake is choosing the biggest model because it looked best in a demo, then finding that cost per ticket or reply time breaks the product. In a running system, a slow model makes agents wait on every screen, and an expensive one erodes margin on every call, so these factors must be measured rather than assumed.

questions.prompt: A law firm wants a tool that reads scanned contract pages, which are images, and answers questions about them. Its data must stay in the firm's home country. The team works through the decision in four steps. Step 1, type: reading scanned pages and answering questions about them needs a model that handles both images and text, so a multi-modal model. Step 2, constraints and compliance: remove any candidate not offered in the home country or whose data handling breaks the firm's policy. Step 3 is missing from their notes. Step 4, cost and latency: a model that answers well but takes 9 seconds per page is too slow for lawyers who review 300 pages a day, so the team picks a faster model that clears the accuracy bar. What belongs in Step 3?
choices: Compare only the monthly subscription price of each candidate to find the cheapest one.
Pick the model with the largest number of parameters, since bigger models are always more accurate.
Test the remaining candidates on about 40 real scanned contracts and score how often their answers are right.
Ask each vendor for a recommendation and go with whichever one answers the email first.
questions.why: Step 3 is the performance check, which means measuring how often each remaining candidate is right on real examples of the firm's own work, and that is the test in option B.

questions.prompt: In the course's vocabulary, what is latency?
choices: The delay between sending a request to a model and receiving its answer.
The share of a model's answers that are correct on the examples you care about.
The rules about where data is stored and which staff may process it.
The range of tasks a model can perform at all, such as reading images.
questions.why: Latency is defined in the teaching text as the delay between sending a request and getting the answer, which is option A.

questions.prompt: A logistics company tests a model on its own shipping-claim examples and finds 94% of answers are correct, which meets its target. But each reply takes about 12 seconds, and the warehouse app needs replies within 2 seconds. Which trade-off is failing?
choices: Capability, because the model cannot read the shipping claims at all.
Compliance, because the model must be sent to a different country to be used.
Performance, because 94% accuracy shows the model is not good enough to use.
Latency, because the answers arrive too slowly for the app even though they are accurate.
questions.why: The model's accuracy is already acceptable, so the failure is the delay between request and answer, which is latency, and option A names that correctly.

questions.prompt: A startup chooses the largest available model because it looked impressive in a vendor demo. Later it finds that, at its expected number of requests per day, the cost per request is higher than the revenue it earns per customer. What is the core mistake?
choices: It chose a model with too much capability, when a model with less capability would have been cheaper.
It judged the model on a demo rather than measuring cost and performance on its own examples at its expected volume.
It skipped fine-tuning, which would have reduced the cost per request for every model size.
It picked a diffusion model, which is always more expensive than a text model for any task.
questions.why: The teaching text warns against choosing the biggest model based on a demo and says cost and speed must be measured at real volume, which is what option C describes.

lessons.explainPrompt: A teammate asks why we did not just use the most powerful model available for our new feature. Explain in your own words how you would decide, and name at least one limit or tradeoff of the choice you would make.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would not start with the most powerful model, because capability is only one input. First I would check hard constraints: the model must accept our input length, support our language, and be offered in the region where our data has to stay. Those rules can rule options out before any testing. Then I would measure performance on a sample of our real requests, not on a public benchmark, and set a target accuracy. Among the models that pass, I would compare cost at our expected volume and latency against what users will tolerate. The tradeoff is that a smaller model may be somewhat less accurate on hard cases, so we would accept that gap only if outputs are reviewed or errors are low-stakes. I would also note that switching models later means retesting, so we should revisit the choice as usage grows.
rubricPoints: Identifies the model type the task needs before comparing options
Filters on hard constraints and compliance before comparing performance
Measures performance on real representative examples rather than benchmarks alone
Weighs cost and latency at expected volume against the quality required
States the tradeoff of a smaller or cheaper model and how the risk is managed

suggested.rationale: The core skill is reasoning through trade-offs and explaining the choice back, which no listed mission or planned engine covers directly.

lessons.plain: Business value metrics are the numbers that tell you whether a generative AI feature is worth what it costs. Generative AI means software that produces new text, images, or code. Before anyone asks whether the model is clever, a team asks whether the feature saves time, brings in more sales, or keeps customers longer. The common metrics are return on investment, efficiency gains, conversion rate, average revenue per user, and customer lifetime value. Think of them as a scorecard, where each measure answers a different question about money and people. Good teams choose their metrics before building, so they can judge later whether the feature paid off.
lessons.guessPrompt: A support team adds an AI tool that drafts ticket replies for agents. What two numbers would you check first to decide whether it is worth its monthly bill, and why might one of those numbers mislead you?
lessons.teach:
Return on investment, or ROI, is the gain from a project minus its cost, divided by its cost, usually written as a percentage. Efficiency means output per unit of effort, such as minutes saved per task or tickets closed per agent per day. Conversion rate is the share of people who reach a page or chat and then complete a wanted action, such as buying: completed purchases divided by visitors. Average revenue per user, or ARPU, is total revenue in a period divided by the number of active users in that period. Customer lifetime value, or CLV, estimates the total profit a customer brings over the whole relationship. A simple form multiplies profit per period by the expected number of periods the customer stays. Each metric connects a generative AI feature to money through a chain you can measure, so you can check whether the feature changed the business rather than just produced impressive output.

Worked example. A support team adds an assistant that drafts ticket replies. Step one: the tool costs 10,000 per month. Step two: it saves 2 minutes on each of 50,000 tickets, which is 100,000 minutes, or about 1,667 hours. Step three: at an assumed loaded cost of 30 per hour, the saved time is worth about 50,000. Step four: the net gain is 50,000 minus 10,000, which is 40,000. Step five: ROI is 40,000 divided by 10,000, or 400 percent.

Common mistake: counting saved minutes as cash. If agents simply take on more work or sit idle, no payroll cost falls, so the 50,000 is not real money. You must check whether the time is redeployed or whether backlog, headcount, or response time actually changes.

Consequence in a running system: generative AI is often billed by usage, such as the amount of text processed, so the bill grows with every request. A feature that succeeds in volume can raise cost faster than its value. The scorecard is only honest when it tracks cost per completed task alongside the value metric.

questions.prompt: An online furniture retailer adds a product-advice chat. Step 1: the chat brings 200 extra orders a month compared with the same traffic before the feature, at 150 per order, so the gain is 30,000 a month. Step 2: the chat costs 8,000 a month to run. Step 3, which is missing: work out the ROI as a percentage, using ROI = (gain minus cost) divided by cost.
choices: 375 percent
27.5 percent
A 22,000 net gain, which is already the ROI
275 percent
questions.why: ROI is (30,000 minus 8,000) divided by 8,000, which is 22,000 divided by 8,000, or 2.75, written as 275 percent.

questions.prompt: A language-learning app's tutor page gets 15,000 visitors in a month, and 2,100 of them start a paid trial. What is the conversion rate for that page?
choices: 0.14 percent
2,100 percent
7 percent
14 percent
questions.why: Conversion rate is completed actions divided by visitors, so 2,100 divided by 15,000 is 0.14, which is 14 percent; 0.14 percent is a decimal slip.

questions.prompt: A meal-kit company's AI recipe feature brings in 480,000 of revenue in one month. It has 20,000 registered accounts, but only 12,000 were active that month. What is ARPU for that month?
choices: 24 per user, counting all accounts
12 per active user, after dividing by months
480,000 per active user, the total revenue
40 per active user
questions.why: ARPU is total revenue divided by active users in the same period, so 480,000 divided by 12,000 is 40; counting inactive accounts is the mistake that gives 24.

questions.prompt: A legal-document drafting tool earns 600 of profit per subscriber per year, and subscribers stay about 3 years on average. Using the simple form of customer lifetime value, what is CLV?
choices: 1,800, profit per year times 3 years
200, profit divided by expected years
3, the expected number of years kept
600, the profit for one year only
questions.why: The simple CLV form multiplies profit per period by the expected number of periods the customer stays, giving 600 times 3, or 1,800.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would decide whether a generative AI feature paid off. Name at least one metric you would use, and state one limit or tradeoff of relying on that metric alone.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would start by choosing a value metric tied to the business goal, such as minutes saved per ticket converted into real cost reduction, or conversion rate for a sales assistant. Then I would calculate ROI as the net gain divided by total cost, including the model bill, engineering time, and human review. I would not stop there, because efficiency numbers can overstate the result. If agents use the saved time to take on more work, or the time is just idle, payroll does not drop and the savings are not real. I would also track cost per completed task, since usage-based billing means a successful feature can become expensive as volume grows. The limit is that every metric depends on assumptions, such as the hourly cost or the baseline, so I would show those assumptions openly and recheck them after a few weeks of real data.
rubricPoints: Defines or applies at least one named metric such as ROI, conversion rate, or CLV correctly
Connects the metric to a measurable business outcome rather than output quality alone
Names a limit or tradeoff, such as unrealized time savings or usage-driven cost growth
States that assumptions behind the numbers should be made visible and checked

suggested.rationale: Building a small cost model lets the learner compute ROI and cost per task from their own assumptions, which this objective requires.

lessons.plain: This objective is about knowing which AWS product to reach for when you build an application on generative AI. Generative AI means software that produces new text, images, or code from a prompt. Think of the services as a set of kitchens and tools: some hand you a ready meal through an API, some give you a full workshop to train your own model, and some are finished tools for specific people. Several are for building AI agents, which are programs that take multi-step actions by calling other tools. You rarely need to build a model yourself to use these. The skill is matching the product to the job and naming its main limit.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your team wants a chatbot that answers questions from its own help articles, and nobody on the team has trained a model before. Which kind of AWS offering would you reach for first: a ready-to-call model service, or a full machine learning training platform? Why?
lessons.teach:
Each service sits at a different layer of the stack. Amazon Bedrock is a managed service that gives you API access to foundation models (large pre-trained models that many tasks can reuse) from several model providers, without you running any servers. Amazon SageMaker AI is a broader platform for building, training, tuning, and hosting your own machine learning models, so you control more and also operate more. SageMaker JumpStart is a catalogue inside SageMaker that offers pre-trained models and ready-made solutions you can deploy in a few steps. Amazon Quick is a business assistant for employees that answers questions and automates work over company information, so it is a finished tool rather than something you build apps on. Kiro is an AI-assisted development environment that helps engineers write and change code. Strands Agents is an open-source software development kit for writing agents, where a model, its instructions, and its tools run in a loop until the task is done. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore is a managed platform for running agents in production, providing hosting, memory, identity, and monitoring.

Worked example: a team wants a support assistant that answers customer questions from its help articles. Step one, pick the model layer: call a foundation model through Amazon Bedrock. Step two, pick the build layer for the agent logic: write it with Strands Agents. Step three, pick the runtime layer: host and monitor it on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore.

Common mistake: choosing by brand name instead of by layer, such as picking SageMaker AI when a managed model API would do, which adds training and operations work without a benefit.

When a limit is ignored, the design fails in production. A catalogue model that does not meet your data-residency rule, or a staff tool that cannot be embedded in your own customer product, will block the launch no matter how good the output is.

questions.prompt: A hotel group wants a chatbot for its own guest app, answering questions from its policy documents. Guests must never see the staff tool. Step one: rule out Amazon Quick, because it is a finished assistant for employees and cannot be embedded in the hotel's own product. Step two is missing. Step three: host and monitor the agent's runtime on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. Which choice correctly fills the missing step two, the model layer?
choices: Call a foundation model through Amazon Bedrock's API, so no model servers need to be run by the hotel
Use Strands Agents as the model host, since it runs the model loop on the hotel's behalf
Use Kiro to generate the chatbot's model weights from the policy documents during the build
Train a new model from scratch in Amazon SageMaker AI so the hotel owns every weight before any guest can use the app
questions.why: Step two chooses the model layer, and Amazon Bedrock gives API access to foundation models without the hotel running servers, which fits a guest-facing app that does not need its own trained model.

questions.prompt: Which description best matches Amazon Bedrock AgentCore?
choices: A managed platform for running agents in production, providing hosting, memory, identity and monitoring
An AI-assisted development environment that helps engineers write and change code
An open-source software development kit where a model, its instructions and its tools run in a loop
A catalogue of pre-trained models that can be deployed in a few steps inside SageMaker
questions.why: AgentCore is the runtime layer that hosts and monitors agents in production, while Strands is the build kit, Kiro is a coding environment, and JumpStart is the model catalogue.

questions.prompt: A regional credit union wants to build and tune its own custom machine learning model, and it wants control over training and hosting. Which service fits this need best?
choices: Strands Agents, because it runs a model, its instructions and tools in a loop
Amazon SageMaker AI, because it builds, trains, tunes and hosts your own models
Amazon Quick, because it answers employee questions over company information
Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, because it hosts agents and provides memory and identity
questions.why: SageMaker AI is the broader platform for building, training, tuning and hosting your own models, giving the most control and the most operating work, which matches the credit union's stated need.

questions.prompt: A small firm building an FAQ bot chooses Amazon SageMaker AI to train its own model, even though a managed model API would answer the questions well. What is the main drawback of this choice?
choices: The bot cannot answer questions at all until it is embedded in a finished staff tool
It adds training and operations work without giving the bot a benefit it needs
It locks the firm out of every model provider, so it can never switch models later
The bot stops being able to call tools, because SageMaker AI removes tool use
questions.why: Choosing a build-and-operate platform when a managed model API suffices adds training and operations effort with no matching benefit, which is the mistake of choosing by brand rather than by layer.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate who has never used AWS generative AI services how you would choose between Amazon Bedrock and SageMaker AI for an internal document assistant, and name one limit or tradeoff of your choice.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would start with Amazon Bedrock because the assistant needs a capable language model, retrieval over our documents, and a quick path to production, and Bedrock gives API access to foundation models without us running servers or training anything. The tradeoff is that we are limited to the models Bedrock offers in the regions where we operate, and we have less control over the model internals than we would with SageMaker AI. If we later needed a model trained on our own labelled data with custom hosting, I would look at SageMaker AI, which gives more control but also means we operate more of the stack ourselves. Before committing, I would check that the chosen model meets our data-residency and cost constraints, because those limits matter more than convenience.
rubricPoints: Bedrock provides managed API access to foundation models without running infrastructure
SageMaker AI offers more control for building, training, and hosting custom models but adds operational work
A concrete limit is named, such as model availability by region or less control over model internals
The choice is tied to the requirements such as compliance, cost, or speed to market

suggested.rationale: This objective is a product catalogue and mapping of services to layers, which is best learned from reading and comparing the descriptions rather than from an existing or planned hands-on engine.

lessons.plain: Building on AWS generative AI services means renting a ready-made AI model instead of building one yourself. Think of it like hiring a commercial kitchen for a day rather than building a restaurant: the equipment, maintenance and expertise are someone else's job, and you pay for what you use. This lowers the barrier because a small team can add a working AI feature quickly, with less money up front and fewer specialist skills, and then learn from real users sooner. The trade-off is that you depend on the provider's models, prices and rules.
lessons.guessPrompt: A three-person startup wants to add an AI feature that writes product descriptions. Why might they start by calling a hosted AI service rather than training their own model, and what might they give up by doing so?
lessons.teach:
A managed service is one where the provider runs the underlying machinery, such as servers, scaling, patching and model hosting, and you use it through an interface, usually an API. An API is a set of request and response rules that your code calls over the network. Building on AWS generative AI services means calling foundation models that someone else has already trained and hosted. A foundation model is a large model trained on broad data that can handle many tasks. Training and hosting such a model is the expensive, specialist part, and that is what you skip.

The barrier drops for four reasons. Accessibility: a developer with an account and an API call can get a useful model response without machine-learning training. Efficiency: the team spends its time on the product rather than on infrastructure. Cost-effectiveness: you pay for what you use, often per token (a token is a small chunk of text, roughly a word or part of one), instead of a fixed server bill sitting idle. Speed to market: a prototype can run in days, so real feedback arrives sooner.

Worked example: a small team builds a tool that summarises support tickets. Step 1: the code sends each ticket's text to a hosted foundation model through the managed service. Step 2: the service returns a summary and reports how many tokens were read and written. Step 3: the team multiplies those tokens by the published price to estimate cost per ticket, then by 2,000 tickets a day. Step 4: they release a pilot to one support team within a week.

Common mistake: treating managed as meaning no design work. Because billing is per token, long prompts and long replies both add cost, and a feature that looks cheap in testing can become expensive at full traffic. The provider secures the infrastructure, but the team still owns its data handling and the quality of the output.

Consequence: if the application calls the model on every page view, both its bill and its response time grow with traffic, so the design must limit how often and how much the model is called. The lower barrier is real, but it shifts the work from building the model to using it well.

questions.prompt: A regional museum builds a visitor guide that answers questions using a hosted foundation model, which is a large pre-trained model that a provider runs for you. The team works through its cost estimate in four steps. Step 1: they log 200 sample visitor questions and find each one averages 120 tokens read by the model and 310 tokens written back. Step 2: they add these to get 430 tokens per question. Step 3 is missing. Step 4: they multiply the per-question cost by 900 questions a day across the museum's five halls. Which action completes Step 3?
choices: Apply the published input and output per-token prices of the chosen model to get the cost of one question
Divide the 430 tokens by 900 to get a per-question token count
Count only the written tokens, because the words the model reads are not billed
Ask the provider for a fixed monthly server fee and treat it as the per-question cost
questions.why: Because billing is per token, the team must convert the token counts into money using the published input and output prices to get the cost of one question before scaling it up.

questions.prompt: In plain terms, what does a managed generative AI service let a developer skip, and what does it let them do instead?
choices: It lets them skip training and hosting a foundation model, so they call one through an API and get a response
It lets them skip the product itself, so they only test the model and never ship a feature
It lets them skip all billing, so usage is free and the model runs without a provider
It lets them skip the API, so they write their own network protocol and host the model themselves
questions.why: A managed service runs the model's servers and hosting for you, so the developer's work is calling the model through an API rather than training or hosting it.

questions.prompt: A small startup has a feature that will be used only a few times a day on most days but occasionally in bursts during a product launch. Which cost arrangement suits this pattern best, and why?
choices: A fixed monthly fee for a dedicated server, because a steady bill is always cheapest
Buying a server outright, because owning hardware removes all usage costs
A per-token managed service with the longest possible prompts, because longer prompts reduce the number of calls
A per-token managed service, because you pay for the tokens used and not for capacity sitting idle between bursts
questions.why: Per-token billing means the startup pays only for usage, so quiet days cost little and bursts cost in proportion to the work done, unlike an idle fixed server bill.

questions.prompt: A product team puts a call to a hosted foundation model on every keystroke in a search box. They assume that because the service is managed, the design needs no thought. What is the most likely consequence for a running system?
choices: The provider automatically caches every keystroke, so the cost stays flat no matter how many calls are made
Nothing changes, because managed services do not bill for calls that happen during typing
The model cost and response time both grow with the number of calls, so the team needs to limit how often the model is called
Response time falls as traffic rises, because the managed service warms up under load
questions.why: Each call adds per-token cost and latency, so calling the model on every keystroke makes both grow with traffic, and the design must limit call frequency and size.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate who has never used a cloud AI service why building on AWS generative AI services lowers the barrier to launching an AI feature, and name one limit or trade-off the team must still manage.
lessons.modelAnswer: Managed AWS generative AI services host the foundation models for us, so we call them through an API instead of training or running models ourselves. That cuts the specialist skills, hardware and setup time needed, so we can get accessibility for developers without ML backgrounds, spend effort on the product, and ship a prototype quickly. Cost is pay-as-you-go, usually per token, so we avoid paying for idle servers. The trade-off is that the bill and latency grow with usage. Every long prompt and reply costs money, so we have to design to limit how many calls we make and how much text each one carries. We also still own our data handling and the quality of the output, because the provider only runs the infrastructure.
rubricPoints: Names the core idea: the provider hosts and runs the foundation model, so the team calls it through an API
Gives at least two of the four benefits: accessibility, efficiency, cost-effectiveness, speed to market
Explains that usage-based (per-token) pricing ties cost to how much the application uses the model
Names a real limit: cost and latency grow with traffic, and the team still owns data handling and output quality

suggested.rationale: The objective is about reasoning and explaining why the approach lowers barriers, and no listed mission or planned engine covers cloud AI service selection.

lessons.plain: When a company runs a generative AI tool, the model lives on computers owned by a cloud provider such as AWS. The question is who protects what. The provider handles the buildings, hardware, network and core software that run the service, and it publishes evidence that independent auditors have checked those controls. The company still decides who may use the tool, what data it sends in, where that data is kept, and whether answers are checked before customers see them. It is like renting a fully staffed office: the landlord locks the building, but you decide who gets a key and what you keep in your desk.
lessons.guessPrompt: A company runs its generative AI assistant on a major cloud provider. Which is the provider most likely responsible for: deciding which employees may call the assistant, or keeping the data centre's physical access controls and servers secure? Give your guess and one sentence of reasoning.
lessons.teach:
The shared responsibility model is the division of labour between a cloud provider and its customer. The provider is responsible for security of the cloud: data centres, physical access controls, servers, storage, the global network, and the managed software that runs the service. The customer is responsible for security in the cloud: its own data, who is allowed to call the service, how its applications are configured, and how outputs are used.

Compliance means meeting external rules and standards, such as privacy law or an industry audit. The provider can show auditors that its infrastructure meets many standards and publishes reports customers can read. That does not make the customer compliant automatically. A healthcare company still has to show that its data handling, retention and access rules satisfy the regulations that apply to it.

Responsibility and safety concern the content and effects of the model. Infrastructure cannot decide whether an answer is accurate or fair. Safety tools such as content filters, often called guardrails, let the customer block topics or harmful output, but the customer chooses the settings and watches the results.

Worked example: a support team builds an assistant on a managed model service. Step one: the provider keeps the model hardware patched and the facility locked. Step two: the team creates an access role that only the support application may use, so a leaked key cannot be used from elsewhere. Step three: they keep customer records encrypted with keys they control and choose a region where their data may be stored. Step four: they enable a guardrail that blocks card numbers, then sample answers each week to check accuracy.

Common mistake: treating 'the cloud is certified' as 'our system is safe'. Certification covers the provider's layer only.

Consequence: if the team skips step two and gives every developer full access, anyone with an account can call the model and read prompts containing customer data. The provider's strong infrastructure does not prevent that. The customer owns that outcome.

questions.prompt: A freight company builds a driver-notes summarizer on a managed model service. Step 1: the company limits the summarizer's access role so only the dispatch app can call it. Step 2: the provider keeps the servers patched and the data centre locked. Step 3: the company documents its own retention and access rules for driver records and checks them against the privacy rules that apply to the company. Step 4: a person reviews a sample of summaries each month for errors. Which statement correctly describes what the company must still do for its own compliance?
choices: Ask the provider to certify each summary as accurate before it reaches dispatch, since the provider owns the model.
Nothing further, because the provider's audit reports make the whole system compliant once the access role is set.
Turn on a guardrail that blocks driver names, which removes the need to review retention or access rules.
Show that its own data handling, retention and access rules satisfy the regulations that apply to it, because the provider's reports do not make the customer compliant automatically.
questions.why: The teaching text says provider audit reports do not make the customer compliant automatically, and the customer must show its own data handling, retention and access rules meet the applicable regulations.

questions.prompt: In the shared responsibility model, which of these is the customer's responsibility rather than the provider's?
choices: Maintaining the global network that carries requests between regions.
Locking the data centre and controlling physical access to storage hardware.
Keeping the physical servers that run a managed model service patched and secured.
Deciding which staff members and applications are allowed to call the model and with what permissions.
questions.why: The customer is responsible for security in the cloud, which includes who is allowed to call the service; the provider handles the data centres, hardware, storage and network.

questions.prompt: A retail team's model service is run by a provider with strong, certified infrastructure. The team gives every developer full access to the account. What is the most accurate description of the resulting risk?
choices: The provider must delete the prompts after each call to protect the customer.
Anyone with an account can call the model and read prompts containing customer data, and the customer owns that outcome, not the provider.
The risk is small, because certified infrastructure blocks unauthorised calls automatically.
The provider's certification has lapsed, so the infrastructure is no longer trustworthy.
questions.why: Strong provider infrastructure does not stop an overly broad access setup; access control is the customer's responsibility, so the customer carries the consequence.

questions.prompt: A team uses a guardrail on a managed model to block certain topics and harmful output. Which statement about guardrails is correct?
choices: They let the customer block topics or harmful output, but the customer chooses the settings and still needs to watch the results.
They guarantee that every answer is accurate and fair, so monitoring is unnecessary.
They are set by the provider and cannot be changed, so the customer does not need to review them.
They replace the need for compliance work, because blocking content is the same as meeting privacy law.
questions.why: Guardrails are content safety tools the customer configures and monitors; they do not decide accuracy, fairness, or legal compliance on their own.

lessons.explainPrompt: A teammate says that because our generative AI service runs on AWS, we are automatically secure and compliant. Explain to them, in your own words, what AWS handles, what we still have to handle, and one limit of what AWS certifications can prove.
lessons.modelAnswer: That is only half true. AWS secures the physical facilities, the hardware, the network and the managed service software, and it provides audit reports showing those controls were checked. We still own what goes into the system: who gets access, which roles and keys they use, where our data is stored and which region it stays in, and whether the model's answers are filtered and reviewed. Compliance is shared the same way. AWS can show its layer meets a standard, but we must show our data handling meets the rules that apply to us. A limit to remember is that no infrastructure certificate tells us whether a model's answer is accurate or fair, so we still need our own evaluation and guardrail settings before going live.
rubricPoints: AWS secures the infrastructure and the managed service layer.
The customer secures its own data, access permissions and configuration.
Provider compliance reports do not make the customer's own system compliant.
Accuracy and safety of outputs remain the customer's to test and filter.

suggested.rationale: The core skill here is explaining who is responsible for what in a shared setup, which is best practised by saying it back to a teammate.

lessons.plain: Generative AI services are often billed by how much text the model reads and writes, and the way you buy capacity changes what you pay and how fast answers come back. Think of a shared taxi rank versus booking a car for the whole day: the taxi is cheap when you need it occasionally, but at a busy hour you may wait, while the booked car is always there and always costs money, even when it sits idle. This lesson compares those choices across AWS generative AI services: how quickly answers arrive, how reliably the service stays up, which regions offer a given model, what tokens cost, reserved capacity, and custom models.
lessons.guessPrompt: Suppose your app answers customer questions with a large language model. Traffic is quiet most of the day but spikes sharply at lunchtime. Would you rather pay per request using shared capacity, or reserve dedicated capacity at a fixed hourly rate? Give one reason for each choice before reading on.
lessons.teach:
A token is the small chunk of text a model reads or writes, often a word or part of one. Most generative AI services bill by counting tokens: input tokens in your request and output tokens in the reply. That is the first cost lever. The second is how you buy capacity, and that is where services differ.

On-demand pricing charges per token with no commitment. You pay only for what you use and start instantly, but the work shares capacity with other customers, so it can be slowed or throttled at busy times, and the per-token rate is usually the highest. Provisioned throughput reserves a fixed amount of model capacity, billed by the hour, often with a term commitment that lowers the rate. Latency becomes more predictable, but you pay whether or not traffic arrives. Batch inference trades speed for a lower price: you submit many requests together and collect results later.

Custom models, made by fine-tuning a base model on your own examples, add a training bill and often need dedicated capacity to serve, so their running cost is higher than the base model's. Regional coverage also matters: a model may be offered in only some regions, and cross-region routing can improve availability by sending overflow to another region in the same geography, at the price of longer distances and less predictable latency.

Worked example. Suppose an assistant sends about 2 million input tokens and 500,000 output tokens a day, and the on-demand rate is one unit per thousand input tokens and three units per thousand output tokens. Input costs 2,000 units and output costs 1,500 units, so the daily cost is 3,500 units. Multiply your monthly volume by the rate, then compare that with the hourly reserved cost multiplied by the hours in a month. If the reservation is cheaper and traffic is steady, reserve; if traffic is spiky, stay on demand.

Common mistake: comparing a per-token price with an hourly reserved price without first estimating real volume, or sizing a reservation for launch-day peak that then sits idle. In a running system, an on-demand app with no headroom can return throttled replies during a traffic surge, while an oversized reservation quietly burns money overnight.

questions.prompt: A support team's ticket classifier sends about 800,000 input tokens and 120,000 output tokens per day, billed on demand at 2 units per thousand input tokens and 5 units per thousand output tokens. Input costs 800 x 2 = 1,600 units and output costs 120 x 5 = 600 units, so the daily cost is 2,200 units. Step left for you: the team runs the classifier every day of a 30-day month, so the monthly on-demand cost is 2,200 x 30. What is that monthly cost?
choices: 66,000 units
6,600 units
62,000 units
2,200 units
questions.why: Monthly cost is the daily cost multiplied by the number of days, and 2,200 x 30 equals 66,000 units.

questions.prompt: A drafting tool sends 300,000 input tokens and 90,000 output tokens each day. On-demand pricing is 1 unit per thousand input tokens and 4 units per thousand output tokens. What is the daily cost?
choices: 360 units
1,020 units
300 units
660 units
questions.why: Input costs 300 x 1 = 300 units and output costs 90 x 4 = 360 units, so the total is 660 units; the other choices count only one side or add the wrong pieces.

questions.prompt: A retail team's shopping assistant has steady traffic all day, with one short surge during a sale. The team is considering staying on pure on-demand pricing. What is the main risk of that choice?
choices: Replies may be slowed or throttled during the surge because capacity is shared with other customers
Batch results arrive too late for shoppers to use them
The reserved hourly charge keeps billing even when no traffic arrives
Fine-tuning the model on sale examples adds a training bill
questions.why: On-demand work shares capacity with other customers, so it can be throttled at busy times, while the other options describe reservations, batch inference, or custom models instead.

questions.prompt: A company's model is offered only in one region, but its users are mostly in another country within the same geography. The company enables cross-region routing to improve availability. What does it give up in exchange?
choices: Fixed, guaranteed response times from the reserved capacity
Longer distances between the user and the model, with less predictable latency
The need to count input and output tokens separately
A lower per-token price than on-demand in the home region
questions.why: Cross-region routing sends overflow to another region, which adds distance and makes latency less predictable, as the text describes; it does not change token pricing or make response times fixed.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate when you would choose on-demand pricing over provisioned throughput for a generative AI feature, and name one limit or tradeoff of the choice you make.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would start on on-demand for a new feature because we do not yet know our volume, and paying per token means no monthly commitment and no idle cost. The tradeoff is that shared capacity can slow or throttle replies during busy periods, and the per-token rate is higher than a reserved rate once volume is steady. So I would measure real input and output token counts over a few weeks, multiply by the per-token rate, and compare that with the hourly reserved cost over a month. If the reserved option is cheaper, traffic is steady, and latency matters, I would move to provisioned throughput. If the work is batch-like, such as nightly summaries, batch processing is cheaper still but returns results later. I would also confirm the model I need is offered in my region before committing to anything.
rubricPoints: Explains that on-demand bills per token with no commitment but can be throttled under shared load.
Explains that provisioned throughput bills reserved capacity by the hour, giving predictable latency while charging even when idle.
Says to compare real token volume against the reserved hourly cost before choosing.
Names one limit, such as regional model availability or a higher per-token rate at steady volume.

suggested.rationale: The planned cost-model engine would let you compare on-demand and reserved costs across volumes in fictional credits, which is the calculation this objective depends on.

lessons.plain: Choosing a foundation model means picking which large, pretrained AI model to use for a job, much as you would pick a vehicle for a delivery route. A small, cheap model handles short, simple tasks well, while a long document in several languages may need a bigger, slower, more expensive one. The useful habit is to write down what the job needs first: how much text goes in and out, how fast the answer must arrive, what kinds of input it takes, which languages matter, and what each request may cost. Then compare candidate models against that list instead of choosing the most famous one.
lessons.guessPrompt: A support chatbot must answer within two seconds, handle customers in Spanish and English, and run about a million times a month on a tight budget. Name two properties of a model you would check first, and say which one you would be willing to give up if the budget breaks.
lessons.teach:
A foundation model is a large model trained on broad data that can be used for many tasks. Choosing one means matching its properties to your requirement. Modality is the kind of data it accepts and produces, such as text, images or audio. Latency is the time from sending a request to receiving the answer. Model size is roughly how many learned numbers (parameters) the model has; bigger models usually reason better but cost more and respond more slowly. Input and output length are limited by the context window, the maximum amount of text the model can read and write in one call, and usage is billed per token, a small chunk of text. Prompt caching means the provider can reuse the processed form of a prompt prefix that repeats across calls, which lowers cost and delay for that repeated part.

Worked example: a firm summarises 2,000 contracts overnight, each about 15,000 tokens, in English and German. Step one: the input is long, so the context window must comfortably hold a contract. Step two: two languages, so the model must be multilingual. Step three: the job runs overnight, so latency matters little. Step four: 2,000 contracts times 15,000 tokens is 30 million input tokens, so cost per token decides the budget. Step five: the same instruction block repeats in every call, so prompt caching can cut the repeated cost. A mid-sized multilingual model with a large window and caching fits; the largest model is not needed.

Common mistake: picking the biggest model by default. In a live chat path, that choice raises latency and per-call cost, and users may hit timeouts before the answer arrives.

Choose the model that meets every stated requirement at the lowest acceptable cost and delay.

questions.prompt: A logistics company classifies 40,000 shipment emails per day, each about 300 tokens, written in Spanish and Korean. A dispatcher waits on each label, so replies must arrive in under one second. Step one: latency is critical because a person is waiting on a live path. Step two: the model must handle both Spanish and Korean. Step three: each email is short, so a modest context window is enough. Step four is left for you to supply. Step five: the same 1,200-token instruction block repeats in every call, so prompt caching can cut that repeated cost. Which statement correctly completes step four?
choices: Choose the largest model available, because classification accuracy matters more than per-token price at this volume.
Work out that 40,000 emails times 300 tokens is 12 million input tokens a day, so price per token is the main budget driver and the cheapest model that handles both languages is the candidate.
Raise the output limit to the model maximum so the dispatcher sees a long explanation with every label.
Ignore token counts entirely, since the one-second limit is the only selection criterion that matters.
questions.why: Step four is the cost calculation: multiplying daily emails by tokens per email gives the daily token volume, and that volume shows that price per token drives the budget, so the cheapest model meeting the language and latency needs is the right candidate.

questions.prompt: A product team's assistant gives accurate answers, but each reply takes about nine seconds to appear on screen. Which selection property is the team measuring when they time that wait?
choices: Latency, meaning the time from sending a request to receiving the answer
Parameter count, meaning the number of learned numbers inside the model
Modality, meaning the kinds of data the model accepts and produces
Context window, meaning the maximum amount of text read and written in one call
questions.why: Latency is defined as the time from sending a request to receiving the answer, which is exactly the nine-second wait described.

questions.prompt: A legal team wants one model to read a 120-page manual in a single request and then answer questions about it. Which criterion must they check first before comparing prices?
choices: Whether the model accepts audio input
Whether the model is the largest available, since bigger always reads more
Whether the model's context window can hold the whole manual plus the answer
Whether the provider offers prompt caching for the manual
questions.why: The context window limits how much text the model can read and write in one call, so it must hold the whole manual before price or other features matter.

questions.prompt: A customer service system bills per token and sends the same 2,500-token set of system instructions with each of 60,000 calls a day. Which selection feature can reduce the cost of that repeated instruction block?
choices: Choosing the largest model, since bigger models lower the per-token charge
Switching to an audio modality, which reduces the number of tokens billed
Raising the output length limit so each reply carries more text
Prompt caching, where the provider reuses the processed form of a repeated prompt prefix
questions.why: Prompt caching reuses the processed form of a prefix that repeats across calls, lowering cost and delay for that repeated part, while the other options either raise cost or do not affect repeated input tokens.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would pick a foundation model for a new feature, naming at least one limit or tradeoff of the choice you would make.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would start by writing the requirements down: the kinds of input and output, the languages, how long a typical request and response are, how fast the answer must come back, and what each call may cost. Then I would shortlist models that cover the modality, languages and context length, and compare their price per token and typical response time. I would check whether prompt caching applies, because a repeated instruction block can make a big difference to cost. The main tradeoff is that a larger model usually answers more accurately but costs more and responds more slowly, so I would pick the smallest one that passes our own test set, not the most capable one. The limit is that a cheaper model may need better prompts or more examples to match quality, and that extra effort has its own cost. I would also re-check the choice when prices or requirements change.
rubricPoints: Start from the stated requirements such as modality, languages, length and latency
Explain cost per token and how prompt caching can reduce repeated cost
State the tradeoff that bigger models are more capable but slower and pricier
Choose the smallest model that meets the requirements, verified on your own test cases

suggested.rationale: This objective is a set of selection criteria and catalogue facts that no listed mission or planned engine currently drills, so reading the reference material is the best fit.

lessons.plain: Inference parameters are the settings you choose each time a language model generates a reply, separate from the prompt itself. Temperature controls how predictable the wording is: low values make the model pick the most likely next word almost every time, while high values let it choose less likely words more often. Input length is how much text you can feed in, and output length caps how much the model may write back. Think of a writer given a brief: you can ask for careful, safe phrasing or loose, creative phrasing, and you can set a word limit on the reply. These settings do not teach the model anything; they only shape one answer.
lessons.guessPrompt: If you ask the same language model the same question twice with its creativity setting at zero, what would you expect to see, and what would change if you turned that setting up to a high value?
lessons.teach:
Inference is the act of running a trained model to produce output from your input. A language model writes text one token at a time, where a token is a small chunk of text such as a word or part of a word. At each step the model assigns a probability to every possible next token. Inference parameters are the knobs that control how that choice is made, and they are set per request rather than being baked into the model.

Temperature rescales those probabilities before one token is picked. At temperature zero the model almost always takes the single most likely token, so the output is close to repeatable. Higher temperature flattens the probabilities, so less likely tokens get picked more often. Temperature changes variety and randomness. It does not make the model more accurate or more truthful.

Worked example: the prompt is 'Name a colour.' Suppose the model scores blue at 0.5, green at 0.3 and purple at 0.2. Step 1: at temperature zero, it picks blue on every run. Step 2: at a higher temperature, the scores are flattened, so blue might fall to about 0.4 and green and purple rise. Step 3: over many runs, you will now see green and purple sometimes. Nothing about the colour answer became more correct; the spread just widened.

Input length is the total amount of text the model can read in one call, including the instructions, the conversation so far and any retrieved documents. If the input is too long, the request fails or the oldest text is cut. Output length is a cap on how many tokens the model may generate. When it is hit, the reply stops mid-sentence, and you still pay for the tokens produced.

Common mistake: raising temperature to make answers more correct. It only adds variety, so a wrong answer may simply become a different wrong answer. In a running system, a low output cap can cut a JSON reply in half, so the parser that depends on it fails in production. A high temperature in a classification pipeline can give different labels for the same ticket on retry, which breaks reproducibility.

questions.prompt: A logistics company runs a nightly job that asks a model to return one JSON record per delivery depot, with six fields. Each complete record takes about 180 output tokens. The team sets the output length cap to 150 tokens and leaves temperature at zero. Step 1: the model begins writing the first record. Step 2: at 150 tokens, the model is stopped by the cap, partway through the record. Step 3: [missing step]. Step 4: the parser that reads the JSON receives an incomplete record and fails the job.
choices: Step 3: raise the input length so the model has more room to finish writing the record.
Step 3: raise temperature to zero so the model writes the JSON more accurately within the same cap.
Step 3: raise the output length cap above the roughly 180 tokens needed, because a reply stopped by the cap is cut off mid-output and the JSON breaks.
Step 3: lower the temperature to shorten the reply so it fits under the cap.
questions.why: The output cap is a hard ceiling on generated tokens, so the cap must be above the length of a complete reply, and the other choices either misuse temperature or confuse input length with output length.

questions.prompt: A bank uses a model to label each card transaction as approved or review. The auditors want the same transaction to get the same label if it is run again. Which setting best supports that requirement?
choices: Raise the temperature so the labels vary less between runs.
Lower the temperature toward zero so the most likely label is picked on each run.
Raise the output length cap so the label has more room to be written.
Increase the input length so the model reads more transaction history.
questions.why: At low temperature the model almost always picks the single most likely token, which makes repeated runs close to identical, while the other settings do not control choice randomness.

questions.prompt: A university tool answers student questions about exam dates. One answer gave the wrong date. The team raises temperature to 1.0, expecting the answers to become more correct. What is the most likely result?
choices: The dates stay the same, because temperature has no effect on randomness.
The answers vary more between runs, and a wrong date may simply be replaced by a different wrong one.
The dates become correct because higher temperature checks the model's facts.
The answers become longer, which makes the date more likely to be right.
questions.why: Temperature changes variety and randomness only; it does not make the model more accurate or truthful, so a higher setting can produce a different wrong answer.

questions.prompt: A legal team sends a 40-page policy document plus a long chat history to a model in one call. The total text is larger than the model's input length. What should the team expect?
choices: The model automatically summarises the document so the call still completes.
The temperature is lowered, which shrinks the document so it fits.
The request can fail, or the oldest text in the call can be cut, because the input exceeds what the model can read at once.
The output cap is raised to make room, and the full reply is returned.
questions.why: Input length is the total text the model can read in one call, and exceeding it causes a failure or cuts the oldest text, while the other options describe behaviour the teaching text does not support.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what temperature and output length each control in a language model, and name one tradeoff you would weigh when setting them for a customer-facing support assistant.
lessons.modelAnswer: Temperature controls how much randomness the model has when choosing each next token. Near zero, it nearly always picks the most likely token, so answers are consistent and repeatable. Higher values make wording more varied, but they do not make facts more accurate, so a wrong answer can just become a different wrong answer. Output length is a hard cap on how many tokens come back. If the cap is too low, the reply can stop mid-sentence, which matters if something downstream parses it. For a support assistant, I would keep temperature low so customers get consistent policy answers, and set the output cap high enough that answers finish, accepting a little extra cost. The tradeoff is consistency and cost against natural-sounding variety.
rubricPoints: Temperature controls randomness and variety in word choice, not factual accuracy.
Low temperature gives more repeatable output; high temperature gives more variety.
Output length is a cap, and hitting it truncates the reply, which can break parsers.
Names a concrete tradeoff such as consistency versus variety, or cost versus complete answers.

suggested.rationale: No listed mission or planned engine covers language model inference settings, and the core skill here is explaining the tradeoff in your own words.

lessons.plain: Retrieval Augmented Generation, usually called RAG, lets a language model answer questions using documents it was never trained on. Instead of relying only on what it absorbed during training, the system first searches your own material, such as manuals, policies, or tickets, for the passages most related to the question. It then gives those passages to the model along with the question, and the model writes an answer based on them. It works like an open-book exam: you may look things up before you write, rather than answering purely from memory.
lessons.guessPrompt: A support chatbot must answer questions about a company's leave policy, which changes every few months. If you relied only on the model's built-in knowledge, what would you expect to go wrong, and what simple change might fix it?
lessons.teach:
Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) is a pattern in which the system retrieves relevant material from a source you control and places it in the prompt before a foundation model (a large pre-trained AI model that generates text) writes its answer. The model itself is not changed; it receives fresh context for each question. Documents are first split into chunks, which are short passages. Each chunk is turned into an embedding, a list of numbers that represents its meaning, and stored in a vector database, a store built to find the items whose embeddings are closest to a query's embedding. Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases is AWS's managed feature for this: you point it at a document source, and it handles chunking, embedding, storage, and retrieval for you.

Why it works: a model's built-in knowledge is frozen at training time and cannot include your private or newest documents. Retrieval brings that knowledge into the prompt at question time, so updating a document updates the answers without retraining.

Worked example: an HR assistant. Step 1, the leave policy is chunked and each chunk is embedded. Step 2, an employee asks how many weeks of parental leave they get, and the question is embedded. Step 3, the system finds the chunks whose embeddings are closest to the question. Step 4, the prompt is built from an instruction, those chunks, and the question. Step 5, the model writes an answer that points to the passage it used.

Common mistake: assuming the model keeps the document's facts after the document changes. Retrieval reads whatever the index holds, so if the source is updated but the knowledge base is not synced, answers quote the old policy with confidence.

Consequence: if the right chunk is never retrieved, the model either declines or guesses, so retrieval quality sets the ceiling on answer quality. RAG suits knowledge that changes often or must stay private; it is a way to supply knowledge, not a way to change how the model behaves.

questions.prompt: A logistics firm loads its 40-page warehouse safety handbook into a RAG setup. Step 1: the handbook is split into 212 chunks, and each chunk is turned into an embedding and stored in a vector database. Step 2: a forklift driver asks, What is the maximum load for the Type B pallet rack in aisle 7? The question is embedded, and the system finds the chunks whose embeddings are closest to it. Step 3 is missing. Step 4: the model writes an answer that points to the chunk it used. Which description fills step 3?
choices: The system builds a prompt from an instruction, the retrieved chunks, and the question.
The system fine-tunes the model on the whole handbook so it memorises each rack limit permanently.
The system renames the handbook file so the index can sort it by aisle number instead.
The system deletes older chunks so only the newest text remains before any answer is written.
questions.why: Step 3 is where the retrieved chunks are placed in the prompt alongside an instruction and the question, because RAG supplies knowledge through the prompt and never changes the model itself.

questions.prompt: A company edits its returns-policy document but does not retrain any model. What changes the answers its RAG assistant gives?
choices: The foundation model's weights are adjusted to store the new policy.
The model's frozen training knowledge is extended to cover the new return window.
The old embeddings are copied into the model's training data.
The new text is chunked and embedded again, so retrieval returns updated chunks.
questions.why: In RAG the model is not changed; answers follow whatever the index holds, so re-chunking and re-embedding the new text is what updates the answers.

questions.prompt: A team edits its leave policy in the source folder but does not sync the knowledge base. Employees then receive the old allowance from the assistant. Which explanation fits the teaching?
choices: The model has learned the old policy in its weights and is ignoring the retrieved text.
The embedding step rewrote the old policy automatically before the question arrived.
The chunks were too long, so the model discarded the new policy as noise.
Retrieval reads the index as it stands, so old chunks still reach the prompt.
questions.why: Retrieval reads whatever the index holds, so when the source changes but the knowledge base is not synced, the outdated chunks are still placed in the prompt and quoted confidently.

questions.prompt: A retailer wants a chatbot to answer questions about its product catalogue, which changes every day, and the catalogue must stay inside the company's own store. Which approach fits the RAG pattern?
choices: Index the catalogue in a synced knowledge base.
Pre-train a new model from scratch on the catalogue every morning.
Paste the entire catalogue into every prompt by hand.
Fine-tune the model once and rely on its built-in knowledge afterward.
questions.why: RAG suits knowledge that changes often or must stay private, and syncing the index after each update refreshes answers without retraining the model.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate, in your own words, what RAG does, when you would choose it over retraining or fine-tuning a model, and one limit or tradeoff it brings.
lessons.modelAnswer: RAG means that before the model answers, the system looks up the most relevant passages from our own documents and includes them in the prompt, so the model answers from current material instead of only from what it learned during training. I would choose it when the knowledge changes often, such as policies or product docs, because updating the source documents and re-syncing the index is cheaper and faster than retraining or fine-tuning. Fine-tuning is better for changing how the model behaves or writes, not for keeping facts current. The main limit is that answer quality depends on retrieval: if the search misses the right passage, the model may decline or guess, and if we forget to re-sync after an update, it can quote stale information confidently. So we need to test retrieval quality and keep the index in step with the source.
rubricPoints: RAG retrieves relevant passages from your own documents at question time and adds them to the prompt
The model itself is not retrained, so knowledge updates come from changing the source and re-syncing
RAG suits fresh or private knowledge, while fine-tuning changes behaviour or style
A key limit is that answers depend on retrieval quality and on the index staying current with the source

suggested.rationale: Choosing between RAG and other customization approaches for a given freshness and cost requirement is best practised as an exam-style scenario to reason through, and no listed mission or planned engine covers it.

lessons.plain: An embedding is a list of numbers that stands for the meaning of a piece of text, an image, or other content, so that things with similar meaning get similar lists. A vector database is storage built to hold very many of these lists and quickly find the ones closest to a new question's list. On AWS, several ordinary database services can take on this job. Think of a library that shelves books by meaning instead of alphabetically: you describe an idea and the nearest shelf gives you the closest books. This objective is about recognizing which AWS service fits that job.
lessons.guessPrompt: If every help article is stored as a list of numbers that reflects its meaning, how could a computer find the article closest to a new question without rereading every article each time?
lessons.teach:
An embedding is a list of numbers produced by an embedding model, which represents the meaning of a piece of content such as a sentence or an image. Similar meanings produce lists that sit close together. Each list is called a vector. A vector database is storage designed to hold very many vectors and answer one question quickly: which stored vectors are nearest to this new one? That operation is called similarity search or nearest-neighbour search. To keep it fast at scale, the database builds an index, a structure that avoids comparing the query against every stored vector.

Why it works: distance between vectors stands in for closeness of meaning, so a question like 'I forgot my login' can match an article titled 'Reset your password' even though they share few words.

Worked example: a company embeds 10,000 help articles and stores each vector with its article ID. A user asks a question. First, the same embedding model turns the question into a vector. Second, the database searches its index for the stored vectors nearest to it. Third, it returns the three closest article IDs, and the application uses those articles to build an answer.

On AWS, several services can do this. Amazon OpenSearch Service has vector search built in alongside text search. Amazon Aurora and Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL store vectors through the pgvector extension, which keeps vectors in the same tables as ordinary business rows. Amazon Neptune is a graph database, so its vector capability suits data where relationships between items matter as much as similarity.

Common mistake: believing the vector database creates the embeddings. It does not; the embedding model does. Query vectors and stored vectors must also come from the same model, because numbers from different models cannot be compared.

Consequence: if the embedding model is changed, every stored vector must be regenerated, or search results quietly become meaningless. The right service is the one whose existing data and operations already match the application's needs.

questions.prompt: Tessaly Freight already keeps its shipment records in Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL. It wants dispatchers to search 48,000 shipment-exception notes by meaning, so that a query like 'truck held at border overnight' finds notes that describe similar delays even when they use different words. Step 1: the team lists the requirement, which is search by meaning over the notes while each note stays linked to its shipment row. Step 2: this step is missing and you must supply it. Step 3: the team chooses Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL with the pgvector extension, so the vectors sit in the same tables as the shipment rows and no separate database is needed. Which completion fills step 2?
choices: They re-embed the shipment rows with a second model so that each row holds two vectors to choose from.
They export the notes to a separate vector database so that the relational tables stay unchanged.
They let the database create the embeddings itself, since pgvector generates vectors from text automatically.
They confirm that the notes and the incoming dispatcher queries will both be turned into vectors by the same embedding model, because vectors from different models cannot be compared.
questions.why: Stored vectors and query vectors must come from the same embedding model, and pgvector stores and searches vectors but does not generate them.

questions.prompt: A product team describes its new feature as 'a vector database that writes embeddings for our documents.' Which statement corrects this description?
choices: A vector database stores and searches vectors, while the embedding model is what turns each document into a vector.
A vector database is a special table type that holds only the IDs of documents, not their meaning.
A vector database compares documents word by word and returns the ones with the most matching words.
A vector database turns documents into vectors and then discards the original text.
questions.why: The teaching text says the vector database does not create embeddings; the embedding model does, and the database's job is storing vectors and answering nearest-neighbour searches.

questions.prompt: A regional museum with 3,200 object records wants to find items connected through donors, loans and exhibitions, where the relationships between items matter as much as how similar their descriptions are. Which AWS service's vector capability best fits this need?
choices: Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL, because it stores vectors as ordinary rows with no relationship support.
Amazon Neptune, because it is a graph database and its vector capability suits data where relationships between items matter.
Amazon Aurora, because it is designed mainly for storing photographs as vectors.
Amazon OpenSearch Service, because it only supports text search over single documents.
questions.why: The teaching text describes Neptune as a graph database whose vector capability suits data where relationships between items matter as much as similarity.

questions.prompt: A support team switches its embedding model from model X to model Y. It re-embeds new articles with model Y but leaves the 10,000 vectors already stored from model X unchanged. A user then searches with a question embedded by model Y. What is the likely result?
choices: The search returns the correct articles because vectors from any two models can be compared once they are indexed.
The database automatically converts the old vectors to model Y, so no problem occurs.
The search still works fine for the new articles only, and the old ones are silently skipped with an error.
Search results quietly become meaningless, because the query and the old stored vectors come from different models and cannot be compared.
questions.why: The teaching text says changing the embedding model requires regenerating every stored vector, or results quietly become meaningless, since numbers from different models cannot be compared.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what an embedding and a vector database are, and why choosing between Aurora and OpenSearch Service for a retrieval store is a tradeoff rather than a single right answer. Name one real limit of this approach.
lessons.modelAnswer: An embedding is a list of numbers that a model produces to represent the meaning of some content, so similar content ends up with similar numbers. A vector database stores many of these and quickly finds the ones nearest to a query's vector, which is how a system finds relevant passages to feed a model. On AWS, OpenSearch Service is built for search at scale and has vector search alongside text search, so it is a natural fit when search is the main job. Aurora or RDS for PostgreSQL with pgvector fits when the vectors should live beside ordinary business tables and transactional data, and the team already runs PostgreSQL. Neptune fits when relationships between items matter as much as similarity. So the choice is a tradeoff among scale, existing skills, data shape, and operating cost. One real limit is that similarity search returns what is close in meaning, not what is correct, so retrieved text can still be irrelevant or outdated.
rubricPoints: Defines an embedding as a numeric representation of meaning produced by a model.
Explains that a vector database performs nearest-neighbour similarity search over stored vectors.
Contrasts at least two AWS services by the workload each suits.
Names a real limit, such as retrieved results being close in meaning but not necessarily correct or current.

suggested.rationale: This objective is a service-selection fact set best learned by reading the product descriptions and fit criteria rather than by a hands-on mission.

lessons.plain: Every time you make an AI model fit your business, you pay somewhere: in money to build it, in effort to teach it, or in extra work on every question it answers. The options run from rebuilding a whole model, which is the most expensive, to pasting the right facts into the question, which is the cheapest to start. The skill is matching the option to how much the model must know, how often that knowledge changes, and how many questions you will answer. This lesson lays out those trade-offs so you can defend a choice on cost and freshness.
lessons.guessPrompt: A company wants a chatbot that answers questions from its 500-page HR handbook, and the handbook changes every quarter. Before reading on, which approach would you expect to be cheapest to start with, and what would make you change your mind?
lessons.teach:
Pre-training means building a model from nothing by training it on enormous amounts of general text. It takes huge compute and data, so almost no business does it. Fine-tuning means taking an existing model and training it further on your own labeled examples, so its behavior or style changes.
