Trusting the model's own confidence statement attached to each description.
Counting how many words each description has and picking the model that writes the shortest ones.
A public benchmark dataset of general language tasks, scored automatically.
questions.why: Tone is hard to measure automatically, so people scoring outputs against a written rubric is the approach that fits this need.

questions.prompt: A team reports a 92% score on a public benchmark for their chatbot and wants to justify using it to process insurance claims. What is the main weakness of that justification?
choices: Automatic scoring cannot run on chatbot answers, so the percentage cannot be interpreted at all.
Benchmarks always contain too few questions to produce a stable number, so any percentage from one is essentially random noise.
It measures general skill, and the model may have seen those questions in training, so the score can be inflated for claims work.
The benchmark is free, so its score is unreliable by default.
questions.why: A public benchmark measures general skill rather than the team's business, and possible exposure to test questions during training can inflate the score, so it does not show fitness for insurance claims.

questions.prompt: A team uses Amazon Bedrock Model Evaluation to compare two models on their own prompts. Which statement is accurate?
choices: The service decides which answers are good for the team's claims process, so the team only needs to read the final ranking.
Because the service is managed, its results replace any need for a test dataset built from the team's own prompts.
The service runs the dataset and scoring, but the team still has to decide what counts as a good answer for its task.
Once the run finishes, the ranking is a certified quality guarantee for the model in production.
questions.why: Amazon Bedrock Model Evaluation, a managed AWS service, removes setup work for running and comparing models, but defining what good means for the task remains the team's responsibility.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would choose between human review, a benchmark dataset, and Amazon Bedrock Model Evaluation when picking a model for a new internal tool. Name one limit of the approach you would not rely on alone.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would start with a small dataset of real questions from our own team, with answers we agree are good. That lets me run candidate models through Amazon Bedrock Model Evaluation or a similar setup, so the comparison is repeatable and cheap. I would then have two or three people rate a sample of outputs on a short rubric, because automatic scores can miss tone, missing details, or confident wrong answers. I would use a public benchmark only as a rough filter to drop weak models early. The main limit of benchmarks is that they measure general skill on someone else's questions, and a model may have seen those questions in training, so the score can look better than real performance. Human review has the opposite limit: it is slow and costs money per item, so I would keep the sample small but representative of the hard cases.
rubricPoints: Names a benchmark dataset and says it measures general skill, not the team's own task
Explains that human review catches qualities automatic scores miss, such as tone and usefulness
Describes Amazon Bedrock Model Evaluation as a managed way to run and compare evaluations
States a real limit, such as contamination of benchmarks or the cost and slowness of human review
Says the team's own representative test data should decide the final choice

suggested.rationale: Choosing an evaluation approach for a given situation is best practised by reasoning through an exam-style scenario, and no listed mission or planned engine covers model evaluation directly.

lessons.plain: When a model writes a summary, a translation, or an answer, someone has to decide whether it is any good. Some checks are automatic: they compare the model's words against a reference answer a person wrote and count how much overlaps. Others use a second language model as a grader that reads the answer and scores it against a rubric, much like a teacher marking an essay. Each method is a different ruler that measures something slightly different, so the job is to pick the one that fits the task and to know what it cannot see.
lessons.guessPrompt: A chatbot answers a customer's question with a sentence that means the same thing as the approved reference answer but uses completely different words. Would you expect a simple word-overlap score to rate it high or low, and why?
lessons.teach: ROUGE, BLEU and BERTScore are automatic scores that compare a model's output with one or more reference texts written by people. ROUGE, short for Recall-Oriented Understudy for Gisting Evaluation, mostly asks how much of the reference shows up in the output. It counts shared word sequences called n-grams, meaning runs of n consecutive words, and it is popular for summaries because a good summary should cover the key content of the source. BLEU, short for Bilingual Evaluation Understudy, asks the opposite question: how much of the output appears in the reference, with a penalty for output that is too short. It was built for machine translation. BERTScore compares meaning rather than exact words. It turns each word into a vector from a language model and matches words by how close their vectors are, so a correct paraphrase can still score well. LLM-as-a-judge uses a capable model, given a rubric such as accuracy, helpfulness or tone, to read an answer and give a score with a reason. It can assess open-ended answers that have no single reference, but the judge carries its own biases, such as favouring longer answers. Worked example: a model compresses a 300-word incident report into a 50-word note. The reference note says the cache was cleared and latency dropped. The model's note says the cache was flushed and latency fell. ROUGE finds few identical word sequences, so it scores low even though the meaning matches. BERTScore, matching by meaning, scores high. An LLM judge asked whether the note is faithful and complete would also pass it. Common mistake: treating a high ROUGE or BLEU number as proof the answer is correct. These metrics reward word overlap, so a fluent wrong answer that reuses the reference's words can score well. Consequence: a team that ships a model on one overlap score may hide regressions that users notice immediately. Overlap metrics measure similarity to a reference, not correctness.

questions.prompt: Harbourline, a shipping firm, wants to know whether a model's German translations of short delivery notes are good enough to use. Their team works through four steps. Step 1: they recognise this is a translation task, so BLEU, a score built for machine translation that measures how much of the output appears in a human reference, is a natural first measure. Step 2: they note that BLEU also penalises output that is too short, so it checks length as well as overlap. Step 3: they test a correct German note that uses different wording from the reference, and BLEU drops because the word sequences differ. Step 4: the team has to decide how to read the BLEU score before shipping the model.
choices: Treat the BLEU score as a pass mark, since it measures whether the translation is correct.
Switch to ROUGE, because ROUGE is the metric built for translation and so will fix the low score.

Pair BLEU with a meaning-based check, such as BERTScore or a human-reviewed sample, because a low BLEU on a correct paraphrase does not prove the translation is wrong, and a high one does not prove it is right.
Ship the model without further checks, because BLEU rewards word overlap, which means a high score shows the translation is accurate.
questions.why: BLEU measures overlap with a reference rather than correctness, so a meaning-based check or human review is needed alongside it before a decision is made.

questions.prompt: Which description best fits BERTScore?
choices: It asks a capable model to read an answer against a rubric and explain its score.
It measures how much of the reference appears in the output and penalises output that is too short.
It compares meaning by matching word vectors from a language model, so a correct paraphrase can still score well.
It counts shared runs of consecutive words between output and reference, and it is popular for summaries.
questions.why: BERTScore matches words by how close their vectors are in a language model, which is why it rewards meaning rather than exact wording.

questions.prompt: A legal-FAQ chatbot team picks between two models using ROUGE. Model B scores higher on ROUGE than Model A. After release, users report that Model B gives confident, wrong answers that reuse the wording of the reference answers. What best explains this?
choices: ROUGE rewards word overlap, so a fluent wrong answer that reuses reference wording can score well, and the team needed a correctness check too.
The team should have used BLEU instead, because BLEU always catches factual errors that ROUGE misses.
ROUGE was the wrong kind of metric for any text, so its scores were meaningless for both models.
Model B's answers were probably too long, which ROUGE penalises heavily but still counted as correct.
questions.why: Overlap metrics measure similarity to a reference, so a wrong answer that reuses the reference's phrasing can score high while being incorrect.

questions.prompt: A retail company uses a judge model to score answers from its shopping assistant. The judge gives longer answers higher scores, even when a short answer is more accurate. What is the most sensible response?
choices: Ask the judge for a rubric-based score, but also check a sample of scores with human reviewers and account for the length bias.
Accept the judge's scores as they are, because a judge model is by definition unbiased.
Discard the judge and go back to using BLEU, since BLEU does not favour long answers.
Add more reference answers so the judge has more text to compare against.
questions.why: LLM judges carry known biases such as favouring length, so their scores should be spot-checked by people and adjusted rather than trusted blindly.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would choose between ROUGE, BLEU, BERTScore and an LLM judge for evaluating a customer-support chatbot's answers. Say what each one measures, and name a limit or tradeoff of the approach you would pick.
lessons.modelAnswer: For a support chatbot there is often no single correct wording, so I would not rely on ROUGE or BLEU, which reward matching the reference's words. BLEU was made for translation and ROUGE for summaries, and neither checks whether the answer is actually right. If we have a set of approved reference answers, BERTScore is a reasonable cheap check, since it compares meaning and tolerates paraphrase, so it catches answers that say the right thing differently. For judging helpfulness, tone and whether the answer used the policy document, I would use an LLM as judge with a written rubric, and spot-check its scores with human reviewers. The tradeoff is that the judge costs money on every evaluation and has its own biases, such as preferring longer answers, so I would calibrate it against human labels before trusting its scores.
rubricPoints: ROUGE measures how much of the reference appears in the output, so it suits summaries.
BLEU measures how much of the output appears in the reference, with a short-output penalty, and was built for translation.
BERTScore compares meaning using embeddings, so it tolerates paraphrase but still needs reference texts.
An LLM judge scores against a rubric and handles open-ended answers, but it has cost and bias and should be checked against humans.

suggested.rationale: Choosing the right metric for a given task is an exam-style reasoning situation, and no listed mission covers foundation-model evaluation directly.

lessons.plain: A benchmark score is a grade a model earns on a standard test that many models also take, like a general exam. Your business objective is the specific job you need done, such as answering a customer's billing question correctly, within three seconds, at a fair price. A model can top the general exam and still fail that job, for example because it is too slow, too expensive per conversation, or weak on your company's own product terms. Deciding whether a model meets the objective means checking it against your own tasks, your own data, and the things your users and budget actually care about.
lessons.guessPrompt: A team picks the model with the highest public benchmark score for their customer support chatbot. Name two things that could still go wrong in production even though the score is high.
lessons.teach:
A benchmark is a standard test set, with agreed questions and agreed answers, that many models are scored on. It tells you how a model performs on that test. A business objective is the outcome your product must deliver. For example: resolve at least 70 percent of billing chats without a human, with each reply arriving in under three seconds and costing less than a set amount per conversation. A model meets the objective only if it does well on the measures that define that outcome, tested on the inputs your users really send.

Why this works: a benchmark samples general ability, while your objective depends on your own vocabulary, documents, tone rules, languages, and budget. So you build a small evaluation set of real or realistic tasks, with expected results written down, and run each candidate model against it. You then score the business measures: task completion rate (the share of conversations finished correctly), user satisfaction (ratings or repeat contacts), and cost per interaction (tokens and infrastructure per conversation). Human reviewers check a sample of answers, which is called human-in-the-loop evaluation.

Worked example. Candidate A tops a public leaderboard. Step 1: collect 200 real billing questions with approved answers. Step 2: run both candidates on all 200. Step 3: A completes 62 percent correctly and B completes 71 percent. Step 4: A's median reply takes 6 seconds and B's takes 2. Step 5: A costs three times as much per conversation. B meets the objective; A does not, despite the leaderboard.

Common mistake: treating the top benchmark score as proof of fit. Consequence: in a running system, a slow or costly model can pass every standard test yet frustrate customers into queues, or its bill can grow faster than the value it returns, and nobody notices until the invoice arrives.

The model is judged by the business objective, measured on your own work, not by the leaderboard.

questions.prompt: A university wants a chatbot to answer enrolment questions. Its team follows this process. Step 1: They collect 120 real enrolment questions from last term's inbox, each with an approved answer. Step 2: They run Model P and Model Q on all 120 questions. Step 3: Model P answers 84 correctly and Model Q answers 91 correctly. Step 4: [missing step]. Step 5: They choose Model Q because it meets every part of the objective.
choices: Compare each model's cost per conversation against the approved budget
Ask each vendor for its list price per thousand words and use that as the cost
Rank the two models by their public leaderboard scores and pick the higher one
Skip cost checks, because accuracy is the only measure that matters for students
questions.why: The objective includes cost per interaction measured on the team's own conversations, so the missing step is checking each model's cost per conversation against the budget.

questions.prompt: In plain terms, what is a benchmark when people talk about evaluating a language model?
choices: A standard test set with agreed questions and agreed answers, used to score many models on the same tasks
A live measurement of how many customers a deployed chatbot has served this month
The exact price a provider charges for each thousand tokens of input
A private set of questions that only one company writes for its own product
questions.why: The teaching text defines a benchmark as a standard test set with agreed questions and answers that many models are scored on.

questions.prompt: An insurance firm is choosing a model to triage motor claims. Model M tops a public leaderboard, answers 58 percent of the firm's own claim tasks correctly, and replies in about 1 second. Model N answers 74 percent correctly and replies in about 4 seconds. Which decision best follows the idea of judging a model by the business objective?
choices: Choose Model N, because it does better on the firm's own tasks, even though it is slower
Choose Model M, because the leaderboard shows it is the stronger model overall
Choose neither, because a benchmark result always means the model is unfit for real use
Choose Model M, because speed matters more than correctness for any claims process
questions.why: The objective is judged on the firm's own work, where Model N completes more tasks correctly, so the leaderboard lead does not decide the choice.

questions.prompt: A retailer runs a returns assistant. Which measure set best shows whether the assistant meets its business objective?
choices: How many tokens per second the hardware can process in a lab test
The vendor's marketing claim about accuracy on general questions
The number of parameters in the model and the model's public leaderboard rank
Task completion rate on real return requests, user satisfaction, and cost per conversation
questions.why: The three business measures named in the teaching text are task completion rate, user satisfaction, and cost per interaction, measured on the retailer's own realistic inputs.

lessons.explainPrompt: A colleague says the new model scored best on the public benchmark, so we should switch to it for our order-tracking assistant. Explain to them, in your own words, how you would decide whether it truly meets our business objective, and name one limit or tradeoff of your method.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would not switch based on the leaderboard alone. A benchmark measures general skill on a shared test, and our assistant has a different job: answering order-tracking questions correctly, quickly, and cheaply. First I would write the objective in measurable terms, such as completing at least 80 percent of tracking chats correctly, replies under three seconds, and a cost ceiling per conversation. Then I would build a set of about 150 real past questions with approved answers and run both the current and the new model on them. I would score task completion, have a human reviewer sample transcripts, and compute cost per conversation from actual token use. The tradeoff is that a small evaluation set can miss rare cases and can drift from what customers ask next month, so after launch I would keep a monitored live sample rather than treating one test run as final.
rubricPoints: Separates a general benchmark score from the specific business outcome the product must deliver.
Turns the objective into measurable targets such as task completion rate, latency, and cost per interaction.
Evaluates candidate models on representative tasks and data from the real use case, with human review.
Names a limit of the method, such as a small test set missing rare cases or drifting over time.

suggested.rationale: Judging a model against a business objective is best practised by reasoning through a realistic selection scenario with competing trade-offs.

lessons.plain: An AI application is more than the model. It is a chain of steps: something looks up relevant documents, a prompt is assembled, the model writes an answer, and sometimes the system calls tools or works through steps in order. Evaluating the whole application means asking whether the finished product does its job for users, at an acceptable cost and speed, and where it breaks when it fails. A model can score well on a general test and still give a wrong answer about your company's refund policy because the wrong document was fetched. So you test the individual parts and the whole, and measure what the business cares about.
lessons.guessPrompt: A support chatbot answers questions from your company's policy documents. Users say the answers sound confident but are sometimes wrong. Before we teach anything, where would you look first to find the cause, the model itself or something else in the chain, and why?
lessons.teach:
A foundation model application is a pipeline of steps, and each step can fail. In a retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) pipeline, a retrieval step searches a document store for passages that match the question, then a generation step passes those passages and the question to a foundation model, which writes the answer. An agent is an application where the model decides which tool to call next, such as a lookup or a calculator, and loops until it finishes a task. A workflow is a fixed sequence of such steps that someone designed in advance.

Evaluating the whole application means measuring the outcome users see and also each stage separately. The end-to-end measures are task completion rate (did the user get what they came for), user satisfaction, latency, and cost per interaction. The stage measures show where a failure lives. For retrieval, ask whether the right passages were fetched. For generation, ask whether the answer is supported by those passages rather than invented.

Worked example: a user asks about the refund window. Step one, retrieval returns the 2019 policy instead of the 2024 one. Step two, the model writes a clear, fluent answer based on the old text. The final answer reads well, so a single 'does it sound good' check passes. Only a stage check on retrieval, or a groundedness check against the current source, exposes the fault.

Common mistake: judging the model alone, or judging only fluency. A good-sounding answer can be wrong, and a model-only benchmark says nothing about which document was fetched.

Consequence in a running system: an application evaluated only end to end can look healthy until customers escalate, and the team may then swap the model when the fix belongs in the document index or how the documents were split into chunks.

questions.prompt: Harbor Tide Insurance runs a claims-help assistant. It fetches passages from its policy handbook, then a foundation model writes the reply. The team's first check was end to end: 92 of 100 test questions were marked complete and reviewers praised the tone. A policyholder then reported a wrong windstorm deductible, so the team traced the failure. Step 1: a retrieval check on 50 test questions with known correct passages found the right passage in the fetched results for only 31 of them. Step 2: a groundedness check on the answers to those questions found that the model's answers mostly matched the passages it was given. Step 3: [missing]. Which step completes the trace so the team knows where the fault lives?
choices: They swap the model for a larger one and re-run the end-to-end completion score.
They ask reviewers to rate tone again, since fluent answers are the best sign that an answer is correct.
They raise the end-to-end task completion target from 92 to 95 percent.
They check the document index and how the handbook was split into chunks, because retrieval is where the wrong passages came from, and fix that stage before judging the model again.
questions.why: The stage checks have located the fault in retrieval, so the next step is to inspect the document index and chunking rather than the model or fluency.

questions.prompt: In a fixed-sequence application, a designer decides ahead of time which steps run and in what order. In an agent, what decides the next step?
choices: The model, which chooses the next tool to call and loops until the task is finished.
The designer's fixed sequence, written before the application runs.
The document store, which returns the next passage automatically.
The user, who must click a button before each tool is called.
questions.why: An agent is defined by the model choosing which tool to call next and looping, whereas a workflow follows a sequence designed in advance.

questions.prompt: A travel-booking assistant at Lark Fare is evaluated only on average response time and cost per interaction, and both look excellent. Which important gap does this evaluation leave?
choices: It cannot measure cost at all, so the cost figure is meaningless.
It measures latency in the wrong units, so the response time is misleading.
It does not show whether users got what they came for, such as a completed booking, and it does not show which stage of the pipeline failed.
It needs a fine-tuning run before any measurement is meaningful.
questions.why: Latency and cost are only part of the end-to-end picture; task completion shows the user's outcome, and stage measures show where a failure lives.

questions.prompt: A recipe-scaling app at Crumb and Co uses a fixed workflow: it looks up the recipe, runs a calculator on the quantities, then has a model write the instructions. A reply states a flour amount that does not appear in the retrieved recipe passage, yet the wording is smooth. Which check would expose this?
choices: A check of the reply's latency against the average for the workflow.
A count of how many tools the workflow called in total.
A groundedness check that compares the reply against the retrieved recipe passage to see whether the figure is supported.
A fluency rating by a reviewer who reads the reply aloud.
questions.why: Groundedness checks whether the generated answer is supported by the retrieved source, which is the only check here that can reveal an invented amount that reads smoothly.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would evaluate a RAG-based support assistant before launch. Name one limit or tradeoff of the approach you choose.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would test the application in two layers. First, the stages: for retrieval, I would take a set of real questions with known correct source passages and check whether the right passages come back near the top of the results. For generation, I would check whether each answer is supported by the passages it was given rather than invented. Second, the whole: I would track task completion rate, meaning whether the user's problem was actually solved, along with user satisfaction, response time, and cost per interaction. The tradeoff is effort and drift. A labelled question set takes time to build, and an automated grader, which is itself a language model scoring other outputs, can share the same blind spots as the model it grades. So I would keep a human-reviewed sample running after launch as well.
rubricPoints: Separates retrieval quality from generation quality when diagnosing a failure.
Measures end-to-end task completion, user satisfaction, latency and cost per interaction.
Checks that answers are grounded in the retrieved sources, not just fluent.
Names a real limit of the chosen method, such as grader blind spots or labelling cost.
Keeps some human review running after launch.

suggested.rationale: No listed mission or planned engine builds judgement about whole AI applications, so explaining the evaluation approach back in your own words is the core skill here.

lessons.plain: When a company adds an AI feature, the technical team can measure how accurate the model is, but the business wants to know whether the feature is doing its job and paying its way. Business alignment metrics are a small set of numbers that answer that: how often users finish what they came to do, how happy they are with the result, and how much each use of the feature costs. Think of a self-checkout kiosk. You judge it by how many shoppers leave without staff help, how annoyed they are, and what each transaction costs the store to run. These three numbers together show whether the AI is worth keeping, and they can pull in different directions, so you read them together.
lessons.guessPrompt: A support chatbot handles 1,000 customer chats in a month, and 600 of them end with the customer's problem solved and no human needed. Which single number would you show a manager first, and why might that number be misleading on its own?
lessons.teach:
Business alignment metrics are measures that tie an AI application to the outcome the business cares about, rather than to how the model scores on a technical test. Three are named for this objective.

Task completion rate is the share of interactions in which the user actually reaches their goal. You count the interactions where the goal was met and divide by all interactions. The goal has to be defined before you count, because a bot that replied is not the same as a customer whose problem was solved.

User satisfaction is how people rate the experience, usually from a short survey such as a one-to-five rating or a thumbs-up share. It catches things completion misses, such as a correct answer delivered rudely or a solved problem that took far too long.

Cost per interaction is the total spend on the feature in a period divided by the number of interactions in that period. Spend includes model usage charges and any supporting services such as retrieval, storage and monitoring.

Worked example: in one month the chatbot handles 1,000 chats. In 720 of them the issue is resolved without a handoff to a person, so task completion is 720 divided by 1,000, which is 72 percent. A survey of 300 respondents averages 4.1 out of 5. Total monthly spend is 1,500 fictional credits, so cost per interaction is 1,500 divided by 1,000, which is 1.50 credits.

Common mistake: reading one metric alone. A cheaper model can lower cost per interaction while completion falls, so more customers reach a human agent, and the true cost per resolved problem rises. Counting every answered message as completed also inflates the completion rate.

In a running system these measures only help if each conversation records whether the goal was met, a satisfaction rating when one is given, and the cost of that interaction, so the three can be tracked over time after each model or prompt change.

questions.prompt: A recipe-app assistant logged 680 sessions in one week. The team reports a task completion rate of 90 percent, calculated as 610 divided by 680, because they count a session as complete whenever the bot sent at least one reply. Of those 680 sessions, 476 ended with the user holding a usable recipe plan, which is the goal the team actually cares about. Step 1 is to count the replied sessions (610). Step 2 is missing from their method. Step 3 is to divide the goal-met sessions by all sessions, giving 476 divided by 680, or 70 percent. What was the missing step?
choices: Define the goal first, then count only sessions where a usable recipe plan was actually delivered
Count sessions where the bot sent at least one reply, because every reply is progress toward the goal
Add the week's spend in credits to the numerator so that cost is folded into the completion rate
Divide the completed sessions by the 610 replied sessions instead of by all 680 sessions
questions.why: Task completion requires the goal to be defined before counting, because a bot reply is not the same as the user reaching the goal.

questions.prompt: A returns-assistant for an online retailer handled 4,000 conversations in May. The total May spend on the feature, including model usage and the retrieval service, was 3,200 credits. What is the cost per interaction?
choices: 1.25 credits
1.20 credits
0.08 credits
0.80 credits
questions.why: Cost per interaction is total spend divided by the number of interactions, so 3,200 divided by 4,000 is 0.80 credits.

questions.prompt: An HR policy bot's latest prompt change raised its average user rating from 3.6 to 4.5 out of 5, but the share of conversations where the employee got the policy answer they needed fell. A manager says the change is clearly an improvement because users like it more. What is the best response?
choices: Both measures must be read together, since satisfaction can rise while task completion falls and the goal is not being met
The change should be judged only by the model's score on a technical test
The manager should ignore the rating and report only the monthly spend on the bot
The manager is right, because a higher rating is the only measure that matters to users
questions.why: Satisfaction and task completion measure different things, so a rise in one cannot prove the application is achieving its goal when the other has fallen.

questions.prompt: A claims-assistant team wants to track its three business alignment metrics over time so it can compare the effect of each prompt change. Which record should each conversation store?
choices: Only the total monthly spend, so the team can compute cost per interaction at month end
Whether the user's goal was met, the satisfaction rating if one was given, and the cost of that interaction
Only the number of messages exchanged, since message count reflects how much work the bot did
The model's score on a general benchmark, recorded once per model version
questions.why: Each conversation needs its own goal outcome, optional rating and interaction cost so all three metrics can be computed and compared after every change.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate why a team should track task completion rate, user satisfaction and cost per interaction together instead of choosing whichever one looks best, and name one limit of each metric.
lessons.modelAnswer: We track all three because each one can look good while the feature is failing. Completion rate tells us whether users reach their goal, but it depends on how we define success, and a message that was sent is not the same as a problem solved. Satisfaction tells us how people feel, but surveys are only answered by a small, self-selected group, so the average can be misleading. Cost per interaction tells us what each use costs, but a cheap model can push more people to a human agent, and then the real cost per resolved case goes up. If completion rises while cost per interaction stays flat and satisfaction holds, the change is worth keeping. If one moves alone, we dig into why before deciding.
rubricPoints: Task completion rate measures whether users reach their goal, and it depends on a clear definition of success.
User satisfaction captures quality that completion misses, but survey responses can be biased or sparse.
Cost per interaction is total spend divided by interactions, and it must be read alongside outcomes because cheap failures raise real cost.
The three metrics should be read together, since optimising one alone can hurt the others.

suggested.rationale: Working out cost per interaction from usage figures in fictional credits is the arithmetic a planned cost model engine would drill, while the completion and satisfaction parts are reading-and-reasoning.

lessons.plain: Responsible AI is a checklist of qualities an AI system should have before people rely on it. It should treat different groups of people fairly, work for a wide range of users, keep working when inputs get messy, avoid causing harm, and tell the truth. Think of a bridge inspector who checks not only that the bridge stands on a calm day, but that it holds in strong wind, under heavy trucks, and for everyone who crosses it. This lesson covers six named features on that checklist and how they differ, so when a model fails some users you can name which feature broke.
lessons.guessPrompt: A loan-approval model is accurate overall, yet it rejects applicants from one postcode far more often than applicants with similar incomes elsewhere. Before reading on, which of these six qualities (bias, fairness, inclusivity, robustness, safety, veracity) do you think is most directly at stake, and why?
lessons.teach:
Responsible AI is the set of properties an AI system should have so that it is reasonable and safe to rely on. The six features in this objective overlap, so keep them distinct. Bias is a systematic tilt in a model's outputs or errors, often caused by the data it learned from or by how people labelled that data. Fairness is the goal of treating people comparably, and it is checked by looking at results for each group rather than only the overall average. Inclusivity means the system is designed and tested with the full range of people who will use it, including their languages, accents and circumstances. Robustness is the ability to keep behaving sensibly when inputs are unusual, noisy or deliberately tricky. Safety means the system does not produce or enable harmful outcomes, and a guardrail is a control that blocks them. Veracity means outputs are true and correctly grounded in reliable sources. A confident invented answer fails veracity, which is the property hallucinations violate.

Why it matters: a model can score well on average while failing a group that was rare in its training data, so the check has to be done per group.

Worked example: a speech-to-text feature transcribes 95 percent of words correctly overall. Step one, split the test set by accent. Step two, find that one accent scores 70 percent. Step three, name the feature: this is a fairness and inclusivity failure, probably traced to bias in the training data. Step four, a test with background noise would be a separate robustness check.

Common mistake: treating one overall accuracy number as proof of fairness. Consequence in a running system: a support bot that is accurate for most callers but fails one language group generates complaints that only appear after launch. Fixing it then means retraining or adding guardrails, and sometimes rolling back the release while that work happens.

The six features are checked with different tests, and you cannot assume passing one proves the others.

questions.prompt: A parcel company uses a model that reads handwritten delivery addresses from photos. It reads 97 percent of addresses correctly overall. Step one: the team splits the test set by the postal style used on each address. Step two: they find that addresses written in one rural postal style are read correctly only 72 percent of the time. Step three: they name this a fairness and inclusivity failure, most likely caused by training data that rarely included that style. Step four is missing. The team next retests the same model on photos taken in heavy rain and at a blur, and records how accuracy changes. Which feature is that retest checking?
choices: Robustness, because the inputs are noisy and unusual
Inclusivity, because the rural style was left out of the design
Bias, because the photos were taken by a biased group of people
Veracity, because the model must give true readings
questions.why: Rain and blur are noisy, unusual inputs, and robustness is the property that checks whether a system keeps behaving sensibly under such conditions.

questions.prompt: A chatbot for a university library is set up with a filter that blocks any reply containing instructions for self-harm. Which responsible AI feature does that filter provide?
choices: Robustness, because the filter keeps working when students type strange text
Fairness, because the filter treats all students the same way
Veracity, because the filter makes sure every reply is true
Safety, because the filter is a guardrail that blocks harmful outputs
questions.why: A guardrail is a control that blocks harmful outputs, and that is what the safety feature is about, not truth, equal treatment or handling of odd inputs.

questions.prompt: A research assistant bot is asked for sources on a medical question. It replies with a citation to a journal article that does not exist, written in a confident tone. Which feature has the system failed?
choices: Robustness, because the question was unusual for the bot
Inclusivity, because the bot did not serve the user's language well
Safety, because the citation could lead to a harmful medical decision
Veracity, because the output is confidently invented rather than grounded in reliable sources
questions.why: Veracity means outputs are true and grounded in reliable sources, and a confident invented citation violates exactly that, which is what hallucination means.

questions.prompt: A loan-screening model approves 91 percent of applications overall. Its error rate for applicants from one region is three times higher than for everyone else. A manager says the model is fine because the overall figure is high. What is the correct response?
choices: It fails fairness for that region, so compare results per group.
It is a robustness failure, because a higher error rate for one region shows that the model cannot cope with unusual applications at all.
It is a veracity failure, because the model is making confident decisions that it cannot fully justify to the applicants affected.
It passes fairness, since a high overall approval rate is the accepted proof that every applicant was treated equally by the model in all circumstances.
questions.why: Fairness is checked by looking at results for each group rather than the overall average, so the regional error rate is a fairness failure that the overall figure hides.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how bias, fairness and veracity differ, using one example of each, and name one limit of checking these features before launch.
lessons.modelAnswer: Bias is a systematic tilt in what a model produces or gets wrong, usually traced to skewed training data or labels. Fairness is the goal that people in different groups are treated comparably, and it is checked by splitting results by group, not just looking at the average. Veracity is whether the output is true and grounded in sources, so a confidently invented policy fails veracity even if the wording sounds fine. Example: a resume screener that ranks equally qualified candidates lower from one group shows bias and a fairness problem. A chatbot that invents a refund policy shows a veracity problem. One limit: pre-launch tests only cover the cases the team thought of, and some groups may be too small in the test data to measure reliably, so monitoring real user feedback after launch is still needed.
rubricPoints: Defines bias as a systematic tilt in outputs or errors, often from data or labels
Explains fairness as comparable treatment, checked per group rather than by overall average
Distinguishes veracity as truthfulness and grounding, separate from group-level bias
Names a limit such as tests missing real cases or small groups, and the need for monitoring after launch

suggested.rationale: Telling six overlapping qualities apart and naming which one failed is best practised by explaining it back, and no listed mission or planned engine covers AI model behaviour.

lessons.plain: Imagine a shop that lets customers talk to an assistant that could say almost anything. Before a reply reaches a customer, a checkpoint reads what goes in and what comes out. It blocks rude or unsafe material, hides personal details, and stops topics the business has ruled out. Amazon Bedrock Guardrails is that checkpoint for generative AI apps built on AWS. It is a configurable filter that sits between users and a model, so the same safety rules can apply whichever model you choose.
lessons.guessPrompt: Suppose a support chatbot answers a customer's question by quoting a stranger's home address it found in a document it was given. Which kind of safeguard would you add, and would you place it on the question going in, the answer coming out, or both?
lessons.teach:
A guardrail is a set of configured rules that inspects text flowing into a generative AI model and text flowing out of it, then blocks, masks or flags anything that breaks a rule. In Amazon Bedrock, the managed generative AI service on AWS, you create a guardrail as a named, versioned resource and attach it to model calls. Because it is a separate layer, its rules do not depend on how the model was trained, and it can also check text from other sources through a standalone check call.

The main policy types work like this. Content filters score text for categories such as hate, insults, sexual content, violence and misconduct, and for prompt attacks, where a user tries to override the application's instructions. Denied topics describe a subject the application should refuse. Word filters block exact terms. Sensitive information filters detect personal data such as names or card numbers and either block the message or mask the data. Custom patterns written as regular expressions, which are rules that match the shape of text, extend this. Contextual grounding checks compare a response against the source material supplied and score how well it is grounded in that material and how relevant it is to the question. Responses that score below your thresholds are blocked.

Worked example: a benefits assistant has the denied topic 'legal advice' and personal data masking turned on. A user asks for help with a dispute and includes a national ID number. Step one, the input is checked and the ID number is masked before anything else happens. Step two, the request matches the denied topic, so the guardrail returns your configured refusal message instead of letting the model answer. Step three, the application logs only the masked text.

Common mistake: assuming a guardrail makes a model fair, accurate or complete. It only enforces the rules you wrote. A content filter cannot catch a bias pattern you never listed, and a grounding threshold set too low lets weak answers through.

Consequence: if the guardrail is missing or not attached to the call, the request goes straight to the model, and whatever it produces reaches the customer.

questions.prompt: A shoe retailer runs a returns chatbot. Its guardrail has a sensitive information filter set to mask card numbers and a contextual grounding threshold of 0.7. A customer pastes a card number and asks whether a 45-day return is allowed, but the supplied policy text says returns are accepted for 30 days. Step one: the card number is masked in the input before anything else happens. Step two: [missing]. Step three: the grounding check scores the reply at 0.4, which is below 0.7, so the reply is blocked and the configured fallback message is returned to the customer. What is the missing step two?
choices: The guardrail lowers the grounding threshold to 0.3 so the reply can pass.
The application retrains the model on the returns policy before it answers the question.
The model drafts a reply, and the guardrail then checks that draft against the policy text supplied with the call.
The card number is unmasked so the refund team can verify the customer's account.
questions.why: Grounding is a check on a response, so the model must first produce a draft that the guardrail can score against the supplied source material; the other choices either change rules that are not changed in this scenario or are not part of a guardrail call.

questions.prompt: In plain terms, what is an Amazon Bedrock guardrail?
choices: A set of configured rules that inspects text going into and coming out of a generative model, then blocks, masks or flags what breaks a rule.
A model trained to avoid bias by reviewing its own training data.
A logging service that stores every prompt and reply for later review.
A dataset audit tool that runs once before a model is launched and never again.
questions.why: The teaching text defines a guardrail as configured rules that inspect text flowing into and out of a model and act on violations, and the other choices describe training, auditing or logging instead.

questions.prompt: A travel app wants its assistant to refuse any question about forging passports, no matter how the user words it. Which policy type fits best?
choices: A word filter that blocks the exact term forge
A contextual grounding check against the airline's fare rules
A sensitive information filter that masks passport numbers
A denied topic that describes forging passports as a subject to refuse
questions.why: A denied topic describes a subject the application should refuse, which covers any wording of the request, whereas a word filter only matches exact terms and the other two policy types do not refuse subjects.

questions.prompt: A bank's loan-rate assistant has a grounding threshold set very low. An answer that quotes a rate not found in the supplied rate sheet gets through to a customer. What most likely went wrong?
choices: The guardrail is working as intended and the rate sheet is the only fault.
The model was biased against customers in one region, which the grounding check should have caught.
The sensitive information filter was switched on, which stops grounding checks from running.
The threshold is set too low, so a weakly grounded answer scored above it and was allowed through.
questions.why: Grounding checks block only responses scoring below the configured threshold, so a threshold set too low lets weak answers through, while the other choices misidentify the cause or invent a mechanism the teaching text does not describe.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what Amazon Bedrock Guardrails does and does not do, and name one limit or tradeoff a team should weigh when setting its thresholds.
lessons.modelAnswer: Amazon Bedrock Guardrails is a configurable layer that checks the messages going into a model and the replies coming out. It can block or mask unsafe content, filter prompt attacks, refuse topics we have ruled out, mask personal data, and check whether an answer is grounded in the source documents we supply. It does not make a model fair, truthful or unbiased on its own, and it only catches what we configured. The main tradeoff is in the thresholds. If we set a grounding or content threshold very strictly, we block useful answers and frustrate users. If we set it loosely, weak or harmful answers get through. So we should test the guardrail against realistic examples, review blocked and passed cases with real users, and adjust the thresholds over time.
rubricPoints: Describes the guardrail as a configurable checkpoint on model inputs and outputs, not a built-in property of the model
Names at least two policy types such as content filters, denied topics, sensitive information filters or grounding checks
States that it enforces only the configured rules and does not guarantee fairness or accuracy
Explains a tradeoff in threshold settings between blocking too much and letting harm through

suggested.rationale: This objective is mostly configuration features and console steps, which a reading with a worked example covers better than any listed mission or planned engine.

lessons.plain: Responsible model selection means choosing which AI model to use for a job by weighing more than how accurate it is. You also ask whether it is fair to the people it will affect, whether you can explain its behaviour well enough to justify it, how much electricity it uses to run and train, and what it costs over time. A very large model may answer every question well but use far more energy per request than a smaller one that handles your narrow task just as well. Choosing responsibly means picking the smallest model that meets the requirement, checking it on every group it will serve, and writing down why you chose it.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your team needs a model to sort short customer emails into five categories. A very large general model scores 2 points higher on a test than a small model. Which would you pick for production, and what would you want to know before deciding?
lessons.teach:
Model selection is the step where a team chooses which trained model will do a job. A model is a learned set of numbers that turns an input, such as an email, into an output, such as a label. Inference means running a model to produce an answer for one request. Training means the one-off, usually much heavier, process of building the model. Each inference uses computing power, and computing power uses electricity, which is the main source of a system's energy footprint. Responsible selection checks four things together: whether the model is accurate enough, whether its errors fall unfairly on some user groups, how well its behaviour can be explained, and how much energy and money each request costs.

Worked example. Requirement: at least 90 percent correct on five email categories. Step 1: build a labelled test set that includes emails from every customer group the feature serves. Step 2: score both models. The small model gets 91 percent overall and 89 percent on one dialect group; the large model gets 93 percent overall and 92 percent on that group. Step 3: multiply per-request energy by expected volume, for example two million emails a month. Step 4: the small model meets the requirement for all groups only if you accept a fix, so you decide to improve the small model's data for that group before launch and record the reason.

Common mistake: choosing the model with the top leaderboard score and assuming bigger is automatically more responsible. The overall score can hide a group that is poorly served, and the extra energy is paid on every request.

In a running system, a larger model also adds latency and cost per call, so a choice made once shapes the bill and the carbon footprint every day after launch.

questions.prompt: A bank wants a model that summarises loan applications. The requirement is at least 90 percent correct for every applicant language group. Model P scores 94 percent overall and 88 percent on applicants who write in a regional second language. Model Q scores 92 percent overall and 92 percent on that same group. Energy is 0.4 Wh per summary for P and 0.9 Wh for Q, with 300,000 summaries a month, so P uses 120 kWh a month and Q uses 270 kWh a month. Steps 1 to 3 are done: the test set includes applicants from every language group, both models are scored per group, and energy has been multiplied by monthly volume. Step 4 is left for you: decide which model meets the requirement and what that means for launch.
choices: Choose Q, since it uses more energy per summary and so must be the more careful model in every respect.
Choose P, since its 94 percent overall score is the higher number and an 88 percent group score is close enough to 90 to ignore before launch.
Average each model's group scores so that P's 88 and 94 become 91, which passes P against the floor.
P fails the 90 percent floor for the regional group, so it is not acceptable as it stands; Q is the choice.
questions.why: P scores 88 percent for the regional group, below the 90 percent floor, so it fails the requirement as it stands, while Q meets the floor for every group, making Q the choice.

questions.prompt: A retailer's product-tagging model took 2,000 kWh of electricity to train once. Each tagging call (inference) uses 0.002 kWh, and the system makes 5 million calls a month. A colleague says training is the only energy cost that matters because it is the biggest single job. What is the best reply?
choices: Inference and training are the same thing, so the 2,000 kWh figure already includes every call the system will ever make.
Energy from inference is free once the model is deployed, so only the training figure belongs in the selection decision.
Training energy is the only cost that matters because it happens once and the monthly calls are too small to count.
Inference is a repeated cost: 5 million calls at 0.002 kWh is 10,000 kWh a month, which exceeds the one-off 2,000 kWh training cost within the first month.
questions.why: Inference repeats on every request, so 5 million calls at 0.002 kWh each (10,000 kWh a month) exceeds the one-off 2,000 kWh training energy within a month, which is why per-request cost matters for selection.

questions.prompt: A clinic's symptom-intake model scores 95 percent accuracy overall on its test set, which had few messages written in teenage slang. In production it scores 81 percent on messages from teenagers. Which check, run before launch, would most directly have revealed this problem?
choices: Confirming the model can be run on a smaller server so it is cheaper to host.
Building a labelled test set that includes messages from each user group and scoring accuracy separately for each group.
Comparing the model's overall score against the leaderboard of other published models.
Checking the model's energy use per request against the monthly budget.
questions.why: Splitting the scores by user group on a test set that includes every group exposes a poorly served group that the overall 95 percent score hides.

questions.prompt: Two models give the same accuracy for every user group in a benefits-eligibility assistant. Model X costs 10 times as much per call as Model Y and draws much more electricity per request. Which conclusion does responsible model selection support?
choices: Choose X, because a higher cost per call usually means better answers that are worth the extra bill.
Choose whichever model has the longer name, since the choice cannot be changed once the system is live.
Choose the model with the cheaper cost and energy per call, since the accuracy is equal and the choice shapes the bill and carbon footprint for every day after launch.
Choose either model at random, since per-call cost only matters during training and not during daily use.
questions.why: With equal per-group accuracy, the tie is broken by cost and energy per request, which are paid on every call after launch, so the cheaper, lower-energy model is the responsible choice.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate, in your own words, how you would choose between a large and a small model for a customer-facing feature. Name one limit or tradeoff of the approach you choose.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would start by writing down the accuracy requirement and the groups of users the feature serves. Then I would test both models on a labelled set that includes every group, not just the overall average, because a good overall score can hide one group getting worse results. Next I would estimate energy and cost per request at our real monthly volume, since a large model multiplies both. If the small model meets the requirement for every group, I would choose it and record why. The main limit of this approach is that the test set may not reflect real traffic, so the decision needs monitoring after launch, and a smaller model may need extra data work to close a gap for one group.
rubricPoints: Checks accuracy against a stated requirement, not against a leaderboard
Tests subgroup performance rather than only the overall score
Estimates energy and cost per request at expected volume
Names a real limit, such as an unrepresentative test set or the extra work a smaller model may need

suggested.rationale: Being able to justify a model choice in your own words, with a tradeoff, is the core skill here and no listed mission covers it directly.

lessons.plain: Generative AI is software that writes text, images or code in response to a prompt. Because it learned from very large collections of material, its output can copy protected work, state false facts with confidence, treat some people unfairly, and reach end users who trust it. These are the main legal and business risks an organisation must weigh before putting such a system in front of customers. Knowing the categories helps you spot which one is at stake when something goes wrong.
lessons.guessPrompt: A company's chatbot confidently gives a customer a made-up refund policy, and the customer acts on it. Which kinds of risk does this touch, and who ends up bearing the cost?
lessons.teach:
Intellectual property, or IP, is the legal right to own a creation such as text, images, code or a brand name. Infringement means using someone else's protected IP without permission. A generative model learns patterns from large amounts of material and can sometimes reproduce passages or images that closely resemble what it saw, so its output may infringe. A hallucination is an output that reads confidently but is false or unsupported by any source. Biased output is a result that treats some groups worse or repeats stereotypes, often because the training data under-represented them. Loss of trust happens when customers stop relying on a product after it misleads them. End-user risk is harm that lands on the person reading or acting on the output, such as someone following wrong medical or financial advice. A guardrail is a rule or filter applied to what goes into or comes out of a model.

Why this matters: the model does not know whether its words are true, copyrighted or fair. It predicts likely words, so the organisation that publishes the output carries the consequences.

Worked example. A retailer uses a model to write product descriptions. First, a staff member sends a prompt asking for a catchy slogan. Second, the model writes a line that closely matches a competitor's trademarked slogan. Third, the retailer publishes it without checking. Fourth, the competitor files an infringement claim. Fifth, the retailer pays legal costs and removes the material. A similarity check and human review before publishing would have caught the problem at step two.

Common mistake: assuming that because a model produced the text, the company is not responsible, or that a disclaimer removes the risk. The business that deploys and publishes the output usually answers for it.

Consequence in a running system: an unchecked support bot that invents a refund rule creates complaints, refunds and possibly legal disputes, and the loss of customer trust can last longer than the fix.

Legal risk is a release decision made by the product team, not only a problem for lawyers to solve later.

questions.prompt: An airline's booking assistant is asked whether a traveller needs a transit visa. Step 1: the model replies with a confident rule that appears in no official source, which makes it a hallucination. Step 2: the airline's app displays the reply to the traveller with no review. Step 3: the traveller relies on it and is refused boarding. Step 4 is missing: before launch, the airline had no control that compared the reply against the official visa source or sent unsupported answers to a person. Which control, added before launch, would have closed that gap?
choices: A longer reply style so the answer sounds more thorough
Raising the model's creativity setting so answers vary less
A footer saying that answers may be wrong, shown beneath every reply
A guardrail that checks visa answers against the official source and routes unsupported ones to a human before display
questions.why: A guardrail that checks outputs against a trusted source and escalates unsupported ones stops the hallucination before it reaches the end user, whereas a disclaimer or style change leaves the false answer in front of the traveller.

questions.prompt: Which description best matches a hallucination as used in generative AI?
choices: A confident output that is false or unsupported by any source
A customer who stops using a product after being misled
A rule that filters what goes into a model
A copy of a protected passage that the model saw during training
questions.why: A hallucination is defined as an output that reads confidently but is false or has no supporting source, which is the only option that matches that definition.

questions.prompt: A furniture retailer's model writes product copy that repeats a stereotype about which customers would use a product. Which risk category fits this output best?
choices: Hallucination, because the model invented a fact
End-user risk, because a shopper reads the copy
Biased output, because the copy treats a group unfairly by repeating a stereotype
Infringement of a competitor's trademark
questions.why: Biased output is the category for results that treat a group worse or repeat stereotypes, which is what the copy does; end-user risk describes harm to the reader, but the defining problem here is the bias itself.

questions.prompt: A company publishes model-written text without human review and adds a line beneath it saying the text was generated by AI and may be inaccurate. Which statement is correct?
choices: Only original text can cause legal problems, so the footer is enough
The published output usually remains the company's responsibility, so the footer does not transfer the risk
The footer moves legal responsibility to the model's vendor
Because the model wrote the text, the company does not need a review step
questions.why: The teaching text states that the business that publishes output usually answers for it and that a disclaimer does not remove the risk, so the first option is the only correct one.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate the main legal and business risks of generative AI in a customer-facing product, and name one limit or tradeoff in managing those risks.
lessons.modelAnswer: The main risks are IP infringement, where generated text or images copy protected material; hallucinations, where the model states false things confidently; biased outputs, where some users get worse or stereotyped answers; loss of customer trust after a visible mistake; and end-user harm when someone acts on a wrong answer. The company that publishes the output usually carries the liability, not the model provider alone. A practical control is human review before publishing and monitoring after launch. The tradeoff is that review adds cost and delay, and filters or guardrails can block some legitimate answers while still missing new failure modes, so the team has to balance speed, cost and safety for each use case.
rubricPoints: Names at least three distinct risk types, such as IP infringement, hallucination, bias, trust loss or end-user harm
Explains that the deploying organisation usually bears responsibility for published output
Gives a concrete control, such as human review, filtering or monitoring
States a real tradeoff, such as cost or delay versus safety, or false blocks versus missed failures

suggested.rationale: This objective is a set of named risk categories and facts that no listed mission or planned engine currently practises directly.

lessons.plain: A dataset is the collection of examples a model learns from. Its characteristics describe who and what appears in that collection, where the examples came from, and how many examples each kind has. These choices shape what the model gets good at. If a face-recognition system is trained mostly on one group of faces, it will work well for that group and poorly for others. Inclusivity means the data covers the people who will actually use the system. Diversity means a range of situations within that coverage. Curated sources are chosen and checked on purpose. Balance means no group or case is badly underrepresented.
lessons.guessPrompt: A voice assistant understands adult male speakers well but often mishears children and people with regional accents. Before looking at any tools, what is the most likely cause, and what would you check first?
lessons.teach:
A dataset is the set of examples a model learns from, and its characteristics are the properties of that set: who or what appears in it, where the examples came from, and how many examples each kind has. Inclusivity is whether the dataset contains the people and conditions the system will serve. Diversity is the range within that coverage, such as different ages, accents, lighting, devices, languages, and situations. Curated sources are inputs selected and checked on purpose, with a known origin and permission to use, rather than whatever was easiest to collect. Balance is the proportion of examples per group or outcome. A dataset is unbalanced when one group dominates so heavily that the model learns its patterns well and treats everyone else as rare noise.

Why this matters: a model can only generalise to cases that resemble the ones it learned from. When a group is missing or thin, the model has little evidence about that group, so its predictions for that group are less reliable, even when the overall score looks high. A held-out set, meaning examples kept aside and never used in training, is the honest way to measure this, and results should be reported per group rather than as one average.

Worked example. A team trains a loan-screening model on five years of past applications. Step one: count applications by region, and find that 85 percent come from two large cities. Step two: check the outcome records, and find that rural applicants are rare and their records are often incomplete. Step three: test on a held-out set split by region, and find 92 percent accuracy overall but 61 percent for rural applicants. Step four: treat the dataset as the first suspect, because the rural pattern was thin from the start.

Common mistake: judging a dataset only by its size. A million examples from one narrow source can teach less than ten thousand examples that cover the users well.

Consequence in a running system: an underrepresented group receives worse decisions without any error being raised, so the problem appears as customer complaints rather than alerts, unless results are monitored per group.

questions.prompt: A wearable-health company trains a model to flag irregular heartbeats using 12,000 recordings from its sports app. Step one: count recordings by age band and find that 80 percent come from users aged 20 to 45, while only 6 percent come from users over 65. Step two: compare that share with the app's real user base, where about 30 percent of users are over 65. Step three: test on a held-out set split by age band and find 94 percent accuracy overall but 68 percent for users over 65. Step four is missing.
choices: Collect and check more recordings from users over 65 with reliable records, then retrain and re-test results per age band.
Drop the over-65 results from the report because that group is small and makes the average look worse.
Report only the overall 94 percent figure to the product team, since it meets the launch target.
Raise the model's decision threshold so it flags fewer heartbeats overall, which will reduce errors in every age band.
questions.why: The over-65 group is thin in the data from the start, so the fix begins with the dataset: adding curated, verified examples for that group and re-testing per band is the step that addresses the cause.

questions.prompt: A startup gathers 40,000 photos of street signs by scraping random websites. Which problem is most directly about the source of the data rather than its coverage or balance?
choices: The photos have no known origin and the team may not have permission to use them.
The photos were all taken in daylight, so night-time conditions may be missing.
Forty thousand examples is too few for any model to learn anything useful from.
Some sign types appear far more often than others, so the label counts are uneven.
questions.why: Curated sources are inputs chosen and checked on purpose, with a known origin and permission to use, so scraped material with unknown origin fails the source test regardless of coverage.

questions.prompt: A speech model is trained on 2 million recordings, all made at one call centre in one region. Which outcome is most likely once the model is deployed nationally?
choices: It will show balanced results across regions because all recordings share one source.
It may perform well for callers similar to the recordings but poorly for accents it rarely heard.
It will be reliable for every caller because the dataset is very large.
It will overfit only if the test set is larger than the training set.
questions.why: A model generalises only to cases resembling its training data, so a huge but narrow dataset can leave whole groups poorly covered, and size cannot make up for missing coverage.

questions.prompt: A resume-screening model scores 90 percent accuracy on a held-out test set. Which reporting approach best exposes whether the model treats different groups unequally?
choices: Evaluate only on the training data, where the model is most accurate.
Remove any group with fewer than 100 examples before computing the average.
Report the single overall accuracy, since an average summarises the model fairly.
Split the held-out results by group and report accuracy for each group separately.
questions.why: Per-group results on a held-out set reveal gaps that a single average can hide, which is why results should be reported per group rather than as one overall number.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate why a model can look highly accurate overall and still fail one group of users, and name one limit or tradeoff of fixing that by adding more data.
lessons.modelAnswer: A single overall accuracy number averages across everyone, so a large majority group can hide poor results for a smaller group. The model only learns from the examples it was given. If a group is thin or missing in training, its patterns are weakly learned and its predictions are less reliable. The first check is to split the results by group and see whether the gap is there. The fix usually starts with the data: collect more real examples for the underrepresented group, confirm the labels for that group are as accurate as the others, and record where the data came from and whether it is licensed. One limit is that more data does not guarantee better coverage. If the collection process itself misses the group, adding volume keeps the same gap. A tradeoff is that rebalancing by copying examples can make the model memorise a few cases, so genuinely new examples are better than duplicates.
rubricPoints: Overall accuracy can hide poor results for a smaller group.
The model only learns patterns present in its training examples, so thin or missing groups are weakly learned.
Checking results per group, using a held-out set, reveals the gap.
Fixing it starts with the data: inclusive collection, balanced coverage, and accurate labels with known provenance.
Adding volume alone may not close the gap if collection itself misses the group.

suggested.rationale: Reasoning through a scenario about which dataset property caused a group-specific failure adds more than reading, and no listed mission or planned engine covers dataset review directly.

lessons.plain: When a model learns from examples, it can go wrong in several opposite ways. Bias is a steady tilt: the model is consistently worse for one group of people or situations, often because the training data left that group out or the labels carried past unfair judgments. Variance is sensitivity: the model reacts too strongly to the particular examples it saw, so its answers swing when the data changes. Overfitting means memorizing training examples, including their noise, so the model fails on new cases. Underfitting means the model is too simple to capture the real pattern, so it is weak everywhere. Both kinds of error can harm real people, and both can often be caught before launch by checking results separately for each group and on data the model never trained on.
lessons.guessPrompt: A loan-approval model is 95% accurate overall, yet it rejects qualified applicants from one postcode far more often than others. Before any teaching, what do you suspect went wrong, and why might one overall accuracy number hide the problem?
lessons.teach:
Bias, in this context, is a systematic error that pushes a model's results in a consistent direction, usually against one group of people or situations. It most often starts in the data: if training examples come mostly from one group, or the human labels reflect unfair past judgments, the model learns that pattern as if it were the truth. Harm to demographic groups is the effect: one group receives worse decisions, lower quality answers, or more errors.

Variance is how much a model's output changes when the training data changes. A high-variance model has learned quirks of its particular sample. Overfitting is the extreme case: the model memorizes training examples, so it scores very well on data it has seen and poorly on new data. Underfitting is the opposite: the model is too simple, or was trained too little, to capture the real pattern, so it is weak on both old and new data. Inaccuracy is the broad effect of all this: wrong answers reaching users.

Worked example. A resume screener is trained on 1,000 past hires, 900 of whom attended one university. Step one: the model learns that the university name predicts success, because most examples show it. Step two: a strong applicant from another school receives a low score. Step three: accuracy broken down by school reveals a much higher rejection rate for that school, even though the overall accuracy looked fine.

Common mistake: trusting a single average metric. An overall score can hide a group that is failing. The checks that catch this are subgroup analysis, which compares results per group, and testing on held-out data the model never trained on, which exposes overfitting.

Consequence: a model that passes an average launch test can still discriminate against people in production, which creates fairness, trust, and reputational problems for the organization that deployed it.

questions.prompt: A regional bank trains a fraud-flagging model on 50,000 past card transactions. About 85 percent come from urban branches. Step one: the model learns that transactions from rural postal codes are unusual, so it associates rural spending with fraud. Step two: legitimate rural customers have their cards blocked more often than urban customers. Step three is missing. Which step completes the way to catch this before launch?
choices: Train the model for more rounds so it learns that rural spending is normal.
Check that the overall fraud-catch rate across all regions is above 95 percent.
Raise the fraud threshold for every customer so that fewer transactions are flagged overall.
Compare the error rate per region using data the model never trained on, which reveals that rural customers are wrongly flagged more often.
questions.why: Subgroup analysis compares results per group on held-out data, which exposes a group that an overall average hides, and that is the check the teaching text describes.

questions.prompt: In plain terms, what does it mean for a model to have high variance?
choices: The model's output changes noticeably when the training data changes, because it has learned quirks of its particular sample.
The model scores the same on every dataset because it has memorized the training examples.
The model's answers are systematically pushed toward one group of people.
The model is too simple to capture the real pattern and is weak on both old and new data.
questions.why: The teaching text defines variance as how much a model's output changes when the training data changes, and high variance means it has learned quirks of its own sample.

questions.prompt: A demand-forecasting model for a grocery chain scores 98 percent accuracy on the sales records it was trained on but only 61 percent on next month's records. Which problem does this pattern most clearly show?
choices: Underfitting, because the model is too simple to capture the pattern.
Inaccuracy caused by a missing guardrail on the output.
Overfitting, because the model memorized its training examples and does poorly on new data.
Harm to a demographic group, because the errors fall on one kind of shopper.
questions.why: Overfitting is the case where a model scores very well on training data it has seen and poorly on new data, which matches the 98 versus 61 percent gap.
