questions.prompt: A health-insurance company launches a claims-triage model that reports 91 percent accuracy on a test set drawn from all members. Two months later, members in one age band are getting slower, worse decisions. Which check, run before launch, would most directly have caught this?
choices: Measuring the training loss curve and stopping when it flattens.
Breaking accuracy down by age band and testing on held-out data, so a failing group shows up before launch.
Adding a content filter that blocks offensive words in the model's replies.
Confirming that the overall accuracy figure is higher than the previous model's figure.
questions.why: Subgroup analysis compares results per group and held-out testing exposes problems the average hides, so this check would have revealed the failing age band before launch.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate the difference between bias and variance, give one user-facing effect of each, and name one limit of checking only overall accuracy before launch.
lessons.modelAnswer: Bias is a consistent tilt in a model's results, usually caused by training data that does not represent everyone or by labels that reflect past unfair judgments. Its effect is that one group gets worse outcomes repeatedly. Variance is sensitivity to the particular training sample: a high-variance model swings when the data changes and tends to memorize. Overfitting is the extreme case, with strong scores on training data and weak scores on new data. Underfitting is the reverse, a model too simple to learn the real pattern, so it is weak everywhere. For example, a face model that performs worse on darker skin tones because few such images were in training shows bias harming a group. A chatbot that repeats its training answers word for word but fails on new questions shows overfitting. The limit of checking only overall accuracy is that an average can hide a group that fails badly, so the team also needs results broken down by subgroup and a held-out test set.
rubricPoints: Bias is a consistent, systematic tilt that often comes from unrepresentative data or biased labels
Variance is sensitivity to the specific training sample, and overfitting is memorizing it
Underfitting is a model too simple to capture the real pattern, weak on old and new data
An overall accuracy number can hide a group that fails, so subgroup analysis and held-out testing are needed

suggested.rationale: Naming what went wrong in a model that fails one group is best practised by reasoning through a scenario, and no listed mission or engine covers machine learning fairness directly.

lessons.plain: When a computer system makes predictions or writes answers, it can be right for some people and wrong for others, or it can state false things with confidence. Detecting and monitoring bias and truthfulness means checking for these problems before launch and while the system runs. Three checks are central. First, you examine the labelled examples used to teach or test the system and ask whether the labels are accurate and consistent. Second, trained people review real outputs and grade them. Third, you split results by group, such as age, region, language or device, and compare error rates. A system can look good on average and still fail one group badly, and these checks help you notice before users do.
lessons.guessPrompt: A loan-approval model is 92 percent accurate overall, but it rejects applicants from one postcode far more often than others. Before any teaching, what single check would you run first to find out whether the problem comes from the data or from how the model behaves?
lessons.teach:
A label is the correct answer attached to an example, such as 'approved' or 'rejected'. Label-quality analysis checks whether those answers are accurate and consistent, usually by having two people label the same items independently and measuring how often they agree. A human audit is a planned review in which trained people read real outputs or decisions and grade them against a rubric, including whether factual claims are true. Subgroup analysis splits results by a group such as region, age band, language or device, then compares error rates for each group. Bias here means a systematic error that falls unevenly on some groups. Truthfulness means an output's claims match reality, which an average score can hide.

Why it works: the system learns whatever pattern the labels contain, so noisy or skewed labels teach skewed behaviour, and an overall average can hide a large failure in one group. Each check looks at a different place where the problem can start.

Worked example: a resume screener learned from past hiring decisions. Step 1: two reviewers independently relabel 200 past records. They disagree on 30 percent of one job family, so the labels there are unreliable. Step 2: subgroup analysis shows qualified candidates from one group are rejected at 21 percent, against 8 percent for others. Step 3: a human audit reads 50 of those rejections and finds 15 were qualified applicants whose experience was written in a format the training data rarely contained. The cause is noisy labels plus a data gap, and a pre-launch check would have flagged both.

Common mistake: reporting only overall accuracy and treating a good average as evidence of fairness.

In a running system, the gap keeps producing unfair rejections on every request, and if monitoring tracks only the average, the drift stays invisible until complaints arrive. Group-level checks and periodic human review must continue after launch as well as before.

questions.prompt: A telecom company uses a model to draft replies to customer support tickets. A team wants to know whether the drafts are unfair to some customers. Step 1: two reviewers independently label 150 past tickets as 'needs escalation' or 'resolve'. Overall they agree on 92 percent of tickets, but on billing-dispute tickets they agree on only 63 percent, so those labels are unreliable. Step 2: subgroup analysis splits the results by ticket language. Portuguese tickets get a wrong draft 19 percent of the time, against 6 percent for English tickets. Step 3 is missing: the team has not yet checked whether the wrong Portuguese drafts are actually false or harmful. The next step is to have trained reviewers read a sample of the flagged Portuguese drafts and grade each one against a written rubric, including whether every factual claim is true.
choices: Remove the language field from the data so that subgroup analysis can no longer split the results.
Report the 92 percent overall agreement as proof that the drafts are fair to all customers.
Have trained reviewers read a sample of the flagged Portuguese drafts and grade them against a rubric, including whether each factual claim is true.
Retrain the model on more English tickets so that the Portuguese error rate falls to match the English one.
questions.why: A human audit that grades outputs against a rubric, including truth of factual claims, is the step that confirms whether the subgroup gap reflects real harm.

questions.prompt: A content moderation team has two reviewers label 500 posts independently. They agree on 97 percent of all posts. Which conclusion do the figures support?
choices: The labels are accurate for every category of post, so no further checks are needed.
Agreement only measures the speed of the reviewers, not the quality of their labels.
The labels are unreliable, because 97 percent agreement is always too low to use.
The overall agreement cannot rule out unreliable labels within a specific category, so agreement should be checked per category.
questions.why: A high overall agreement can hide a narrow category where reviewers disagree, which is why label-quality analysis should look at each category.

questions.prompt: A voice assistant's speech recognizer is tested before launch with a single overall word error rate of 5 percent. After launch, users on smart speakers report far more errors. Which check would most likely have revealed this before launch?
choices: Subgroup analysis that compares error rates by device type, such as phones and smart speakers.
Asking the engineering team to review the source code of the recognizer.
Counting how many total users tried the assistant during the test.
Measuring the average response time across all devices.
questions.why: Splitting results by device and comparing error rates per group would expose a large failure that a single overall average hides.

questions.prompt: A medical-information chatbot has an average user rating of 4.6 out of 5. A team then runs a human audit in which trained reviewers check each dosage claim against reference material, and they find that about 1 in 10 dosage claims is wrong. What is the best conclusion?
choices: The user ratings were collected incorrectly and should be discarded entirely.
The high average rating can hide untruthful claims, so the audit results show a truthfulness problem that the rating does not reveal.
The chatbot is truthful, because users rate it highly.
The problem is only one of wording, so the dosage claims are acceptable as long as they sound confident.
questions.why: Truthfulness means claims match reality, and an average satisfaction score can conceal false claims that only a checked audit will find.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate why a model with high overall accuracy can still be unfair or untruthful, and name one limit of the checks you would use to catch this (label-quality analysis, human audits, or subgroup analysis).
lessons.modelAnswer: Overall accuracy is an average, so a model can be right for most users while failing a smaller group badly, and the average hides it. Subgroup analysis fixes that by splitting error rates by group and comparing them. Label-quality analysis asks whether the answers the model learned from were accurate and consistent in the first place; if two reviewers disagree often, the model is learning from guesses. Human audits catch what numbers miss, such as a fluent answer that is simply false, but they are slow and cover only a sample, so a rare failure can slip through. Subgroup checks also need enough examples per group to be meaningful, since a group of twenty records can swing wildly. So I would use all three together and treat small groups as a warning sign rather than a confirmed result.
rubricPoints: Overall accuracy can hide a failure that falls on one group.
Subgroup analysis compares error rates across groups.
Label-quality analysis checks whether training answers are accurate and consistent.
Human audits catch false or unfair outputs that metrics miss, but only cover a sample.
Small groups give unreliable numbers and need caution.

suggested.rationale: Reasoning through an exam-style scenario where a model fails one group adds the most, and no listed mission or planned engine covers this topic.

lessons.plain: When a computer system makes a decision about a person, such as approving a loan or flagging a message, people often want to know why. Some models are built so you can read their logic directly, like a short list of yes-or-no rules. Others are so tangled that even their builders cannot point to the reason for a single answer. A transparent model shows its workings. An explainable model may be harder to read, but it can still give a reasonable account of why it produced a given answer. A model that is neither leaves you with an answer and no usable story. This lesson is about telling these three kinds apart and knowing why the difference matters before a model reaches real users.
lessons.guessPrompt: A bank uses a model to approve or decline loan applications. A customer is declined and asks why. Which kind of model would make it easiest to give a truthful reason: a short set of readable rules, or a model with millions of internal numbers that nobody can inspect? Why do you think so?
lessons.teach: A transparent model is one whose internal logic a person can read and check directly, such as a short decision tree or a handful of weighted rules. An explainable model is one whose individual outputs can be justified after the fact, usually by a separate method that reports which inputs pushed a given answer up or down. A model that is neither is a black box: its internal workings are too numerous to read, and no reliable account of a single answer is available. Why does this matter? A transparent model gives you the reason as a by-product of how it computes, while an explanation method is an approximation layered on top, so it can be incomplete or wrong. Worked example: a bank declines an applicant whose income is 28,000 and whose debt ratio is 45 percent. A transparent rule set says: if income is under 30,000 and debt ratio is over 40 percent, decline. Step one, the first condition is true. Step two, the second condition is true. Step three, the rule fires, and the decision and its reason are the same thing. Now take a neural network that scores the same applicant at 0.31. An attribution method might report that debt ratio contributed most to the low score. That is useful, but it is an estimate of the network's reasoning, not the reasoning itself. Common mistake: assuming an explanation tool proves the model is fair or correct. Consequence in a running system: when a customer appeals or a regulator asks why one group is declined more often, a black box with no explanation method leaves the team unable to answer, which is why a simpler model may be chosen even at some cost in accuracy. Interpretability and performance often pull in opposite directions, so choosing between them is a deliberate decision that must be made before launch.

questions.prompt: A regional hospital schedules reminder calls using a short rule set that a clinic manager can read. The rule says: if the patient is over 75 and has missed 2 or more appointments in the past year, flag the patient for a reminder call. Patient A is 80 and has missed 3 appointments. Step one, the age condition is true. Step two, the missed-appointment condition is true. Step three, the rule fires, so Patient A is flagged, and the flag and its reason are the same thing. Patient B is 70 and has missed 4 appointments. Step one is shown: the age condition is false. Step three is left for you to complete: state whether Patient B is flagged, and why.
choices: Flagged, because the rule produces a high score and the explanation names the missed appointments
Not flagged, because the age condition is false and both conditions must be true for the rule to fire
Flagged, because missed appointments alone are enough to trigger the rule
Not flagged, because a transparent rule set cannot give a reason for a decision
questions.why: The rule requires both conditions to be true, and Patient B fails the age condition, so the rule does not fire and the reason is the failed condition itself.

questions.prompt: An online store uses a neural network to decide which shoppers get a discount code. Support staff can only see a ranked list of inputs produced by a separate tool after each decision. Which label best fits this model?
choices: Black box with no explanation method, because the network is too complex for any account of a single answer
Explainable, because individual decisions can be justified after the fact by a separate method
Neither transparent nor explainable, because the ranked list proves the network is accurate
Transparent, because staff can see the ranked list of inputs
questions.why: The model is explainable because each output can be justified afterward by a separate method, but it is not transparent because its internal logic cannot be read directly.

questions.prompt: A logistics company uses a short set of weighted rules to rank delivery routes. A planner reads every rule. Separately, an attribution report shows that distance contributed least to the route scores, and the team concludes the rules are fair across all depots. What is the best response?
choices: Accept the conclusion, because an attribution report that shows which inputs mattered is proof of fairness
Recognise that reading the rules is not the same as proving fairness, and test outcomes across depots, because attribution is an estimate and does not prove fairness
Accept the conclusion for distance only, since the attribution report covers every input
Drop the rules and switch to a black box, because transparent models can never be fair
questions.why: Transparency lets you read the logic, but fairness still has to be checked against outcomes, and an explanation method only approximates the reasoning rather than proving the model is fair.

questions.prompt: A city council is choosing a model to prioritise pothole repairs. Option X is a large neural network that is three percentage points more accurate but cannot be read or explained case by case. Option Y is a short decision tree that is slightly less accurate but its reasoning can be read directly. What should the council do before launch?
choices: Use option Y only if its accuracy is higher than option X
Choose the more accurate option automatically, because accuracy is always the most important property
Make a deliberate choice between accuracy and interpretability before launch, weighing how much the council must justify individual decisions to residents and regulators
Use option X and add a black box explanation later if residents complain
questions.why: Interpretability and performance often pull in opposite directions, so the council must make that trade-off deliberately before launch, based on how much it needs to justify individual decisions.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate the difference between a transparent model, an explainable model, and a model that is neither, using the loan example. Name one limit or tradeoff of choosing each kind.
lessons.modelAnswer: A transparent model is one we can read, like a few if-then rules or a small decision tree, so the reason for a decision is the same thing as the logic that produced it. An explainable model is harder to read, but we can attach a method that tells us which inputs most influenced a particular answer. A model that is neither gives us an answer with no usable account. For loans, a transparent model is the easiest to defend to a customer or regulator. Its limit is accuracy, since simple rules can underperform on complex patterns. An explainable model keeps more accuracy, but its explanation is an approximation, so it can mislead if we treat it as proof. A black box may have the strongest performance but the weakest accountability, so it needs stronger testing and monitoring before launch to catch unfair or wrong outcomes.
rubricPoints: Defines a transparent model as one whose logic can be read directly
Defines an explainable model as one whose outputs can be justified by a separate method
Identifies a model that is neither as a black box with no usable account of its answers
Names a tradeoff, such as accuracy against interpretability, or explanation approximation against proof

suggested.rationale: Explaining the three kinds of model back to a teammate and naming their tradeoffs is the core skill here, and no listed mission or planned engine targets it directly.

lessons.plain: Before a model goes live, someone needs to answer basic questions: what was it built for, what data taught it, how well does it work for different groups of people, and are we allowed to use it at all. This lesson covers the tools AWS offers to record and check those answers, plus the questions to ask about open-source models and licensing. Think of it like the label, test report, and receipt that come with a product you are about to sell. These tools do not make a model fair by themselves, but they make gaps visible before customers find them.
lessons.guessPrompt: A team wants to launch a model but cannot say what data it was trained on or whether they are allowed to reuse that data. Which two kinds of record would they need to find, and why might a fact like 'it is open source' fail to answer either question?
lessons.teach:
Transparency tools are records and tests that let people see how a model was built, what it does, and whether they may use it. Four ideas matter here.

A model card is a structured document describing one model: its intended use, the data it was trained on, its known limits, and its evaluation results. Amazon SageMaker Model Cards is the AWS service for keeping these records for models you build or host. The card is a governance record that can be reviewed and versioned. It describes the model; it does not test it. A card that says nothing about a particular user group is a warning sign, not proof of fairness.

Model evaluation means running a model against a test set and scoring its outputs. Amazon Bedrock Model Evaluations lets you compare foundation models (large pre-trained models you reach through an API) using automatic metrics or human reviewers, and you can supply prompts that reflect your real users. This works because a model that looks fine on average can fail one subgroup, and only a test that slices results by group reveals that.

Open-source models have publicly available weights, so you can inspect and self-host them. That gives visibility into the model artifact, but not automatically into the training data or into whether the license allows your commercial use.

Data and licensing asks where training data came from, whether it was curated, and what terms attach to it. Every model and dataset carries a license that sets permitted uses.

Worked example: a loan-scoring model declines applicants from one postcode area far more often. Step 1: check the model card for training data sources and whether that area was represented. Step 2: run an evaluation sliced by postcode. Step 3: confirm the data license permits this use. The gap shows up in step 1 or step 2, before launch.

Common mistake: treating a model card or an open-source label as a fairness certificate. The consequence in a running system is that a feature quietly disadvantages customers, and no test ever looked at them.

questions.prompt: A recruiting firm uses a self-hosted open-source model to rank job applications. Its model card says the training data came mainly from résumés submitted to one large employer, and it reports no results broken down by applicant group. The firm's review so far: Step 1, the card shows the training data was narrow, so this is a dataset concern to check before launch. Step 3, the firm confirms its data license allows commercial hiring use. The missing step is Step 2, the test that would show whether the ranking treats applicant groups differently. Which completion fills Step 2?
choices: Rely on the public model weights to confirm the training data was fair.
Ask the open-source project's maintainers to certify the model as unbiased.
Run an evaluation of the ranking outputs, sliced by applicant group, before launch.
Accept the model card as a fairness certificate, since it lists no complaints.
questions.why: Only an evaluation whose results are sliced by group can reveal a subgroup failure before launch, while the other choices treat a card, public weights, or a maintainer's word as proof of fairness.

questions.prompt: Which statement correctly describes what an Amazon SageMaker Model Card is for?
choices: It runs a test set against a model and scores its outputs for fairness.
It stores the model's live traffic logs so engineers can debug errors.
It is a versioned governance record describing a model's intended use, training data, known limits, and evaluation results, but it does not test the model.
It is a license agreement that grants commercial rights to a foundation model.
questions.why: The teaching text defines a model card as a structured, reviewable record that describes a model and explicitly says it does not test the model.

questions.prompt: A team self-hosts an open-source model and argues it is cleared for commercial product use because its weights are publicly downloadable. What is the flaw in that reasoning?
choices: Self-hosted models cannot be used commercially under any license.
Public weights make the model artifact inspectable, but they do not establish that the license permits commercial use or reveal the training data.
Open-source models must be evaluated by Amazon Bedrock Model Evaluations before any use at all.
Public weights prove the training data was curated, so only the license needs checking.
questions.why: The teaching text says open-source weights give visibility into the artifact but not automatically into training data or whether the license allows commercial use.

questions.prompt: A retailer's support chatbot scores well on average in a pre-launch review, but customers who write in a regional dialect get poor answers. Which pre-launch practice would most likely have caught this?
choices: Checking that the foundation model's license names the retailer as a permitted user.
Adding a card entry that states the chatbot is fair to all customers.
Reading the model card's list of intended uses and confirming the dialect is not mentioned.
Running a model evaluation using prompts that reflect real users, with results sliced by user group so the dialect gap shows.
questions.why: A model that looks fine on average can fail one subgroup, and only an evaluation with realistic prompts sliced by group reveals that gap, whereas a card or license check does not test outputs.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would decide whether a model is safe to launch for a customer-facing feature. Name which tool or record you would use for each check, and name one limit of those tools.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would split the check into three questions. First, what do we know about the model? The model card, or the vendor's published documentation for a foundation model, tells us the intended use, training data sources, and known limits. Second, does it work for everyone who will use it? I would run a Bedrock Model Evaluation using our own realistic prompts, and I would look at results sliced by user group or language rather than only the overall average, because an average can hide a failing group. Third, are we allowed to use it the way we plan? That means checking the license on the model and on any dataset, including commercial use and attribution. The limit I would name to the team is that none of these tools proves fairness on its own. A card only records what someone wrote down, and an evaluation only covers the prompts we chose, so we still need human review of failures and monitoring after launch.
rubricPoints: A model card records intended use, training data, and known limits, but it documents the model rather than testing it.
Bedrock Model Evaluations compares models on metrics using your own prompts, and results should be sliced by user group.
Open-source weights give visibility into the model artifact, not automatically into training data or usage rights.
Licensing and data provenance determine whether the planned use is permitted at all.
Each tool has a limit, so human review and post-launch monitoring still matter.

suggested.rationale: Matching a badly behaving model to the right transparency tool is best practised by reasoning through an exam-style scenario, with the tool names learned as reference facts.

lessons.plain: Some decisions made by software need two things that can pull against each other. One is safety: the system should not produce harmful or unfair results. The other is transparency: people should be able to see how it reached a result. A very simple, easy-to-read rule is easy to check but may miss subtle cases. A very powerful, complicated system may be more accurate but hard to inspect. This objective is about recognizing that tension and choosing the balance that fits the job, instead of assuming more of one is always better.
lessons.guessPrompt: A bank wants software to approve or refuse loans. Option A is a short list of rules anyone can read, and it is right about 80 percent of the time. Option B is a complex model that is right about 92 percent of the time, but nobody can say why it rejected a given person. Which would you pick, and what would make you change your mind?
lessons.teach:
Definitions. Interpretability means how easily a human can see which inputs drove a particular decision. Performance means how often the system does its job correctly, such as its accuracy. Transparency is broader: documenting what a system was built from, what it is meant for, and where it fails. Safety means limiting harmful outputs and unfair treatment, often with checks such as guardrails that block certain content.

Why the tension exists. Simple models, such as a short scoring formula or a shallow decision tree, have few moving parts, so a reviewer can trace each step. Large neural networks can capture far more patterns, which often raises accuracy, but their internal calculations are not readable by people. Explanation tools can approximate what drove a decision, but an approximation is not the true reason, and it can mislead.

Worked example. Take the loan case. Model A is a weighted formula, so a refused applicant's reason is the two factors with the largest negative weights. Model B has 92 percent accuracy, but to explain a refusal the team runs an approximation tool, which says income and recent missed payments mattered most. Step one: check whether the approximation matches what the model actually does on test cases. Step two: if a regulator or customer needs a reason, weigh whether the 4-point accuracy gain justifies a harder audit. Step three: record the choice and its limits in a model card.

Common mistake: treating the most accurate model as automatically the best choice, or trusting an explanation tool without testing it.

Consequence: an opaque model that starts drifting can refuse people for reasons nobody can name, and the team cannot find the fault quickly.

Safety and transparency also pull apart. Publishing exact safety filter rules can help attackers avoid them, so good practice is to disclose a system's purpose and limits rather than every internal rule.

questions.prompt: An insurer runs two models to flag suspicious car claims. Model P is a shallow decision tree with 91 percent accuracy, so each flag can be traced along a short path of yes/no questions. Model Q is a large ensemble with 94 percent accuracy, and its reasons come from an approximation tool. For a flagged claim from Model Q, the approximation tool says claim amount and claim filed within 7 days of policy start mattered most. Step one: test whether the approximation tool's reasons agree with what Model Q actually does on a sample of held-out claims. Step two is missing. Step three: record the chosen model and its limits in a model card. Which step two completes the process?
choices: Retrain the decision tree on the same claims data to raise its accuracy before deciding anything else.
Publish the exact fraud-scoring thresholds on the public website so that every customer can see every rule.
Skip any further checks, because the model with the higher accuracy is automatically the right choice.
Weigh whether the 3-point accuracy gain is worth a harder audit, given that customers or regulators may need a reason for each flag.
questions.why: Step two is the trade-off decision: the team compares the accuracy gain against the extra cost of auditing an opaque model when a reason must be given, which is the same logic the teaching text applies at its own step two.

questions.prompt: In plain terms, which statement best separates interpretability from transparency?
choices: Interpretability is how well a system is documented, while transparency is how often it answers correctly.
Interpretability means blocking harmful outputs, while transparency means measuring the error rate on test data.
Interpretability and transparency are two names for the same property, both describing model accuracy.
Interpretability is how easily a person can see which inputs drove one decision, while transparency is documenting what a system was built from, what it is for, and where it fails.
questions.why: The teaching text defines interpretability as seeing which inputs drove a particular decision and transparency as the broader documentation of origin, purpose, and failure points.

questions.prompt: A content team uses a summary tool whose reasons for rejecting a draft come from an approximation tool. Reviewers accept each reason without checking it. What is the most likely failure?
choices: The tool is safe because approximation tools always reveal the exact internal calculations of a neural network.
The summary tool has no accuracy, so its rejections cannot be measured at all.
The reviewers are required to publish every internal rule to the public before any draft can be rejected.
The approximation may not be the true reason the model rejected the draft, and nobody has tested whether it matches the model's behaviour.
questions.why: The teaching text warns that an explanation is an approximation, not the true reason, and that trusting an explanation tool without testing it is a common mistake.

questions.prompt: A company publishes a full list of the exact keyword rules its safety filter uses to block harmful text. Why does this work against the goal of safety?
choices: Publishing exact rules lets attackers study and avoid them, so good practice is to disclose the system's purpose and limits instead of every internal rule.
Publishing the list has no effect on safety, because filters are never bypassed in practice.
Publishing the list makes the filter faster, which always reduces harmful output.
Publishing the list makes the filter more accurate, because outside reviewers will fix every error.
questions.why: The teaching text notes that exact safety filter rules can help attackers avoid them, so practice favours disclosing purpose and limits rather than every internal rule.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate why a more accurate model is not always the right choice when the system must justify its decisions to customers. Name one specific limit or tradeoff of the option you would choose.
lessons.modelAnswer: A more accurate model is only better if it meets the whole requirement. If customers or regulators must get a reason for each decision, a model whose decisions cannot be traced is a problem even at higher accuracy. A simpler model, such as a weighted formula, shows which factors pushed a result up or down, so the reason can be given directly. Its trade-off is that it may miss subtle patterns and be wrong more often on complex cases. An opaque model can be paired with an explanation tool, but that tool gives an approximation, so the team should test whether its reasons match what the model actually does. Safety adds a second pull: exposing exact filter rules can help people evade them, so we share purpose and limits instead. I would pick the simplest model that clears the accuracy bar and document the gap.
rubricPoints: Defines interpretability and performance and says they can conflict.
Notes that simple models are easier to trace but may be less accurate on complex data.
Explains that explanation tools give approximations and must be tested against real behaviour.
Connects safety and transparency: full disclosure of rules can help attackers, so disclose purpose and limits.
Names a concrete trade-off of the option the learner would choose.

suggested.rationale: Weighing safety, transparency and accuracy against each other and justifying the choice is best learned by explaining it back, since no listed mission or planned engine practises this reasoning.

lessons.plain: Human-centered design for explainable AI means building an AI-assisted product around the people who use its output. The goal is that they can tell when a machine made a decision, get a useful reason for it, and flag mistakes so the team can fix them. Think of a clerk who stamps a form and also shows you which rule they applied, and gives you a way to ask for a second look. A good design treats the person as the final checker, not as someone who must simply accept the answer.
lessons.guessPrompt: An AI tool quietly declines a customer's request and gives no reason. Before reading on, what would you add to the screen so a person could trust the decision or challenge it, and why?
lessons.teach:
Human-centered design for explainable AI means shaping an AI-assisted product around the people who use its outputs, so they can understand what the system did and correct it when it is wrong. Explainable AI, often shortened to XAI, is the set of methods that make a model's behaviour understandable to people. Transparency is the broader practice of openly telling users that a machine is involved, what the system is for, what it cannot do, and what evidence it used. A user-feedback mechanism is any channel, such as a flag button, a reason menu, or an appeal form, that lets users send a bad output back to the team.

It works because people calibrate trust. When users know an answer came from a model, roughly what it relied on, and how to challenge it, they can rely on it appropriately instead of over-trusting or ignoring it. Feedback also shows the team real failures that no test set covered.

Worked example: a support assistant suggests refusing a refund. Step 1: the screen labels the suggestion as AI-generated. Step 2: it shows the policy clause and order facts it used. Step 3: the agent clicks 'this is wrong' and picks 'policy changed'. Step 4: the case is logged with input, output and reason, and the team reviews a sample from that reason each week. Step 5: they find the model read an outdated policy document, and they fix the source.

Common mistake: adding a feedback button and never reviewing it, or writing an explanation that sounds plausible but is not what actually drove the output. In a running system, users then stop using the button, errors go unseen, and the same wrong refusals keep repeating.

Good explanation design therefore treats the user as a checker and the feedback as data the team must act on, not as decoration.

questions.prompt: A regional bank uses an AI tool to pre-sort small business loan applications into 'likely approve' and 'send to underwriter'. Its designers follow a human-centered pattern. Step 1: the screen labels each sorting result as produced by an AI tool. Step 2: it shows the income and debt fields the tool relied on. Step 3: an underwriter clicks 'this sort is wrong' and picks 'missing document'. Step 4: [missing step]. Step 5: the team finds that the tool ignored a tax form that some self-employed applicants upload as a scanned image, and fixes the document intake. Which step completes the pattern?
choices: Log each flagged case with its input, the tool's output and the chosen reason, then review a sample from each reason every week.
Turn off the flag button for underwriters with high case loads so they can work faster.
Retrain the sorting model overnight on only the flagged applications, then remove the feedback button to cut noise.
Publish the tool's weighting of each field to every applicant so no decision is hidden.
questions.why: Step 4 is the point where feedback becomes data the team acts on, which means logging the input, output and reason and reviewing them regularly, the step that leads to finding the scanned-form problem in step 5.

questions.prompt: A grocery chain adds a feature where its app shows a delivery-time estimate produced by a model. Which term names a channel that lets customers send a wrong estimate back to the team, such as a report button with a reason list?
choices: A user-feedback mechanism
An explainable AI method
A dataset audit
A model card
questions.why: A user-feedback mechanism is defined as any channel such as a flag button, reason menu or appeal form that sends a bad output back to the team, and the other options describe different ideas.

questions.prompt: A city housing office uses an AI tool to rank rental applicants. The office's explanation for each ranking is a fluent paragraph written by a second model after the ranking was made, and it cites reasons the ranking tool never actually used. Which failure does this design show?
choices: Good transparency, because a clear paragraph tells users what the system is for.
A missing feedback mechanism, because users cannot flag the paragraph.
An explanation that sounds plausible but is not what actually drove the output, so users calibrate trust on a false picture.
Variance in the ranking model, because the paragraph changes from one applicant to another.
questions.why: The teaching text warns that an explanation which sounds plausible but is not what actually drove the output misleads users, and a fluent post-hoc paragraph citing unused reasons is exactly that failure.

questions.prompt: A streaming service's AI recommends a bundle of shows to a family account. Which set of design choices best follows the human-centered approach for explainable AI?
choices: Label the bundle as AI-suggested, show the viewing history and genre signals it used, and let viewers flag a bundle with a reason that the team logs and reviews.
Show only the final list with no label, since viewers will assume a human chose it and trust it more.
Let the model write its own marketing copy claiming it understands the family perfectly, which builds confidence.
Hide the recommendation source so the interface feels simpler, and collect feedback only through a yearly survey.
questions.why: Labelling the source, showing the signals used, and offering a reasoned flag that the team reviews covers the transparency and feedback parts of the approach, while the other choices hide, mislead or ignore user input.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what makes an AI-assisted screen human-centered, using the idea of a user-feedback mechanism. Name one limit or tradeoff of showing explanations to users.
lessons.modelAnswer: A human-centered AI screen makes it clear that a model produced the output, shows the main facts or policy it relied on, and gives the user a simple way to say the output is wrong, with a reason. The feedback matters only if the team reviews it regularly and traces it back to the data or documents that caused the error. The main tradeoff is that a detailed explanation can make users trust the output too much, especially when the explanation is only a plausible story and not the true reason the model acted. There is also a cost in clutter and in the effort of building the explanation itself. So the design should show enough to let people check the decision, and be honest that the explanation is approximate.
rubricPoints: Defines transparency: users know a model is involved and what it can and cannot do
Explains that user feedback is a channel that must be reviewed and acted on
Names a tradeoff, such as overtrust in a plausible but unfaithful explanation, or added complexity
Notes that explanations should be honest about being approximate

suggested.rationale: Explaining how transparency and feedback work, and their limits, to a teammate is the core skill here and no listed mission or planned engine covers it.

lessons.plain: Keeping an AI system safe means controlling who can touch it, locking up the data it uses, keeping its traffic off the open internet, finding sensitive information you did not mean to store, and filtering what it says. On AWS, five building blocks do this work. Roles and policies decide who or what may act. Encryption scrambles stored and moving data so only key holders can read it. Macie hunts for personal data hidden in storage. PrivateLink keeps traffic on a private path. Guardrails screen what goes into and comes out of a model. Think of them as locks, sealed envelopes, a private corridor, a metal detector, and an editor checking what leaves the building.
lessons.guessPrompt: An AI chatbot needs to read customer records from a storage bucket and call a model. Without looking anything up, what two or three ways would you use to stop an attacker or a bug from reading those records?
lessons.teach:
An IAM role is an identity with no fixed password that a person or service can temporarily take on. IAM stands for Identity and Access Management. An IAM policy is a JSON document that lists which actions are allowed or denied on which resources. Anything not explicitly allowed is denied, and an explicit deny beats any allow.

Encryption at rest means stored data is scrambled. Encryption in transit means data is scrambled while it moves between machines. AWS Key Management Service (KMS) holds the keys. A reader without permission to use the key sees only unreadable bytes, even if they copy the file.

Amazon Macie is a discovery service. It scans Amazon S3 buckets, where many AI documents and training files live, and reports where personal or financial data appears. It finds and reports; it does not block access by itself.

AWS PrivateLink creates private interface endpoints inside your virtual network. Calls to an AWS service then travel on AWS's internal network instead of the public internet.

Amazon Bedrock Guardrails are configurable checks applied to prompts going into a foundation model and to responses coming back. They can block denied topics, filter harmful content, and redact sensitive information such as names or account numbers.

Worked example: a support assistant reads tickets from a bucket. Step 1: its role may read only the tickets prefix, so IAM limits it. Step 2: the bucket is encrypted with a KMS key that only that role may use. Step 3: model calls go through a PrivateLink endpoint, so no public path exists. Step 4: Macie reports that some tickets contain card numbers. Step 5: a guardrail redacts card numbers from replies.

Common mistake: treating guardrails as the security boundary. A guardrail filters content; it does not stop an over-permissioned role from reading every bucket. Consequence: if the role has broad rights and its credentials leak, one stolen credential exposes every customer file, however good the output filter is. Controls must be layered.

questions.prompt: A freight company runs an invoice-summary assistant that reads files from one storage bucket (a container of files in Amazon S3). Step 1: its IAM role (an identity it temporarily takes on) may read only the invoices folder prefix, and an explicit deny blocks deleting anything there. Step 2: the invoices are encrypted with a key from AWS Key Management Service (KMS) that only that role may use. Step 3: model calls travel through a PrivateLink endpoint (a private connection inside the virtual network), so no public path exists. Step 4: [missing]. Step 5: a guardrail stops replies from quoting bank account numbers. Which completes step 4?
choices: Macie blocks the role from opening any file where it finds bank account numbers.
Macie scans the bucket and reports which files contain bank account numbers, without blocking access on its own.
Macie rotates the KMS key every time it finds sensitive data, so older copies become unreadable.
Macie encrypts each flagged invoice in transit so the assistant cannot read the numbers.
questions.why: Macie (a discovery service) finds and reports where sensitive data sits in S3 but does not block access by itself, so option B is the only accurate completion.

questions.prompt: A nightly report job runs on a server and needs permission to read a storage bucket. Which description fits an IAM role rather than a stored password?
choices: An identity with no fixed password that the job temporarily takes on to get permissions
A long-lived username and password saved in the job's configuration file
A list of allowed and denied actions attached to a single file
A key that scrambles the report files while they sit in storage
questions.why: An IAM role is an identity with no fixed password that a person or service can temporarily assume, which is what the job would do here.

questions.prompt: A team's assistant role has an allow policy for reading all storage buckets. A second policy explicitly denies reading the payroll bucket. Can the role read files in the payroll bucket?
choices: Yes, because anything not denied is permitted
Only if the payroll files are stored unencrypted
No, because an explicit deny beats any allow
Yes, because the allow policy was written first
questions.why: In IAM, an explicit deny overrides any allow, so the role cannot read the payroll bucket despite the broader allow.

questions.prompt: A security reviewer says a chat app's guardrail, which redacts card numbers from replies, is enough to protect the customer database. What is the flaw in that reasoning?
choices: Guardrails can only redact names, never card numbers
Guardrails only run during model training, not at answer time
Guardrails filter content and do not stop an over-permissioned role from reading the stored data, so access control needs its own layer
Guardrails encrypt the customer database at rest
questions.why: Guardrails check prompts and responses but do not limit which identities can read the underlying data, so access must be controlled separately through IAM and encryption.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate why an AI application that handles customer data needs more than one of these controls, and name one limit of the guardrail feature.
lessons.modelAnswer: No single control covers every failure. IAM decides who and what can act, so a leaked credential with narrow permissions does limited damage. Encryption with KMS means copied files stay unreadable without key access. PrivateLink keeps model and storage traffic off the public internet, which reduces exposure. Macie tells us where sensitive data actually sits, so we can clean it up instead of assuming it is absent. Guardrails screen prompts and replies. Their limit is that they only filter the content the model handles. They do not control who may call the API or read the bucket, and their detection is not perfect, so they cannot be the only defense. A sensible design layers all of them and checks that each one still works.
rubricPoints: IAM roles and policies control which identities may perform which actions on which resources.
Encryption with managed keys keeps copied data unreadable without key access.
PrivateLink keeps traffic on a private network path instead of the public internet.
Macie discovers and reports sensitive data in storage; it does not block access by itself.
Guardrails filter prompts and responses but do not replace access control.

suggested.rationale: Working out whether IAM allow and deny statements grant a given action is closest to the authorization policy evaluator planned here.

lessons.plain: When a company runs an AI tool in the cloud, the work of keeping it safe is split between two parties: the cloud provider and the company using it. The provider looks after the buildings, the hardware, and the underlying platform the tool runs on. The company decides who can use the tool, what data it may see, how that data is protected, and how its use is watched. This split is called the shared responsibility model. Knowing where your side of the line sits tells you which controls you must set up yourself and which ones you can assume are already in place. When an auditor asks how customer data is kept in bounds, the answer is about your side of the line.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your team uses a managed AI service from a cloud provider to summarise customer support chats. A staff account with far more access than it needed exports the chat logs and they leak. Who was most responsible for preventing this, the provider or your team, and why?
lessons.teach:
The shared responsibility model is the agreed division of security duties between a cloud provider and the customer. Security of the cloud is the provider's job: the physical data centres, the hardware, the core network, and, for a managed service, the software platform that runs the model and keeps it patched. Security in the cloud is the customer's job: the data you send, who holds access and how that access is granted (identity and policies), the encryption and network paths you choose, the logs you keep, and how you use the outputs. It works this way because the provider can see the hardware but not your business rules, while you can see your data but not the data centre floor.

Worked example. A claims team uses a managed text-generation model. Step 1: the provider keeps the service running, patched, and physically secure. Step 2: the team creates an identity that lets only the claims application call the model, not every engineer. Step 3: the team decides that prompts must not include national identifiers unless a claim needs them. Step 4: the team turns on logging of who called the model and when. Step 5: the team reviews a sample of outputs before customers see them. The provider owned step 1; the team owned steps 2 to 5.

Common mistake: assuming that a managed, secure platform makes the data inside it secure. The platform does not know which records are sensitive or who should see them. Consequence in a running system: if the claims application is given a broad administrator key, one leaked key exposes every customer record, and the provider is not responsible for that outcome. The split also moves with the service type. If you run a model yourself on a virtual machine, you own more of the stack than you do with a managed model service.

The provider secures the platform; you secure what you put on it and who may touch it.

questions.prompt: A regional university runs an open-source text model on a virtual machine it rents from a cloud provider, to summarise student support tickets. The team writes its own plan. Step 1: the provider keeps the data centre, the physical hardware and the core network secure. Step 2: the university allows only the support-desk application role to call the model server. Step 3: the university encrypts the ticket summaries stored on the rented disk. Step 4: the university keeps a log of which service calls the model and when. One step is still missing from the university's own duties. Which step completes the list?
choices: Applying security patches to the operating system and the model server running on the rented virtual machine
Deleting the access logs every 24 hours to save storage cost
Replacing the failed cooling unit in the provider's data centre
Asking the cloud provider to read a sample of the ticket summaries before staff see them
questions.why: On a self-managed virtual machine the customer owns the operating system and the software it runs, so patching those is the university's duty, while the provider owns the physical facility and the hardware.

questions.prompt: Which statement best describes the shared responsibility model?
choices: The cloud provider is responsible for all security once a service is labelled as managed, so customers need no further controls.
The customer is responsible for physical data centre access, hardware replacement and core network cabling.
Security duties are divided between the provider, which secures the cloud itself, and the customer, which secures its data, access rules, encryption choices and logs.
Every security duty is split exactly 50/50 between provider and customer no matter which service is used.
questions.why: The model is an agreed division where the provider secures the underlying cloud and the customer secures what it places in the cloud, including data, access and logging.

questions.prompt: A small recipe app uses a managed image-generation model. A developer stores a long-lived access key in a public code repository, and an attacker uses it to call the model and pull stored prompts. Who owns the failure under the shared responsibility model?
choices: Nobody, because the attacker used a valid key and the platform worked as designed.
The app team, because managing access keys and keeping credentials out of public code is a customer-side duty.
Both equally, because the provider and the customer each own half of every security event.
The cloud provider, because the model service was managed and the provider keeps its platform patched.
questions.why: Who holds access and how credentials are handled is the customer's responsibility, so a leaked key in the customer's repository is the customer's failure even on a managed platform.

questions.prompt: A hospital runs its own self-hosted language model on virtual machines it rents from a cloud provider. Which set of duties falls to the hospital rather than to the provider?
choices: Maintaining the physical security of the building where the provider's servers sit.
Patching the virtual machine's operating system, setting network rules, and choosing how patient text is encrypted and logged.
Replacing failed drives in the provider's racks and keeping the facility's power supply running.
Patching the hypervisor that divides the physical host into virtual machines.
questions.why: Running a model on a virtual machine moves the operating system, network rules, data protection and logging to the customer, while the provider keeps the physical facility, the hardware and the hypervisor layer.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate who has just joined: for an AI feature that answers customer questions using our customer records, what the cloud provider is responsible for, what we are responsible for, and name one limit of this split that we still have to plan for.
lessons.modelAnswer: The provider is responsible for security of the cloud: the data centres, the hardware, the core network, and the managed platform that runs the model, including its patching. We are responsible for security in the cloud for this feature. That means deciding which engineers and services can call the model and which customer records the feature can read, which is set through identity and access rules; choosing encryption and private network paths for the data; keeping logs of who asked what and when; and checking answers before they reach customers. One limit we still have to plan for is that the provider cannot know which of our records are sensitive, so we must classify and filter that data ourselves before the model sees it. Without that step, a correctly secured platform can still expose data we never should have sent.
rubricPoints: Provider secures the underlying infrastructure and managed platform.
Customer secures its data, identities and access rules, encryption and network paths.
Customer keeps logs and reviews outputs for the AI feature.
Names a limit: the provider cannot judge which data is sensitive, so the customer must classify and filter it.

suggested.rationale: Explaining the split to a teammate, including its limits, is the core skill, and no listed mission or planned engine practises this directly.

lessons.plain: When an AI agent can take actions, such as looking up an order or sending an email, two questions matter. Who is the agent acting as? That is its identity, like a badge that tells a guard who you are. What may it do? That is its policy, a set of rules listing permitted actions and their conditions. Both checks should happen outside the AI model, because a model can be talked into things its instructions forbid. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore is the AWS platform for running agents, and it includes components for both jobs.
lessons.guessPrompt: A customer-support agent can look up orders and issue refunds. If a customer types a clever message telling it to refund everything, what should stop it: the model's good judgment, or a separate rule checked before the refund runs? Which would you trust, and why?
lessons.teach: An agent is an AI model that can call tools, such as reading an order record or issuing a refund. Identity means who the agent acts as. Inbound identity is the verified caller reaching the agent. Outbound identity is the credential the agent uses when it reaches other systems. In Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, the Identity component verifies callers and stores outbound tokens or keys in a managed vault, so secrets are not pasted into prompts or code. A policy is a rule set checked on every tool call before it runs. It is deny by default: an action proceeds only if a rule explicitly allows it, possibly with conditions such as amount limits. AgentCore Policy provides this check, so the decision sits outside the model. Worked example. A support agent, acting for verified customer Ana, asks to refund order 512 for 80 dollars. Step 1: Identity confirms the request came from Ana's signed-in session and that the agent uses its own limited refund role. Step 2: The model proposes refund(order=512, amount=80). Step 3: The policy checks the rule 'refunds up to 50 dollars on orders the caller owns'. The amount is over 50 and no rule allows it, so the call is denied. Step 4: The denial and its reason are logged, and the agent tells Ana a person must approve it. Common mistake: writing 'never refund over 50' only in the system prompt. A prompt is guidance the model can be argued out of, for example by instructions hidden in a customer's message. Put the limit in the policy. Consequence: with the rule only in the prompt, one crafted message could push many refunds through, and nothing outside the model would stop them. Identity and policy checks outside the model keep the agent inside its bounds even when the model is fooled.

questions.prompt: Brightline, a travel company, runs a booking agent that acts for verified employee Priya. Priya asks the agent to cancel booking 7731, and the policy contains the rule 'cancel bookings the caller owns'. Step 1: Identity confirms the request came from Priya's signed-in session and that the agent uses its own limited booking role. Step 2: The model proposes cancel_booking(booking=7731). Step 3: [missing]. Step 4: The cancellation runs, and the event is logged with the rule that allowed it. Which entry correctly fills step 3?
choices: The model rereads its system prompt and decides whether cancelling is acceptable for this employee.
The cancellation runs first and the policy reviews it afterward, so the log can record the outcome.
AgentCore Policy checks the proposed call against explicit rules before it runs, and the call proceeds only because a rule allows it.
The agent writes Priya's session token into the tool call so the booking system can check it.
questions.why: The policy is a check outside the model that runs on each tool call before it executes, and it allows the call only when an explicit rule permits it.

questions.prompt: Which pairing correctly matches each AgentCore part to its job, as described in the teaching text?
choices: Identity and Policy both only write logs after a tool has already run, so they never stop anything from happening in the first place.
Identity stores outbound keys in a vault; Policy verifies inbound callers.
Identity verifies callers and keeps outbound tokens in a managed vault; Policy checks each tool call first.
Policy verifies callers; Identity decides which refund amounts are allowed.
questions.why: The teaching text says Identity verifies callers and stores outbound tokens or keys in a vault, while Policy checks every tool call before it runs.

questions.prompt: A developer building a parcel-tracking agent pastes the carrier's API key directly into the agent's prompt so the model can call the carrier. What is the main risk, and what fix does the teaching text describe?
choices: Risk: the key loads slowly; fix: cache it in the model's working memory.
Risk: the key sits in prompts and code where it can leak; fix: keep it in the managed vault that Identity uses for outbound credentials.
Risk: the carrier charges more per call; fix: rotate the key monthly inside the prompt.
There is no risk, because the model never repeats its prompt; no fix is needed.
questions.why: The teaching text says secrets should not be pasted into prompts or code, and that Identity stores outbound tokens or keys in a managed vault instead.

questions.prompt: A hospital scheduling agent has a policy with one rule: 'reschedule appointments the caller booked'. A request arrives to cancel an appointment that a different patient booked. Under a deny-by-default policy, what happens?
choices: The call proceeds, because the policy only blocks actions that a rule specifically forbids.
The model decides from its prompt whether the cancellation is reasonable before any check runs.
The call proceeds with a warning in the log and a staff member reviews it later, since the agent is trusted to act on requests.
The call is denied, because no rule explicitly allows cancelling a booking the caller did not make.
questions.why: Deny by default means an action proceeds only when a rule explicitly allows it, and no rule covers cancelling someone else's booking.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate who is building a support agent why identity and policy are separate controls, and name one limit or tradeoff of relying on a policy check.
lessons.modelAnswer: Identity and policy answer different questions, so they are separate controls. Identity establishes who is calling the agent and which credential the agent uses to reach other systems. Policy decides, for each specific action, whether it is allowed. An agent can have a valid identity and still be denied a refund above a limit, and a policy is hard to audit if you cannot tell which identity made the call. The main limit is that a policy only covers the actions and conditions someone thought to write down. Anything not explicitly allowed is blocked, so an incomplete rule set breaks legitimate work, while overly broad rules let risky actions through. Policies also need review as tools and business rules change. The tradeoff is precision against maintenance: tighter rules are safer but block legitimate requests more often, so test them against realistic requests and keep the log of every allow and deny.
rubricPoints: Identity answers who the agent acts as, covering both inbound callers and outbound credentials.
Policy checks each tool call before it runs and is deny by default.
Policy enforcement sits outside the model, so manipulated prompts cannot override it.
A named limit: policies only cover what was written, so gaps or overly broad rules are the tradeoff.
Logged identity and allow or deny decisions give an auditor evidence of what the agent did.

suggested.rationale: The core skill is explaining why identity and policy are separate controls and where each one stops, which is best practised by explaining it back.

lessons.plain: When an AI system gives an answer, someone should be able to ask where the information came from, what the model was built on, and who checked it. Documenting data origins means writing that trail down: where each dataset came from, how it changed on the way, and where it is listed so others can find it. Data lineage is the map of that journey. Data cataloging is a searchable index of which datasets exist, who owns them, and whether they may be used. A model card is a structured record for one specific model that states its purpose, its training data, how it was tested, and its known limits. Auditors and teammates use these records to answer questions about trust and origin without re-running everything.
lessons.guessPrompt: Imagine a company chatbot starts giving wrong answers about refund rules, and a regulator asks which documents the model learned from and who approved using them. What records would you need to answer that, and where would you look for them?
lessons.teach:
Data lineage is the recorded history of a dataset: where it originated, which systems copied, filtered, or joined it, and what transformations were applied before a model used it. A data catalog is a searchable inventory of datasets that stores each one's description, owner, sensitivity label, and location, so people can find the right data and check whether it is approved for a given use. A model card is a structured document about one trained model. It states the model's intended use, the data it was trained and evaluated on, the metrics used to judge it, its known limitations, and who is accountable for it.

Why this works: each record answers a different auditor question. Lineage answers where did this come from. The catalog answers what data exists and am I allowed to use it. The model card answers what was this model built for and how well does it perform.

Worked example: a support-ticket dataset is exported from the helpdesk system. The export job is logged as the first lineage entry, with source, date, and version. A cleaning job then removes customer names, and that transformation is logged with the operator and the rule used. The cleaned set is registered in the catalog with an owner and a label saying it holds no direct identifiers. A classifier is trained on that exact version, and its model card cites the dataset version, the evaluation results, and the approved use of routing tickets. An auditor questioning any output can now walk backward through each step.

Common mistake: documenting the model but not the exact data version. A card that says trained on support tickets becomes useless once the export has been re-run with different filters. Record the version and the transformation steps.

Consequence: if a retention rule requires deleting one customer's records and the lineage is missing, the team cannot tell which trained models used that data, so every model trained on the export must be treated as affected.

questions.prompt: A logistics firm exports 4.2 million shipment delay records from its warehouse system as version 3 on 14 March. Step 1: the export is logged in lineage with its source, the date, and version 3. Step 2: a filter job removes rows with a blank carrier code, and the operator and the rule are logged. Step 3: the filtered set is registered in the catalog with an owner and a label saying it holds no direct identifiers. Step 4: a delay predictor is trained on that filtered set. Step 5, which is missing from the team's records: the model card is written. What must the card cite so an auditor can walk back through the chain?
choices: The filtered dataset's exact version together with the lineage entries for the export and the filter job
The predictor's accuracy figure, with no dataset reference, because the metric is what matters most
The catalog's sensitivity label, since that is what the auditor checks first
Only the name of the warehouse system the records came from
questions.why: The model card must name the exact dataset version and the transformations applied, because a card that names only the source cannot be traced back to the data the model actually used.

questions.prompt: A bank's data team keeps a searchable inventory where each dataset has a description, an owner, a sensitivity label, and a location. Which record is this, and which auditor question does it mainly answer?
choices: A model card, which answers how well the model performs
A data catalog, which answers what data exists and whether it is approved for a given use
A lineage record, which answers where the data came from
A training log, which answers how long the job ran
questions.why: A data catalog is the searchable inventory with owners and sensitivity labels, and it answers whether a dataset exists and is allowed for a use.

questions.prompt: A retailer trained a recommendation model on a customer purchase dataset. Two months later the team re-ran the export with different date filters, but the model card still says trained on purchase data with no version recorded. What is the main problem?
choices: The problem is only cosmetic, since the evaluation metrics are unchanged
The card is fine because the model name still matches the dataset name
The card cannot show which data version produced this model, so an auditor cannot verify the training inputs
The card must be deleted because any change to a dataset invalidates all cards automatically
questions.why: Without the exact dataset version and transformation steps, the card no longer identifies which data the model was trained on, so the chain of evidence breaks.

questions.prompt: A health insurer must delete one member's records after a retention request. Its lineage shows that the dataset was copied into a staging area and then used to train two fraud-scoring models. What does the lineage let the team conclude?
choices: Only the staging copy needs attention, since the models are unaffected by deletions
The team must retrain nothing but must rewrite the catalog owner field
Neither model is affected, because the catalog label says the data holds no direct identifiers
Both trained models must be treated as affected and reviewed, because lineage identifies which models used this data
questions.why: Lineage records which systems copied the data and which models trained on it, so the team can identify both models as affected instead of guessing.

lessons.explainPrompt: A teammate says we do not need to document data origins because the model is already tested and works. In your own words, explain what data lineage, a data catalog, and a model card each add, and name one limit of these records that the team should still keep in mind.
lessons.modelAnswer: Testing shows how the model performs, but it does not show where the training data came from or whether it was allowed to be used. Data lineage records each step the data went through, from source to model, including the transformations that removed or changed information. The data catalog lists each dataset with its owner, sensitivity label, and approved uses, so someone can check permission before using it. The model card ties one model to its purpose, data versions, evaluation results, and limits. A real limit is that these records are only as good as their upkeep: if a dataset is re-exported and the lineage or card is not updated, the documents describe data that no longer matches what the model learned from.
rubricPoints: Lineage records the path of data from source through transformations to the model
The data catalog records ownership, sensitivity, and approved use for each dataset
A model card links one model to its intended use, data versions, evaluation, and limitations
Records go stale if datasets change and documentation is not updated

suggested.rationale: Explaining how these three records answer different audit questions, and where they fall short, is the core skill and no listed mission or planned engine covers it.

lessons.plain: Before an AI system learns from or answers questions about company data, someone has to make sure that data is good enough, that personal details are shielded where they should be, that only the right people and programs can touch it, and that nobody has changed it without anyone noticing. Secure data engineering is the set of habits and checks that do this work. Think of a hospital pharmacy: the stock list must be accurate, patient names are hidden from people who only need to count pills, only authorised staff open the cabinet, and every shelf count is recorded so tampering shows up. The same four concerns apply to the data behind an AI app.
lessons.guessPrompt: An AI assistant answers questions using a copy of customer records. Name two things that could go wrong with those records before the assistant ever sees a question, and say how you would notice each one.
lessons.teach: Data quality assessment means measuring whether data is fit for its purpose. Common dimensions are completeness (are required fields filled in), validity (do values match the expected format, such as a real calendar date), uniqueness (no duplicate records), and timeliness (is the data recent enough). You measure these with automated checks that run before data is used, and you record the results so a failed check holds a bad batch back rather than quietly feeding it to a model.  Privacy-enhancing technologies, often shortened to PETs, are techniques that reduce how much personal information a system exposes. Masking replaces a value with a placeholder such as asterisks. Pseudonymisation swaps a direct identifier for a random token and keeps the lookup key stored separately. Anonymisation removes identifiers so individuals cannot reasonably be picked out, though re-identification risk still has to be judged. Each technique trades some usefulness for less exposure.  Data access control answers who may read or change which data. The principle of least privilege means each person or program gets only the permissions its job needs, granted through roles rather than shared accounts, and reviewed regularly.  Data integrity means data has not been altered, lost, or corrupted without authorisation. A checksum or hash is a fingerprint: you recompute it on arrival and compare it with the value recorded at the source.  Worked example: a customer export of 10,000 rows arrives. Step 1, the quality check finds 312 rows with an empty postcode, above a 1 percent completeness threshold, so the batch is held. Step 2, the email column is pseudonymised before the data enters the AI workspace. Step 3, the file's SHA-256 hash is compared with the hash the exporter published; they differ, so the file is rejected and fetched again.  Common mistake: treating a hash as protection against everyone. A hash shows that a file changed, but if an attacker can also replace the recorded hash, the check is worthless unless the reference value is stored where they cannot write.  A model trained on unchecked records learns wrong answers silently, and an over-permissioned service account lets one bug expose the whole customer table.

questions.prompt: A clinic sends a nightly file of 4,000 appointment rows to an analytics team. The team's rule is that every appointment ID must be unique, and any batch with duplicate IDs is held back. Step 1: the uniqueness check finds 58 rows whose appointment ID appears twice, so the batch is held. Step 2: the patient phone column is pseudonymised, with each number replaced by a random token and the lookup table kept in a separate store, before analysts can open the file. Step 3 is missing. The exporter published a SHA-256 hash for the file. What should happen at Step 3 so that the file's integrity is confirmed before use?
choices: Recompute the file's SHA-256 hash on arrival and compare it with the value recorded at the source; accept only if they match.
Ask the exporter to email the hash, then accept the file if the email arrives on time.
Copy the file's hash into the same storage folder as the file so analysts can check it later.
Replace each pseudonymised token with the original phone number so the file's contents match the published hash.
questions.why: Integrity is checked by recomputing the fingerprint on arrival and comparing it with the reference value recorded at the source, and the file is accepted only on a match.

questions.prompt: A retail chain's marketing team wants to follow the same anonymous shopper across months of purchases to see repeat buying patterns, but nobody on the team should be able to see the shopper's name or email. Which privacy-enhancing technique fits best?
choices: Anonymisation, by deleting every identifier from the purchase table.
Deleting the email column and keeping only the purchase amounts.
Pseudonymisation, by replacing the email with a random token and storing the lookup key separately.
Masking, by replacing the email with asterisks in the purchase table.
questions.why: Pseudonymisation keeps a consistent token per person so records can still be linked over time, while the key that reveals the real identity is held apart from the data.
